div.head: AMBULANCE WORK.
div.p: AMBULANCE WORK.
Competition for the Crosfield Challenge
Shield at Warrington.

Nine ambulance teams from various parts of Lanca- shire and Cheshire competed at Warrington on Saturday afternoon for the erodeld Challenge Shield presented by the firm of Messrs. Joseph Crostleld and Sons, Ltd., for annual competition in the number 4 (North-Western) district of the St. John Ambulance Brigade. The pro- ceedings took place in the workmen's dining hall at Messrs. Crosfields' works and were followed with con- siderable interest by a fair attendance of the public. The judges were District Chief Superintendent A. L. Garnett, of Burnley (practical test) and Dr. Davies, of Shaw (viva voce). Athough Warrington was not repre- sented in the competition, many local ambulance workers attended, including Captain Waring (chief superinteudant of the Warrington division), and Mr. A. E. Spann (secretary). The tests occupied about four bours,and at the close Chief Superintendent Garnett announced the results as follows :—Cromptma, 3114 'points Horwich, 297 k; Nelson, 2591; Northwich,2ssl-; Colne, 29;2 Hindley, 2131 ; Preston, 2c53 ; Waterloo, 165 ; Sale, 1524'. Crompton thus became the holders of the challenge ;Held for another twelve months, having now won it four years in succession. Captain G. It. CROSIIELD presented the trophy to the winning team and congratulated all who had taken part in the competition upon their excellent display. He must especially congratulate the winning team who had now carried off the shield for four years in succession. That fact inclined him to make a suggestion to the deputy-commissioner, to the effect that it might be a good thing to introduce some regulation that no man should be allowed to compete in a team for more than two years—that was to say, it might be found advantage- ous to change the team every two or three years. That would give other towns a chance and as going in for the competition was most beneficial to their ambulance efficiency and they wanted to spread the advantage of that training as much as possible, it would be well if they could induce more men to com- pete. He thought very few of those present who were not actually members of the ambulance corps could realize the amount ef time, work and self-sacrifice which ambulance work entailed. The most distinguishing feature of the work was accuracy because the slightest inaccuracy might result in a precious life being lost. Accuracy meant discipline, self-restraint, and a good, honest, steady life and he congratulated the ambulance men who had sheen by their work that day the value of their lives. They could not have arrived at the pitch of perfection which most of them had attained without leading good,honest, sober lives, and in the present rather complex state of affairs there was the greatest need for such lives—lives which were always ready to fortify the right, to arouse sloth and dispel eepression. In conclusion Captain Croafield thanked Colonel Trimble, District Chief Superintendent Garnett and the other members of the brigade staff for the great interest they had always shown in that competition. He had great pleasure in handing the shield to the Crompton team. (Applause). Each member of the Crompton team also received a clock, while the Horwich competitors were presented with barometers and the Nelson team with umbrellas. Colonel Tatatnta proposed a vote of thanks to Captain Crosfield for hi presence and to the firm for their generous gift of the shield and prizes. Captain' Crcsfleld's remarks with reference to the constitution of the teams in future years would have his (Colonel Tumble's) attention and be would take into consulta- tion the members of his district staff. No doubt they would be able to devise some method of arranging the competition roes to get the very hest out of it. Captain Crosfled in making the suggestion was most desirous of making the competition 03 useful as possible in the interests of ambulance work. These competitions thould rot be stereotyped year after year for the object was to ensure general and not limited efficiency. In lgorth-East Lancashire they had had to introdrce measures to enlarge the scope of the contests, thereby enabling ambulance men to become more efficient and extend their knowledge of first aid. Col. Trimble warmly acknowledged the encouragement which Messrs. Crosfield always gave to ambulance work. No volun- tary organization involved more self-denial than the ambulance brigade, and the well-being and progress of the work depended upon the unselfishness of the mem- bers which brought out true manliness. As deputy- contmissioner he hoped the shield would not go to Crompton every year. (Laughter.) Ile was much obliged to all the men for the smart and soldier-like way in which they had ternd out, and credit was due to all concerned. (Applause). District Chief Superintendent GARNETT seconded, and said Messrs.erosfield were deserving of the warmest thanks for the great interest they had taken in the move- ment for so many years. . _ _
The vote was ily accorded. Col. 'TRIMBLE also voiced the indebtedness of the teams to the judges for their arduous work._
After the competition a large company, including the members of the teams, partook of tea in the girls' dining rcom.

div.head: SELF-DESTRUCTION
div.p: SELF-DESTRUCTION

Food .repairs the ks& to some extent, but the power to digest food grows less from year. to year with use. That is the reason, sooner or later, we must die.
Now take ncte. The faster you live, the more you waste; the mote you throw away, the sooner you rate to the end.

Once mote. The great waster, the great thief of life is innesm. Then, you may lose in a month what might have lasted a year, and (remember!) not merely of flesh and strength, but of the "power to get it hack. Here is where Mother Seigel's Syrup does its wonderful work. It gives you back lost power. Not all of it, for then you could live fer ever ; but most of it. Ilefore it was completed I began to suffer from bilious- ness and indigcstion. div.head: SMART EVENING BLOUSE.
div.p: A SMART EVENING BLOUSE.

The winter dance season is very close at hand now, and many of us are beginning to make preparations for coming" evening festivities. In anticipation of such festivities, I am giving you in the accompanying sketch an illustration of a

dainty and charming evening blouse, which is quite an ideal garment for a very slight figure, as it gives fulness and softness of outline. The original was carried out in delicate grey mous- soline-dersoie- powdered with tiny glittering cut- steel discs. A wide band cf grey insertion mounted over white chiffon edged the decolle- tage all round the shoulders. Beneath this band the corsage was gathered all round the top, both back and front. Three bands of grey satin held the blouse into the figure, and gave an appear- ance of plump roundness. The sleeves were simple, slightly full affairs, caught dew!) to the arm by bands of grey satin, whi,eh finished in little, showers of sparkling cut-steel beads. A blind of grey insertion finished the alcoves at the elbow. WHY TEACH GIRLS LATIN?

In the November number of the Oirre Own Paper and IVoinan'e Migraine, Dr. Emil Reich starts the first of a series of articles on the modern method of educating girls, in which he deals very frankly with the weak points in our present educational system. Among other things, he objects strongly to a girl spending time siu °dyin" Latin. He says: As the main function of the sun, so far as we are concerned, is the diffusion of light, even so in social life a woman's most desir- able quality is tact. It is by tact, and by tact alone, that women can largely regulate and better , the general. conditions of life. Every man who has closely studied life knows that owing to a curious process in our nature, and more especially in that of women, the force and delicacy of tact has a tendency to diminish with the accumulation of mere un- digested/ knowledge. It is, I admit, impera- ti re Ls know Latin if one aims at becornmg a scholar. Ildwever it ' may be with regard to men, it is indubitable that Roman literature, or the writings of the ancient Romans, have little value as an asset for the mind of young girls . . . Roman literature is mostly written either for men only, or for students of politics. and law. It is scarcely—even in its more pleasing aspects—meant to be read by girls or women. What use, then, can a lengthy and fatiguing study of Latin be to young women? It will certainly not increase their tact; rather it will blunt it. It is not Latin, but Greek, which ought to be studied by women."

div.head: NEW COIFFURE.
div.p: A NEW COIFFURE.

Quite one of the most important items in a smart and well-turned-out toilet is a well ana modishly-drcsied head. Our present '3l:etch pic- tures a new coiffure of particularly becoming styla, that is typical of the latest and most

fashforal.ile ideas on the subject. In thistcoitTur6 the I4[r is waved all over the head in wide and seern.r.gly careless waves. The hair is parted a little to the left; and the big waves drawn away to either side and arranged in innumerable •soft little curls and puffs. These curls go ail the way round the back of the head, and shew no trace of comb or ornament of any kind. When a hat is worn they shOw beneath the brim at the back and sides, though they are only carried half-way down the head at the back, and leave the tie:s end lower part of the head quit clear. A pan ticularly smart and. attractive coiffure.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street.

Anniversary sermons were preached at this Church on Sunday by Mr. R. Pinches, of Chester. There were large congregations. At the morning service the solo "-Jesu, Lover of my soul" was vety sweetly sung by Miss Lomax, and in the evening an anthem was very creditably sung by the choir, the solo parts being taken by the Misses N. Lomax, F. Adams, and Messrs. J. R3der, P. Kean and H. Woolley, Mr. J. Ryder (con- ductor), end Mr. J. Bats (organist). In the afternoon a musical service was given and was sustained by Miss Lina Plinston, Mr. G. Gough, and Mr. A. Spruce's Quartette Party. Miss M.PI inston was the accompanist. The Chairman. Mr. John B. Starkey, spoke Upon "Ideals," and the Rev. J. F. Matthews gave an address on "Religious problems."

div.head: Wycliffe Congregational Church.
div.p: Wycliffe Congregational Church.

Harvest thanksgiving services sere held on Sunday at this church which had been most tastefully decorated with floweryorn, &c. There were large congregations. At the morning service the pastor (Rev. John Yonge) preached on the joys of harvest. Stainer's anthem "Ye shall dwell in the land " was very creditably inter- preted by the choir, Mr. P. 0. Bailey taking the solo. In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. W. L. Roberts, of Liverpool, who based his discourse on the words "Consider the lilies." Mr. Frank Brown sang ale solo " The Sower went forth sowing." The choir rendered the anthem " The heavens are telling" (Haydn). Mr. A. Griffiths being responsible for the tenor solo "In splendour bright." The trio was inter- preted 14 Miss Griffiths Mr. A. Griffiths awl Mr. Bowman Hibbert. Mr. V. H. Payton, Mug. Bac., pre- sided at the organ.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

There were large congregations at the harvest thanks- giving services held at the above church on Sunday. The Rev. T. Galland Hartley (chairman of the district) preached both morning and tvening, and his discourses were listened to with keen interest. The church had been prettily decorated by lady members of the con- gregation. In the morning the choir gave an admirable interpretation of the anthem "Sing to the Lord of harvest," the solo being well taken by Miss Kershaw, whilst In the evening they acquitted themselves equally Well in " Praise the Lord, 0, Jerusalem," the soloist being Miss Carrie Hastings. Special hymns were also ung. Mr. Frank Hickman was at the organ. The offertories were in aid of church funds.

div.head: Bishop of Liverpool at Winwick.
div.p: The Bishop of Liverpool at Winwick.

There was a large congregation at Winwick Church on Sunday morning when the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) preached. His Lordship took for his text the words" Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption." Eph. iv. SO. At the close of his sermon his lordship appealed for liberal contributions in aid of the new church at Orford. "As I came along from Newton-le- Willows "he said "sad saw the noble spire of this church rising up above the trees, and thought of the little church in the valley below, between here and Warrington, which is to be consecrated next Saturday afternoon I thought that the old Church was putting forth a new shoot." Continuing, he pointed out that the new parish of Orford contains 700 people, and in it there formerly lived and laboured a moral and devoted Christian in the late Mr. Beamont. It was not his happiness to know Mr. Bement, who was one of the great saints and benefactors of this neighbourhood. He knew Mrs. 13eamont durin.g his first years as Bishorcand he knew she was very much what her husband was, and it was in memorial to this devoted family that the church bas largely been built. There was still the sum of £4lO owing before the church could be free of debt. The collections amounted to £l5 lls. Id.

div.head: Late Rev. J. Calvert.
div.p: The Late Rev. J. Calvert.
Memorial Service at Legh street Church.

At Legh•ztreet Primitive Methodist Church on Sunday evening a memorial service to the late Rev. J. Calvert, a former minister in the circuit, was held. There was a lirge congregation. • The anthem " Vital spark "was rendered by the choir, and the Dead March in Saul "was played at the close by Mr. Clatworthy, the organist. The Rev. J. &iglus preached and after- wards read the following memoir :—The Rev. J. Calvert whose departure we have to mourn, was formerly a minister of this church, and was no doubt well known to most of us. From what I have gathered since I came to this circuit I am convinced that he was held in very high esteem by both the members and officials of the Warrinaton and Widnes circuit. It is about 18 years since I became acquainted with him. I was ' preaching missionary sermons in the circuit and was , introduced to him at Widnes on the Sunday morning. ' and had the privilege of dining with him. I shall always remember with pleasure our meeting together on that occasion. He was remarkably approachable— one no sooner came into his presence than he felt at I home with him at once. I bad for sometime cherished the hope that I should see him again in Warrington and have the pleasure of grasping his hand and enjoy- ing his brotherly fellowship, bnt, alas! this has been denied. However, we live in hope that we shall meet him again when the clouds of earth have rolled away. Our departed brother came to the Warrington and Widnes circuit at a very critical period of its history The circuit was like a ship in a storm and needed skilful navigation. It is almost needless for me to say that Mr. Calvert turned out to be just the captain that was required to bring the ship safely into port. I , think we may say without any exaggeration that our i late brother was always diligent n his Christian work, 11 earnest and faithful in his preaching, careful and correct in all the details of his circuit administration, and Christly to all who came( in contact with him. The springs of his religious life lay deep. He was at once upright, sympathetic, devout, just and good. Through failing health be was compelled to superannuate in ISS9, after having served tho Connexion faith- fully for 34 years. Since his retirement he has done occasional preaching and in other ways rendered valuable service to the cause of Christ. Since his superannuation he has crossed the Atlantic several titucs a-cl was in America at the time of his death. Some weeks ago he went from Pittsborough to a hospital at Norfolk, Virginia, to undergo an opera- tion. At first it was pronounced successful, hot unfortunately pneumonia supervened and he began to sink. From Sunday afternoon, September 27th, till he died, he seemed to have been unconscious, although there is no doubt that he had some rational moments, for on Monday, September 28th. we are told, he said to his wife several times that be wanted "To go and be with Jesus." His wish was soon granted, for on Wednesday, September 30th, at 4.15 in the morning, his happy spirit passed into the heavens, to be for ever with the Lord. The funeral took place at Pittsborough, the service being conducted in the Methodist Church. As a proof of the esteem in which he was held by the people at Pittsborough, we are told that there gathered at the funeral a very Large number, of both blacks and h ites.

div.head: Theft of Clothes.
div.p: Theft of Clothes.

Annie Mather, of Philip-street, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday with stealing a boys suit of clothes valued at 13s. Ild, from the shop of Benedict Tyrer, of 75, Orford-lane, on Saturday, October 24th. The Chief Constable stated that the clothes were seen safe hanging outside the shop at 5.30, and at 6 o clock the clothes were misted. Information was given to the police and the usual inquires wete made, it was found by P.C. Gilchrist, that a woman by the name of Kitchen, of Elizabeth-strc at, had pawned the clothes at Mr. Deacon's pawnshop. Gilcrist took the clothes and Mrs. Kitchen to the police station and from what she told him, he at-tested priscner outside the house in Philip-street. The officer questioned her about the theft and she said that a Scotchman, +rho came from Manchester, had given them to her, but after being further questioned, she admitted that she bad stolen them from the shop of Benedict Tyter, of 75, Orford-lane. It appears that she gave the clothes to Mrs. Kitchen to paw. Prisoner, whe appeared in the dock- with a child in her arms, said she stole the suit to ray a fine for not sending her clii!then r:gularly t school. She had twice previously been ornvicted of theft and she was ordered to pay 20s. and costs, or in default go to gaol for cne month.

div.head: ." SMOTHERED WITH ECZEMA."
div.p: ." SMOTHERED WITH ECZEMA."
20 Years' Suffering from Itching Sores. Turned 60, but Zam-Buk Cured Her.

Mn. P. Lamer, of Brook-street, Chipping, Sodbury near Bristol, though turned seventy and having suffered for twenty years from terrible eczema, has been perfectly cured by Zam-Buk. "Twenty years ago I began to suffer from eczema," Mrs. Lamer, told a Biistol journalist: " It started first corny body and hands, and then spread all over until I was nearly smothered with the terrible disease. My legs were in a shocking condition. They were simply a mass of running sores. The pain was ternble, and the only way I could get a little ease was by bathing my legs in cold water. The legs swelled to a frightful size, and gave me no peace night or day. " For twenty years I endured this daily torture, and became very ill from want of rest and the constant pain. I tried almost every kind of ordinary ointment, salve, etc., and spent several months in hospital, but the eczema continued to eat into my flesh. Doctors were. powerless to check, the disease. I spent almost all my time in bed or on the sofa, quite unable to move about, and my skin constantly peeled off. "1 bad given up hope of ever being cured until Mrs- Greenaway, a neighbour, showed me how Zam- Buk bad cured her little boy of eczema, and per- suaded me to try this rich balm. The result was magical. Right from the first applications Zam-Buk brought improvement. The terrible itching pain got less, and the discharge was Charge was stopped. New healthy akin began to grow as the sores dried up and peeled off, until, after carefully persevering with Zam-Buk, not a trace of the eczema was left. Zant- Bult has worked a perfect cure, and enabled me to get about again better than I had done at least for twenty years.

I "How can it be that she is so hopelessly plain," ! she said to herself, with a side-glance at a full- length mirror which showed her whole figure as she sat. It was a graceful, if angular, form, and • had the merit of a certain air of distinction. .11er face had no beauty, yet it could not be called plain; there was in it a look of power which redeemed it. But poor Margery! She came. into the room at the Moment, ,and timidly approached the fire. She was not only plain, but absolutely commonplace. If she had ever possessed any character it had all been crushed out of her long ago. Mrs. Armstrong's look of dis- approval was sufficient to make her quite nervous.; and she never expected to meet any other look, so used was she to it. She certainly encountered it now; for Mrs. Armstrong was thinking very earnestly how she could add to her chances in life and make her more attractive. And, indeed, it seemed a hopeless task. Her cold, dissatisfied regard went over Margery's face and figure as she walked down the great room towards the hearth ; and at this moment the door of the room opened and Frank came in, accompanied by a very pretty young woman, pale and delicate, with quantities of fair hair and a fragile figure full of grace. She was very simply dressed in rather shabby black. Mrs. Armstrong sat up in her chair and sur- veyed the two arrivals in amazement. Frank took the girl's hand and drew her forward, saying "Mother, this is my wife." And then he hastily began to tell an incoherent story. It appeared that the girl's father had kept a little shop in a village to which Frank had gone for fishing; for several years he and Lucy had "kept company," as she called it—probably he had never seriously thought of the affair going any further. But now she had written him a strange, illegible, illiterate little note, begging him to come to her; and when he went he found her father had died suddenly and left her worse than penniless, for the business consisted only of debts. He felt that he must come to the rescue, and insisted upon marrying her at once. As lie intended to marry her he showed wisdom in this; he knew well that if he introduced her as his proposed bride the wedding would never be permitted. So .he determined to take her to Armstrong Court as his wife. And he had done it. Now came the awful moment which lie had dreaded all along, the moment in, which his mother had to be encountered. He suffered acutely. His wife was too ignorant and inexperienced to suffer as he did, or td have any idea of what he was enduring. But she was horribly frightened. She had never been so stared at in her life, and she would have run away if she had not been too terrified to move. Margery steed perfectly still with her eyes, round and staring like a doll's, fixed immov- ably upon her; Mrs. Armstrong slowly lifted . herself up in her chair with flaming eyes. She ' wore a bodice covered with jet, and something , that glittered in her hair; to Frank's poor little ; wife she looked like a great serpent rising up to strike her. And so she was—a human serpent which strikes a more cruel blow than that which deals death. I "Take that girl out of my house, Frank,' she said. "How dare you bring her into the stuno room with your mother and sister I " "She is my wife, mother," he repeated. "More fool you!,, was all she said, in tones of such intense rage and scorn that the girl shrank and turned away and began to blindly stumble towards the door of the room. Tears had come, and she could starcely see. She never knew how ! she got out of the house. It seemed to her that someone helped her, and she concluded after- -1 wait's that it must have been a servant—probably ; the grand ,manservant who had admitted them. I She hurried down the long avenue, almost , running in her great desire to get right away. ! Before she reached the lodge gate her hand was caught and drawn in under an arm. Frank had overtaken her. They went out into the high road and walked away. It was long before the girl was able to look at Frank, and then she was more frightened than ever' he looked so white and Wild. They entered the first inn they came to, and he ordered brandy and drank it in a reckless way. He hardlV spoke to her. At last he exptained in a few words what had happened after she had gone out of the house. "It's all over," lie said. "I am ruined. Eiomo-
SAFETY IN EINETOGRAPSY.

One of the greatr-de-;ideitiialti—cOniteCtloW with the universally popular kinetographic living picture exhibi- tions has long been an absolutely non-inflammable film. This has just been satisfactorily manufactured by the Lumiere Company, which was responsible for the introduction of the Autochrome single-exposure natural colour plates. Even when exposed to a blaze, the new film will only fizzle and crumple up, without any attempt to take light. One of the enormous advan- tages of such a film is that it will make the exhibitors independent of the restrictions, which vary greatly in different parts of the country, and which are specially stringent in certain towns. Several non-inflammable celluloids have been pushed before now, and in many cases the non-inflammaMe property has been present. but combined with mechanical or other difficulties. I have seen several subjects on the new film, and they scam to be in every respect as good as those on the on the very best celluloid base. OLD AIITOCEIROME PLATES.

_ Many people have hild the idea that the autochrome plate would probably prove useless after it had been kept for a length of time before exposure, and even the manufactrrers have not made any very confident state- ments on this point as, of course, the only absolute, test for permanency is the test of time. I saw, the other day, however, a very interesting proof of their confidence in old plates in the form of a number of Ibrge size specimen autochromes, which had been made on plates more than twelve months old. The London ' manager, knowing that a very good antochromist was going to a district where he would have exceptionally fine opportuCties of photographing beautiful gardens in full bloom, gave him a number of boxes of the oldest plates in the place, from some of the very earliest batches which were put upon the market, and asked Lim to use them in making specimens. The results are in every way comparable to the very best that are obtain- able on the latest batches of plates, and there will noc be the slightest need to make any apoligies for them when they are shown for specimens. ' PHOTOGRAPHIC " BOUNDER 3." The discourtesies of some of the would-be press photographers are rapidly bringing our charming craft into serious disrepute, and it behoves everyone who cares for the good name of photography to do all that he can to check and discourage the photographic " bounder." It seems to show a curious lack of gentle- , manly feeling when a man can boast (as a writer does in a long article contributed to contemporary) of his clandestine efforts to photograph a gentleman ,Who objected to the process. He tells how he climbed over a garden wall and hid himself in the branches of a tree, where be waited for hours eventually failing of his purpose because he discovered himself unwillingly through getting on to branches that the gardener threw stones at him, and to regret that although he hired a bedroom which had the only window overlooking the gentleman's garden, he was foiled in his effort to photo- graph his victim from that point of view, because the gentleman ceased to use his garden. I can only express surprise that anyone who is reduced to such subterfuges is willing to write about them, and that gentlemen are so long-suffering as to submit to such espionage, with- out having resource to either a horse-whip or police protection.

boy fetched the governor, and he was as bad as Imy mother. I never expected it of him. He has I always stood by me so far. I suppose I've drivcn him a bit too hard lately. Well, he has turned me out, Sophy, and we must make the best of it. I've got a few pounds to go on with, and I must get something to do. I'm sorry for you, little girl." It was terrible for the two poor weak creatures. They clung together, and made all kinds of plans and efforts. Sophy had a certain amount of sense of a very narrow kind; she soon found that she was the more capable of the two, and she went back to her old trade before the last of the few pounds (really a few hundreds) were spent, and before Frank's valuable trinkets and curios had been sold. While there was still just enough money to stock it and pay a few months' rent in advance, she took a little shop in a London suburb and set to work to try and make it pay. But it was no easy task with Frank to take care of; as soon as he saw her take up the responsi- bility he ceased to look for work himself arid began to drink steadily. He drank himself to death.

Poor dull Margery was now the only child of a rich man an heiress worthy the attention even of titled fortune hunters. She was dressed like a princess, and guarded like one. All Mrs. Arm- strong's ambition was now centred upon her. She, at all events, should not throw herself away like her brother. The rage which possessed her at his marriage never faded—it burnt like a fire in her heart. His death had no softening effect upon her. It was different with Henry Armstrong. When he learnt that his boy was dead and that he had died in such a dreadful manner, his heart was pierced. Ile had loved his son. Ho heard at the same time that a child was born—a girl. He sat brooding and thinking a long time, and eventually went to his lawyer and made a will by which, in any ease, half his fortune was to go to Frank's child at his death, and in the event of Margery's remaining unmarried or dying childless this little girl Was to be the next heir. He left his wife an income for her life, but nothing over which she had absolute control. He did all this secretly, taking no one into his confidence but his lawyer. The longing to see the little child who was his own flesh and blood was very strong; but he withstood it, chiefly because he lacked courage. It seemed to him that in making this will he had done all that was possible. .lle dared not face tha unhappy young widow. So,like Frank, he drowned his conscience with drink, And soon his health began to give way and he followed his son to. the grave.

a 'ow Mrs. Armstrong,alone with Margery and in a position which should have been all-powerful, found herself handicapped by that will. It was like a hand from the grave raised against her. In any ease the child of Frank and his poor young wife must benefit—that was a terrible blow to her. There was no possibility of evading that, nail she could only hope in her wicked heart that the child would die before Margery. But that was not to be. There was a strange and dreadful fate attached to the Armstrong riches. They hardened the heart of their owners, and lives seemed to fall before them as though mowed down by a discriminating destiny. The little frail child, born in a poverty-stricken home, and reared with the greatest difficulty, grew up a fair young girl, tall and straight, with beautiful fair hair like her mother, and Frank's dark eyes. The heiress of Armstrong Court, always per- fectly strong and healthy, and guarded from every possible ill, took the fever in Rome and died of it, in the sudden way in which strong people succumb to illness. Mrs. Armstrong went back alone to Armstrong Court and entered upon a strange, silent phase of her life. She managed everything with care and with businesslike ability. She did not shut herself up even during her period of mourning, but went about among the people as usual. She was like a queen who was making the utmost of a period of sole authority; ordering, arranging, taking a great interest in all details. She took as much care of herself as of the estate, and evidently intended to live as long as possible. Many people thought her intention was to marry again. No one know her heart or her thoughts. She apparently lived a busy life among people with whom she consulted and talked over matters of mutual interest. No one knew that she had one absorbing and overwhelming interest, veritable master passion. She left home occa- sionally alone, and stayed away long enough to do some business and shopping in London, which amply accounted for her time. No one guessed that one afternoon was spent in going to an obscure and dingy suburb of London. She timid herself always to reach it after dark, when the lights were lit, and she could walk about unobserved. She went quietly and without hesi- tation to a certain little sordid street of shops. She kept on one side of the way, never crossing over, but walking slowly up and down opposite a shop window which had her own name--" Ar- mstrong "—over it. She could see the counter from one point on the pavement where she stood, and is sad, shabby woman who served at it—a woman whose grey hair had once been fair. This was her daughter-in-law. Sometimes she caught sight of a tall slip of a girl, with waving clouds of golden hair about her face, and eyes with a strangely familiar look in them. The haunting memory which they awakened stirred the fire that burnt in the grandmother's heart to a stronger flame. She went back to her hotel, as soon as she had caught sight of the girl, aatisfied so far as any sense of satisfaction could ever be possible to her. The girl was growing up a poor girl, uneducated, untended, her hands coarsened with work, her speech vulgarised, her mind attuned to the sordid life she led, and per- fectly ignorant of any possibility of any other for her. Mrs. Armstrong intended to keep her out of her inheritance as long as possible, so that if she had to come into it she should be utterly unfitted for it. Fired by this one mean and dreadful ambition, the proud and haughty woman lived on, steadfast in her purpose, alone in her thoughts and feelings. And pretty young Fanny Armstrong was as gay as the poor caged thrush seemed to be which hung over tha cobbler's shop next door, and sang ceaselessly to his mate, calling, calling, calling in vain. Fanny took him bits of green fail, trying to solace his sad lot, and he loved her dearly as did everyone else who knew her. She had been christened Frances, after her father; and that was all she knew about him. She had not the remotest idea that she was the child of a rich man or had in any way been deprived of his heritage. She was a poor girl, born among poor people, and she never dreamt of any other lot. ller mother's bitter disappointments had nia,de her silent; her only sensation when she thought of Mrs. Armstrong and of Armstrong Court was a deep feeling of shame and humiliation. She said nothing about it to Fanny, letting her grow up in complete ignorance of her father's family. All that the girl knew of him was that he had been very kind to her, and she had loved him dearly, in spite of his being a poor drunken fellow and a sore trial to her mother.

Fanny coUld not grim; up in this dull spot like a Hower in a dark court without having lovers already—inost of them very undesirable. All the men looked admiringly at her; and everyone brightened up at her smile. Of course there was a favoured one. In such a life as Fanny's it was not possible for her, young as she was, to avoid selecting ore among her rough-and-ready admirers who would be her guard and companion, and keep the others at bay. It was inevitable that 1 this must happen. Sometimes she had to be in the shop alone when her mother,was cooking lor unpacking goods or doing any col the things which she thought too difficult or heavy for the girl • and rough fellows would come in and IFerliaps linger. Then it was the time for a neigh. I tour to look in, or to stand at the door within call—a sturdy, stalwart young greengrocer, whose hands wer6 stained with the vegetables and fruit, and whose workaday clothes bore many marks of his trade.

But be was pleasant to look at, all the same; he bad a bright, intelligent expression, keen, kind blue eyes, and thick curly brown hair. He wit§ the son of an ald friend of Sophy. By reason of this connection, Jack Marton had first claimed the right to be Fanny's champien and watch-dog; he retained it by reason of his owr sterling character and his lovableness. Fanny trusted him. Ho was very proud of this.

One day Jack saw a stranger come slowly dowr the street, scrutinising the shops and readir4 the natues over them. He was unusually wolf dressed for the neighbourhood. The gentle. man went into the little general shop. "Are you Mrs. Armstrong ? " he said to thi widow, and when she answered yes, he asked if he could sneak to her alone for a few minutes. With a fluttering, frightened heart she led him into the little parlour, leaving Fanny in charge of the shop. Jack quickly discovered this and came to ask her if she knew who the visitor was; tut she knew nothing. Presently the door of the

• parlour was hurriedly opened and Fanny called in. Her mother had fainted and lay with her head on the table unconscious like one dead. Of coarse, Jack soon knew all this, and came to. fetch and carry and do what he could. And sopa he knew much more—it all came out, and Fanny nearly fainted too. The strange gentleman was lawyer, who had come to find the girl and tell her that her grandmother had died suddenly of heart disease, and that she was the sole heiress to. Armstrong Court and forty thousand a-year. "Oh! Jack, what shall I do ? " she exclaimed,. her eyes full of alarm and fear. " We will instruct you in all matters of detail,- with great pleasure, madam," said the lawyer. ! "Thank you," she murmured. Then she bent over her unconscious mother. "Jack," she said.. , "you had better fetch a doctor." I But it was not necessary. Mrs. Armstrong (slowly recovered consciousness, and by-and-bye sat up again in her accustomed wooden chair by the hearth. The lawyer took his departure, having I extracted a shy, reluctant promise from Fanny te !..-..-ome to his office at a certain hour on the follow- ing morning. He gave her the address and ex- plained to her carefully how to find it; then be spoke to Mrs. Armstrong and begged her to come with her daughter. She only stared at him in a distracted, dazed manner. He went away absorbed in thought and wonder. He had known Henry Armstrong intimately, and had never even guessed that Frank had married till the will was made which made his child the heir. The lawyer was a kind-hearted man, and was fond of his own grown-up daughters. "A wicked, wicked thing," he said to himself ninny times as he went back to his office. "A cruel, wicked thing not to have educated this girl and fitted her for her position in life." Fanny was obliged to close the shop; she could not attend to it. Her mother seemed very strange, and she could not bear to leave her alone. Jack's- father was out with the cart selling vegetables* from door to door; when he came home Jack came in and left him to look after their shop while he talked to Fanny. It was a dreadful ordeal that the girl was going through, for as soon as her mother began to be able to speak it was evident that she shrank from her and looked on her with distrust. It became clear at last that She looked upon her as having done some wrong and wicked thing; suddenly it was revealed t 0 both Jack and Fanny that she thought her daughter had been accused of being a thief. Her mind had given way under the sudden shock; perhaps it would be nearer the truth to say that it had been so over-strained by the long anxiety and distress of the past years that it succumbed when the strain was suddenly relaxed. Through the long, bitter nights she had brooded silently over the wrong done to Fanny; and to see it suddenly righted in so unexpected and over' whelming a manner was more than her brain could stand. She had lost her reason. "This dreadful money will kill us all !" eZ- claimed Fanny, in terror and dismay. 'Oh! Jack, I don't want it. I would much rather bo poor always. What shall I do ? " "Marry me, dear love," he said instantlY; "and we will goat once to my cousins in AUS- tralia, and you shall never have any more trouble or bother in all your life. I'll see to that." , Fanny stared at him in amazement. He had never yet spoken a word of love. She knew about the cousins; they had a large farm and had long wanted him to go and join them. Jack had been thinking hard ever since the lawyer made his errand clear. He was convinced that this was his one chance of winning the girl he loved. He looked down at his hard, wore - soiled hands and wondered how they would seem to Fanny after she had been in possession et forty thousand pounds for a single year. He must take her right away from it all or lose her for ever; of that he was convinced. "We'll take your mother with us," he said. "I've got money enough saved up for the journey. And father will come with us ; it will be far , better for him when he is getting old than stopping here. There is work and pay for every man that knows how to work out there. Sav yes, dear, and I'll go and break it to him; and I'll get a special licence first thing in the more:. ing. You must run away from all this now, et,.! you never will be able to escape." Fanny sat and thought earnestly. Her hand stole into his softly and said "Yes " for her. But she did not speak for some time. She had read many penny novelettes, and she knew that 3 life was described in them as being led by rielt people which would fill her with despair. She would never learn how to behave ! And then herr dreadful to have no one to help and advise her or tell her what to do. Tier mother would never have been able to help her much—but now! She glanced at her with infinite love and pity. Slla would have to care for her henceforward as for a- baby. Jack would be a perfect friend and pro- tector on an Australian farm, as he had been here—but at Armstrong Court ? She glanced at him. She knew he would not be able to help her there. "Yes," she said at last, and in such a tone of love and abandonment and utter relief that Jack almost shouted for joy. He folded her tight and close in a long embrace. The lawyer waited expectantly the next and was much surprised when Fanny actually ilia Lot come at all. As soon as it was possible be left his office and went to the shop. It was closed ; so was the greengrocer's next door. He made inquiries of the neighbours, but could learn nothing, for no one knew anything; they were all RS much in the dark, in as complete 4,110' ranee, as he was himself. He at last found the landlord of the two shops, and learnt that messenger had brought him a note giving the els ' months' notice due and the rent for that period. Ile knew nothing else. Fanny had run away from forty thousand

n-year 1 The estate went into Chancery. Twenty years later a handsome, stalwart young man came from Australia and proved himself the heir to the great Armstrong property. lie baa just laid his beloved, beautiful mother in her grave. She had told him who he was, and giver; him the proofs of his identity. His father hau been thrown from his horse and killed some years before. "Go, dear," she said, as she lay dying—"g° and claim mine and your own. Use it well! Promise me you will um it well. Igo to mY beloved, whom I loved more than any gain or gold on earth!"

Margery Armstrong was the only daughter of a man of great wealth, which had ben made in trade, and, as so;na people thought, not by very desirable methods. Enormous profits flowed in, and each of the partners became men of great possessions, and developed ambition accordingly. Henry Armstrong's ambition was to get inty society, and to this end he bought a great estate in a fashionable county and married the daughter of an impoverished county family. His wife dis- liked him from the first, and married him solely as a matter of business. She had a fixed idea that he came of a common origin and could nevet be anything but a common person, nor could any child of his. In time she grew to positively hate him, and the children became objects ol dislike. it was a desolate family that dwelt in the groat house in the midst of its beautiful old pia*, which Mr. Armstrong had bought from a ruined lord. He had found everything neglected and shewing signs of need; he improved and altered and raised the standard all over the estate, which soon became a show-place. He built acres of hot-houses, and kept armies Of gardeners, so that the flowers were a sight to ace when Mrs. Armstrong gave one of her great parties. Everyone who was asked came to het house—she could afford to be very exclusive. She had great ambition for her children, and believed the could secure for them a future which would lift them above their vulgar origin. Her methods were severe, and added to the desolateness of the household in which family ties existed without family affection. She kept Margery always with her, and gave her the highest education possible under those circumstances. Masters and gover- nesses came to Armstrong Court ; and while Margery was still a child her mother took her . .

The House Committee considered a resolution of the West Ham Union on the question of unemployment, remitted to them by the Boar' The communication pointed out the extreme urgency of the question and the great amount of distress prevalent among the work- ing class, and requested the Board to urge the Prime Minister and the President of the Local Government Board to legislate in the present autumn session on the lines of providing usefel productive work for the unemployed workers. SALARIES AT THE COTTAGE HOMES.
MR. FURNESS AND THE BOARD'S FINANCIAL METHODS.

Mr. E. L, BEST moved: That subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board, the salary of Mr. Arthur Wright, superintendent of the Cottage Homes, Ea increased from .£35 to £6O per annum. Mr. FLANAG AN seconded.

The CIIAIRMAN said if ever an officer of the Board deserved an increase it was Mr. Wright and after he bad waited so long for the Guardians should grant it without question. The resolution was unanimously approved. Mr. BENT then moved : That the salary of Miss J. Bennett, industrial trainer at the Cottage Homes, be increased from £2.0 per arnum to a maximum of £23 by annual increments of .Cl. iss BROADBENT seconded. They came to Board meetings and signed cheques for thousands of pounds,and passed thousands of accounts w hi.:l were not considered five minutes. They were well paid, well fed, and not over-worked, and had plenty of assistance in the houses. The salaries were quite ample end to go and advance one of the junior officials after two years' service would be a great indiscretion. Mr. JOLLEY supported Mr. Houghton's objection. The :lledical Officer reported that the work of medical inspection of school children was commenced on the 14th October. Councillor EVANS explained that an assistant medical officer of health and is school nurse bad been appointed and were engaged in the work under the supervision of the Medical Officer of Health. For the first year those children who had recently entered school and those who were about to leave would be examined. Arrangements had been made between the Medical Officer of Health and the Director of Education for the examination of the scholars at the schools. At the same time the Director would advise the parents when the inspection would take place and ask them to be present. After each child had been examine 1 the parents, if they were in attendance, were informed by the doctor of the physical condition of the child and were advised as to what, if any, remedial measures should be taken. Should the parents not attend the inspection, the defects found by the doctor and the advice given by him for their remedy would be for warded by letter to the parents. It was a part of the duty of the school nurse subsequently to visit the homes of those children who had been found to be defective in order to see that the instructions given were being carried oat. The school nurse was also for the present assisting the doctor at the inspec- tion of the girls, and she was visiting at their homes those children who had been reported to be absent from school on account of some non-infectious ailment and who had no private medical practitioner in attendanc3 on them. Before the end of the year the Medical Officer of Health and the Coief Inspector would have visited all the schools of the borough and reported on their general sanitary condition. Alderman BURTON seconded.

Billinge, \V. Gill, NV. C. Brooks, IL Bolton, W. Flanagan, IL Lee, A. J. Jolley, J. Ball, \V. Houghton, J. Backhouse, A. Brooks, M. W. Setoc, E. L. Bent, J. Evans, \V. Furness, A. div.head: TOOTH BRUSH QUESTION,
div.p: THE TOOTH BRUSH QUESTION,

Mr. BEST, inmoving the adoption of the minutes of the Padgade Cottage Homes Committee, said that in view of the decision of the last Board meeting he went away under the impression that tooth brushes were to be provided for the children. It appeared, however, that the matter was only referred back to the com- mittee for re-consideration and he thought that was a ridiculous idea, seeing that it had already been fully discussed.
Mr. EvAss said he was onder the same impression as Mr. Bent. . _ _
The CLERK said the record on the minutes was simply that the minutes of the Cottage Homes be approved with the exception of that relating to the purchase of tooth brushes.

Miss BRO kDIIENT : I did not understand that. I thought the decision of the Board was final. Later when the Superintendent's list of requisites was submitted, Mr. JOLLEY moved that it be amended by the addition of an order for the supply of tooth brushes for the children. Mr. BENT seconded. I Mrs. WILKINSON : As a noint of order, it should go before the Cottage Homes Committee. Mr. FURNESS : I think it is a reflection on the intelligence of the committee to deal with the matter in this informal way. You should at least give them the opportunity of judging once more whether the tooth kuushes are absolutely essential or not. The CHAIRMAN said that as a member of the Cottage Homes Committee be took very strong objection to the procedure that day. The Cottage Homes Com- mittee were entrusted with the management of the institution and by 7 votes to 11, they expressed them- selves against the provision of tooth brushes. It would be a slight on the members of that committee, who attended regularly and know the needs of the institu- tion, for the Board to go over their heads in the way suggested. Mr. JOLLEY thought it was the committee who were attempting to over-ride the Board in not carrying out what was strongly felt to he desirable by the majority of the Board.

Mr. HOUGHTON objected to tinkering with such a trifling matter, as it was not maintaining the dignity of the Board. He was in favour of its being again dis- cussed by the committee. Mies BROADBENT : It is not a trifling matter. It is the foundation of health to have good teeth. If we do not look after the children in that particular, we are absolutely unworthy of the positions we hold on the School Committee, and we ought to be stopped. Mr. IiouGHTON : You will have a dozen cases of appendicitis before twelve months have p9ssed, through children swallowing the bristles. (Laughter). Mr. FLA NAG AN : I have had aupeudicitis, but I never used a tooth brush in my life. (Laughter). Mr. Jolley's proposition was defeated by 11 votes to eight, and the matter vill again come before the Com- mittee,

" Lewis Rand " by Mary Johnston ; Archibald Constable and Co., Ps." The fiction-loving public will cordially welcome a new novel from the pen of so accomplished a writer as Mary Johnston, the author of " By order of the Company," " Audrey " etc In Lewis Rand" she has fully maintained the high literary standard of her previous works and at the same time concocted a story which will vie with any for sustained interest. Miss Johnston has once more pitched her scene in one of those pet iods of American history, of which she has an apparently profound knowledge. Lewis Rand, the dominant character in the b rok, rises from humbie beginnings to the leadership of the Republican party. His rise is rapid, for Rand is a forceful man and makes light of obstacles. To his ambition, there il,ho-vever, no limit. The friendship and support of President Jefferson do not suflize ; he would be a conqueror, a Napoleon. Ambition oe'r reaches itself and while Lewis Rand dues not come a " cropper " politically—Jefferson's magnanimity saves him _from that —his disappointed hopes bring abut rein in another dirc2tion. The character of Rand is one of deep interest. He has qualities which win the allegiance and admiration or the multitude and secure the unswerving devotion of his friends, but like many great men he is not over scrupulous. Had he been so lie would have been the hero of the story instead of " Lurlwell Cary, his greatest opponent on the Federal side, and a man possessing all the attributes of great- " ness combined with true nobility of character. Though a "foe " he was mt far from being Rand's ' truest friend, and at a critical point in the story he has the following fine words to say ia extenuation of Rand's lapse from loyal adherence to his party and . the State :
A STREET ACCIDENT.
The Gas Committee received a_letter. chtel the 17th

ins-t7,-fr-o; lir:W. W. Shaw, of Pen-loth, chiming com- pensation for an accident which his wife met by tripping over one of the gas boxes hi the street. The committee decided that no further action should be t ikon ;ti the matter._ . _ _
The letter having been read to the Coun2P the re'autes were adopted.
TEIE "MERRY-GO-ROUNDS."

At a meeting of the Fire Engine Committee it was resolved that the attention of the Markets Committee be called to the noise in the Fair Ground caused by " Merry-go-rounds," &c. awl that they be vsked to pre- vent a continuance of it. _
The minutes were passed, on the motion of Alderman BURTON, seconded by Councillor BARTON.
THE TRAMWAYS. INTERMEDIATE STAGES WANTED.

At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee, a deputation appointed by the Stockton Heath Parish meeting, waited on the committee and asked that the fare to Stockton Heath be reduced to Id., or in the event of the corumitte not being willing to agree to that proposal then to dilide the Wildeispool route into Ad. stages. After fully con- sidering the matter, it was !resolved that the deputation be informed that this committee cannot see its way to accede to either of their requests. A letter from Nfr. Nlawson asking for the introduc• tion of an intermediate Id. stage on the Latchford and Sankey route was considered and declined. The MAYOR having proposed, and Councillor WILK INSON seconded, the adoption of the minutes, Alderman BENNETT thought the adoption of the intermediate id. stage would be financially justified. It simply meant that anyone who wanted to get on say at Bridge Foot and go to the Conservative Club would have to pay Id. At present 2d. was charged for that short journey, which was unreasonable. Councillor BARTON said this question could be settled by the adoption of half-penny stages—say from Sankey Bridges to Green-street, Green-street to Ilvlands- street, Rylands-street to Victoria Park and Victoria Park to the Swing Bridge. Councillor PEMBERTON said the slme difficulty arose in other towns, the centre of the town being the place where the fares started and ended. Half-penny fares did not pay in any town of the size of Warrington. The tramways were barely paying now. The MAYOR said the question had been considered several times. They weredisposed to try the suggestion, but were afraid it would not pay. In the matter of tramways, Wariington was well blessed, but whatever the committee could do for the benefit of the public— and do it it in a businesslike way—they would do without much asking. They were trying to da bettor for the public than other towns were doing. He hoped that those who kept grumbling about the price of electricity would take notice that Warrington had been held up as an example of cheapness both for power and lighting puiposes. Alderman TINN:ON called attention to the squealing noises which were made by tramcars in turning round the corner near the County Court offices, and said he had received several complaints from his neighbours about the matter. He thought something might be done to obviate the terrible row, which was very dis- agreeable to:the residents, especially if they were not well. He believed the lines were laid under the direction of the Board of Trade, but they were not laid as they ought to have been. The noises went on from 5 o'clock in the morning until 11.30 at night and 12 o'clock on a Saturday. Alderman BOLTON said there was a bylaw by which the owners of squealing carts could be prosecut ad. fie hoped someone would prosecute the Tramways Com- mittee for not oiling their lines. (Laughter.) Councillor EVANS said he had noticed the noises complained of. Did the Board of Trade enforce a double set of lines round that corner? If not, he was satisfied that a single set of rails could be laid in a manner which would cause a good deal less friction. He hoped the committee would take that into serious Iconsideration. _ .

Councillor ROGERS said the noises round Itylands- street corner were quite as bad. The Mayon said he was of opinion the Urns by the County Court were not laid as they ought to have bsen. He had no doubt the committee would do their bast best to prevent the noises. The minutes were adopted. ADVERTISING THE TOWN. -

Ido not think that you know—l am not sure that I know—the iron strength of the laws that rale an ambitious nature: Ambition becomes an atmosphere; the man whose temperament and self- training inure him to it, breathes it at last es though it were his native air. It becomes that— an inner and personal clime, the source and spring of countless actions great and small. The light, too, is refracted, and the great background of life is not seen quite truly. It is, I think, an enchanted air, into which 6 man drifts upon a river of dreams and, imaginations—and how hard to re-ascend against the current !" S 3 much for Lewis Rand'e persenality. He falls in Jove with,and marries Jacqueline Churchill, one of the most aristocratic of Federalists, or the tale need hardly have been written. Ii Jacqueline and her cousin, [Jolty Dandridge, Miss Johnston has given us two of the most charming women in fiction. No man , could have had a truer helpmeet than .Tacqueline, and Unity was equally qualified to fill the role of R and's wife. More fortunately for her, however, she is espoused by the younger Cary, a bright and high- spirited fellow thoroughly typical of the Federals of the day. The book is fall of quaint characters, and in addition to :its ever attractive love interest it culminates in trage ly, the horror of which is deeply impressed on every 'page of the closing chapters. "Lewis Rand" should sem become one of the dis- tinguished books of the year. It is fit to rank with the best that American brain has produce I in the 're altu of fiction. There are a number of fine illus trations in celonr by F. C. Yohn. "The Forbidden Boundary and Other Stories " by B. L. Putnrin Weals; Macmillan and Co., Us. That Mr. Fatima Weale should appear alse in the field of fiction w ill not supris3 the readers of the vivid and dramatic pages of his well-known series of treatises on the Far E ist which began with the publication of " Maachu and Muscovite." It is the East, too, which he k tows so intimately, that has tarnished him with material for the eight realistic and unconventional tales that make up this new book. They have a peculiar and absorbing interest both for the travelled and untravelled reader. "The Diva's Rahy," by F. Marion Crawford, Macmillan and Co , Us. - Mr. Crawford'e latest novel is the sequel t "Soprano " and " Primadonne," and com- pletes a remark able trilogy of novels. Probably no other writer bat Mr. Crawford could have given us three stories in succession with the same heroine in each and to a great extent the same characters. But in Morgaret Donne, the queen of lyrical opera singers, he created a woman as complex as any of her sex. Perhaps she hardly appeals to the reader's imagina- tion in the way that a lady who cal live through three volumes ought to do. But she certainly gathers round her a few admirers who give Mr. Crawford full opportunity for displaying his intimate knowledge of characier. In the find volume we have Mr. Edward Lushington, an English journalist, as the favoured suitor for the primadonna's hand, but Lushington disc avers that he is not so much in love with Margaret Donne as la Cordova as he was with her as the English girl. Consequently the ways of the two part,and the contest for Margaret's hand is waged with keen- ness by Logotheti the Greek and Van Torp the hard- headed American. Both men start fair as millionaires and the Greek becomes the accepted lover. It is then that the American's fighting qualities are roused, and even with such a handicap against him he wins. Much of the interest is centred round a ruby which the Greek presents to the primadonna, and the adven- tures of the principals concerned excel in point of romance and excitement even those of " Soprano " and '" The Primadonna." It would seem that Mr. Crawford has hardly known which of his heroes to awa d the 1 prize to, but he has chosen wisely. Van Torp earns the reward of pertinacity, and lest we should be dis- appointed on Logotheti's account he finds consolation , in the charms of the young maid from the East, Barak, whose touch of wildness, and natural beauty, appeal to the Greek's love of the romantic, artistic and sensuous. The 6-at chapter of "The Diva's Ruby " in itself a masterpiece of descriptive writing, with an undercurrent of savagely which illustrates the author's remarkable knack of pourtraying man's elemental passions without the slightest straining for effect. We felt quite loth to part with the primadonna and her lovers. Perhaps Mr. Crawford will weave further romance roved Logotheti and his strange bride. There are endless possibilities. She always tells a pretty story and The Sunny Side of the Hill" should become one of the mot popular of her pro- I ductions. It relates the love stories of a brother and sister who are both under twenty-five, but its dominant theme is the romance of a lady who has lived nearly I twice as many years —a romance of so unusual and attractive a kind that it sh luld be learnt at first hand. `• The Woman and tho Sawd," by Rupert Lorraine ; T. Fisher Unwin, Cs. Mr. T. Fisher Unwin's prize novel scheme has proved a good success in every way, and the public o;ves some gratitude to its originator for having intro- duced such authors to the world as Mrs. B rilee- Sauncers, Mrs. Philip Champion de Crespigny, Rosa- mund Langbridge and others. Mr. Rupert Lorraine is the last winner of the .£lOO prize for the best novel from a writer who has not hitherto had anything published, and his romance entitled " Woman and the Sword " laity maintains the high standard of fiction for which Mr. Una in's debutantes have hitherto been responsible. Mr. Lorraine has given us a story which approaches "Rupert of flentzan " for sensation and thrill. As may be guessed from the title, the sword plays no little part in the sequence of events ; never was a story perhaps in which there was more sword-play. The circatnstances of the tale largely account for this, for its action mostly takes place in •Germany during the grim and almost unimaginably turbulent period of the Thirty ' Years' War, in which Gilbert Chareington, the hero, has in fact when the reader first meets him already seen long set vice. A soldier of fortune in the Protestant cause, he has been in the service of half the captains of Europe. The abducted heroine of the story, the " Woman" of the title, is the young, charm- ing, though rather hot-tempered Mistress Hilary Page, only daughter of one Sir Mortimer Page, and the abductor is an Austrian Cont who has a way with women, a black heart, and an incomparable skill at sword-play. The violent historic back-ground of the ably is presented with dignity and knowledge, but what will probably astonish the reader most is the number and vatiety of the "thrills" the book has given hhn. Yet on recalling them, he will see that these were, so to speak, legitimate thrills, due to the natural evolution of a powerlul story, in which, if the characters have often to pass through scenes more than usually appalling, the terror of them is founded on historical fact, and is no mere invention of the author. Readers howe.ver need not fear a sombre hook: they will undoubtedly find "The Woman end the Sword" exciting to an unusual degree.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN
COUNCIL.

IThe final meeting of the Warrington Town Council for the municipal year was held at the Town Hall on ! Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) presided and there were also present :—The Deputy- mayor (Alderman Bolton),Aldermen A.Bennett,T.Burton, IL. Elison, John Evans, W. J. Forshaw, D. Tinnion ; Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, T. Barton, W. Benson, J. Broadhurst, T. Chantler, J. O. Craik, J. Dickenson, James Evans, .1. Hawthorn, Dr. Joseph, T. Locker, J. J. : Nield, J. Pemberton, W. B. Roberts, \V. RogerF, J. Sankey, H. Singleton, J. Skelland, T. S. Steel, J. Fulton-Smith, J. Wilkinson, \V. J. Wilson; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (Town Clerk), A. T. Hallaway (Deputy Town Clerk), J. Fairhurst (Borough Treasurer), TS Longdin (Borough Surveyor), J. Deas (Water Engineer), C. Madeley (Librarian), F. V. L. Mathias (Electrical Engineer), J. M. Murray (Director of Education), F. G. Ruddock (Borough Analyst), and Dr. J. C. 'libber t (Medical Officer).
SOLDIERS' MEMORIAL.

The Borough Treasurer having submitted to the Finance Committee a statement with reference to the Soldiers' Memorial in Queen's Gardens, showing 'a deficit of .f.'26 7s. 9d.,it was resolved that an account for that amount be passed for payment. Alderman BENNETT moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said the account had been adjusted and the amount of the deficit was smaller than they had expected. They were glad to have such a valuable permanent memorial in Queen's Gardens. (hear, hear.) Councillor WILKINSON seconded. ALTERATIONS AT THE TECUNICAL INSTITUTE. The Finance and Estate Committee resolved, on the recommendation of the Education Committee, that application be made to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £2,97,7. for the purpose of altera- tions at the above institute.

--640-uWcillo-r"IrAV:t:TsiIOTZ'N-a-siled for some information with reference to the above minute, pointir'r. out that some of the members of the Council were not members of the Education Committee. Was the amount included in the estimates? Councillor FULTON-SM ITIt said the matter had been duly arranged and agreed to by resolution at several meetings of the Education Committee. Councillor PEA, lERTON while agreeing with what Councillor Hawthorn had said, observed that the altera- tions were absolutely necessary. The matter had been forced upon them by the Board of Education. Councillor Fur:roN-Smtalt said it would be as well to tell the Council that the Board was not satisfied that the alterations would be permanently satisfactory.
The minutes were carried. ADMINISTRATIVE BLOCX AT SANKEY.

A meeting of the Health Committee was held on October 20th, when the deputation appointed by the committee to wait upon the Local Government Board I with reference to the erection of an administrative block at the Sankey Hospital, end the sanctioning of certain amounts overspent, reported that they had now interviewed the Board thereon, and that their explanation both as to the necessity and expediency of the amounts overspent had been approved by the Board. The sub-committees also pointed out that it would be impossible without further borrowing powers, fcr which they were unwilling to apply, to build an adminis- trative block such as had been originally contemplated. They also suggested that in view of the fact that the hospital was so rarely used, it was not good policy t) put up an expensive building, and asked ;the Board to sanction a corrugated iron and wood structure. The Board were favourably impressed with the arguments of the sub-committee, and while dissenting from the ercc • tion of a wood and iron building, said that they now felt that the Health Committee should not be called upon to erect a building which would unduly strain their resources, and they suggested that if the com- mittee would bring a plan before them fora small brick administrative block which could be used as enucleps" in the remote event of an epidemic, they %could be pre- pared to favourably consider it, and this they were of opinion could be done without any increase of the existing.lo£4l%, . .

Coun-cillor EVANS moved the confirmation of the minutes, and alluding to the last-narued minute, said the opinion of the committee was that the work could be finished well %Rhin the present losn. (Hear, hear). Alderman BURTON seconded. MEDICAL INSPECTION. HOW THE WORK IS BEING CARRIED OUT.
At a meeting of the Health Committee it was resolved that Miss Annie Spence, of Grappenhall, be appointed to the position of school nurse at a salary of .£SO per annum.

div.head: BLACK SMOKE.
div.p: BLACK SMOKE.
The Health Committee ordered a letter from a certain firm as to the abolition of black smoke" to lie on the table."
Alderman BENNETT aske4 for information with refer- ence to this minute.

It wr I explained by the MAYou that the letter was really a circular from a firm trading in appliances for burning smoke and accompanying it were photographs of smoking chimneys—not In Warrington. The com- mittee, therefore, decided to take no r ;don in the matter.
The DEPUTY MAYOR : It is a cheap advertisement, and it is as w 1 to let such matters " lie on the table."

Councillor EVANS said the photographs did not apply to Warrington. The circular sent to the committee was purely an advertisement. The committee az d the manufacturers did their best to minimize the smoke nuisance but because a particular firm advertised, the committee were not going to embark on anything which might hamper manufacture's. The minutes were then agreed to. THE WORK OF THE MUSEUM AND LIBRARY. COUNCIL ADVISED_ TO STUDY POETRY AND

div.head: THEOLOGY.
div.p: THEOLOGY.

Alderman BENNETT, in inoving the adoption of the minutes of the Museum Committee, pointed out that they had arrived at an interesting period in the history of the institution. November let would be the 60th anniversary of the opening of the Museum and Libiary cud Warriugtou had cause to be proud of the fact that it possessed the first free rated supported library to be established in the United Kingdom. There were a few facts in the annual repot t of the director and librarian (Mr. C Madeley) to which he would draw attention. The accessions to the Museum during the year were 5,055 which included a very handsome gift of 3,503 specimens from the representatives of the late Mr. T. G. ltylauds, of Thelwall. Ile believed they had now no fewer than 77,000 more or less interesting specimens to show to the public. It had often been said that the !museum was practically an effete institution in which 'no one took any interest and that the money spent on it was practically wasted. He thought the fact that the total attendances of the public last year numbered over 43,00 gave a negative answer to that allegation. The total accessions to the library during the year numbered 1,575 and there were now nearly 4(3,600 volumes in the institution. A cause of special gratification was that nearly 5,000 local books, pamphlets, and manuscripts were included, so that 1 Warrington might fairly claim to have an almost unique local collection. The total circulation at the central library for the year was 89,529, while 11,954 books bad been issued through the branch delivery stations, 14,312 through the juvenile department and 16,730 through the ! school library. One could hardly regard with satisfac- tion the percentages of the different classes of books issued. hile only '7 per cent, of theological works and *9 per cent. oPpoetry and drama were demanded, the issue of prose fiction represented 05.5 per cent Alderman Bennett advised the Council to study the theological works. To listen to the conversation of some of the members of the Council, he said, seemed to indicate they would be the better for a course of theology. (Laughter.) As for poetry, they wanted saturating with it. (Laughter.) It was the very best antidote for the materialistic and somewhat sordid views which so many members of the Council took with reference to their public duties. Once imbue them with a love of poetry and the higher kinds of literature, and they would look on public ques- tions with broad Ind more intelligent ideas and bring to their work that touch of imagination which was absolutely essential. He hoped that during the coming year the members of the Council would do their best to increase the circulation of theological and poetic works. In conclusion Alderman Bennett paid a tribute

1 At a meeting of the Towns Committee, the Tow.) Clerk reported that the Town Council bad voted the sum of 47,0 from the Walker Gift Account for the pur- poses of the committee. It was resolved that the Town Clerk approach the land agents in Warrington and invite them to meet the committee to consider the steps to be taken with a view to the disposal of avail- able sites for works. The Town Clerk was also requested to consider brvi repoa on the F2st toeing to be adopted for the pr' , oose of bringing the available sites to the notice of those reiniting them. The minutes were passed, on the proposition of Councillor PEMBERTON, seconde i by Councillor WILK] NSON.

"Paths of the Righteous," by L.Dougall ; Macmillan and Co:, Os. "Paths of the Righteous," the new novel by Miss L. Dougall, author of "Beggars 'All," is Rely to arouse a good deal of discussion. It is a frankly serious book, and brings before the reader the startling difference between the ideal and actual relations of Christians who differ in forms of worship. The scenes are laid in an English rural parish at the time of the last General Election, and the excited feeling stirred up by the question of Religious ternbing in the schools enters largely into the thread of the story. The author throughout maintains a.- detached attitude, and describes the various types of village society with keen insight and subtle humour. Among new hooks for the young which Messrs. Macmillan have just published are the following : "Fairies of Sorts," by Mrs.Molesworth, with illu- strations by Gertrude Demain Hammond. 3s. Oil. " Fairy Tales from South Africa," collected from original native sources and arranged by Ms. E J. Bourhillr at* Mrs. J. B. Drake, with illustrations by W. H. Holloway. ' This is a volume of fairy- tales quite out of the ordinaa.t. The price is 3s. 61 Among reproductions in miniature editions at Is. each are " Through the Looking Glass," by Lewis Carroll, and " The Rose and the Ring," by W. M. Thackeray, both with the original illustrations. In the Family Herald series of publications Messrs. W. *evens, Limited have just issued "The Parson's Daughter "at 33. GI and 61, and "The Marsdens of Herouleigh " at 3d.

div.head: "The Odd Volume."
div.p: "The Odd Volume."

A prayer by Robert Louis Stevenson concludes "The Odd Volume "which is now on sale through- out the country at the price of one shilling. It reads: "Be with our friends, be with onrselige. Go with each of us to rest; if any awake, tempt to them the dark hours of watching; and when the day returns, return to us. Our sun and comforter, and call us up with moining faces and with morning hearts, eager to labour, eager to be happy, if happiness shall be our portion, and if the day los marked for sorrow strong to endure it." The openimr eontribut;on is a poem entitled " Woodland Peace" by George Meredith, OM., while there are stories, articles, and poems by F. Anstey, J. J. Bell, Marie Corelli, G-. K. Chestertoa, Austin Dobson, Keble Howard, A. E. W. Mason, George Meredith, Alfred Noyes, Baroness ()rev, Sir Gilbert Parker and" Arthur Waugh. The book is pro- fusely illustrated with eight coloured pictures and thirty-two other full-page illustrations, the artists including George Baxter, C. E. Brock, H. M. Brock, Tom Bro.vne, RentS Bull, Dudley Hardy, Bernard Partridge, Frank Reynolds, Byam Shaw, J. A. Shepherd, G. L. Stampa, Lance Thaekeray, Thorpe, Lawson Wood and many others. This wonderful shillings-worth, bound in red with a coloured illus tratiou on the cover, is published in aid of the Nationnl Book Trade Provident Society, the prime objects of which are "to provide temporary or permanent assistance to members in distressed circa ostances, and to coatributi to the funeral expenses of members, and to provide temporary assistance to the widows and children during minority of deceased memberg klI qa 'lifted at their death." "My Story," byHall Caine; W. Heiuemann. In Mr. Hall Caine's new work entitled "My Story," reference is made to the effect produced in the Isle of man when his novels first appeared. He says: "For the first time a writer of story-books had penetrated into its households, getting into' the heart of the conntry, going into the farm-houses, and deliberately sitting dowa by the turf fire in the • chollagh.' The outside world cannot understand what that means; hut we who are of the soil an i have visions of stern old Churchmen and grim old Methodists in every village, who never saw a novel in their lives, and would n)t have touched oae with the longest 'grip' if it had been tossed over the tail-board of a cart, can realise the feelings with which the island mast have grasped the fact that a degenerate son of her own was (as the worthy preacher on the 'plan-beg' put it) 'actually earning his living by telling lies.' "
