Whatever may be the view THE PROBLE.II regarding policy, the
OF THE HOUR. Government is to be con-

gratulated on having attacked the problem of Unemployment with the determination to lessen its evils, at any rate for the present winter. Mr. A soma's statement, supplemented as it has been by Mr. Burixs's explanation of the measures which the Government propose, will satisfy most people that Ministers are doing what they can to alleviate distress, and to help those who would otherwise be out of work over the worst part of the winter. The attack made upon Mr. BURNS by Mr. KEIR HARDIE and the Labour Party was of a particu- larly violent character. The President of the Local Government Board was once one of them— now he is in the safe haven of the Front Bench. They regard him as a traitor. The truth, of course, is that Mr. BURNS is a sensible man who, having got into a job, intends to use his faculties to do the work properly. Time was when the panaceas that appeal to the Labour Party were endorsed by the MEMBER FOR BATTEttsai. But experience has taught a lot. The Government has made provision for the unemployed in various ways—first by expediting naval and other works, by opening the Special Reserve of the Territorial Army during the winter months, and finally by the provision of an increased grant to the Unemployed Fund. It is said that these measures are inadeq . Mr. KEta HARDIE, arguing from the returns of trade unions, sought to show in the House of Commons that there are nearly seven millions of people affected by the present unemployment. The figure, as Mr. Beaxs replied, is illusory. The Poor Law returns show no increase in the applications for relief which could in any degree support such an assertion. It is to be hoped that the Labour Party will see the folly of pursuing a line of argument such as this. Mr. BURNS is doing his best in a difficult position. Those who have the true interests of the poor working man at heart will adopt the attitude of Mr. LONG and Mr. BALFOUR, who refused to assist in hampering the President of the Local Government Board.

The Unemployed problem will take a good deal of attention yet. This year the Government is trying to alleviate distress ; next year it will have to go deeper, and try to find a permanent cure for the evil of unemployment. What that cure may be is still on the lap of the gods,but there are definite indications that the means whereby it will be effected will be found in the taxation of land values. Side by side with that measure must come the reform of the Poor liaw. What is required more than any thing else is the classi- fication of the recipients of relief. At the present moment the loafer and the wastrel get exactly the same treatment as the genuine work- man. We must separate the sheep from the goats, the "won't works" from those who will, but cannot get a chance. Long ago it was suggested that the professional tramps and loafers should be put into colonies and made to work, as is the case in some of the Continental countries. We see no objection to such a course. It would, at any rate, leave the genuine workman a chance of being free from associates who are a drag upon him, and by whom the public are prejudiced against the labouring classes generally.
No one will wish to question COMMONS CLOSED TO the decision of the Speaker STRAN GERS. that the House of Commons

should be closed to strangers in consequence of the disturbances caused by the suffragettes. He must be the best judge of what is necessary, and he has the full support of the Prime Minister and of Mr. Balfour in the course which, as he says " most reluctantly," he thinks must be adopted to maintain order and decency. There is no blame to the officials for what has happened,nor would it be fair to assume that at this stage Members of Parliament who unwittingly lent themselves to the business could have prevented it. The most ugly thing about the affair is that the women disturbers are said to have been asked if they were suffragettes, and by implication gave a sort of understanding that they were not, and might be trusted. If the House of Commons

were to invest itself as it might with simple dis- ciplinary powers to rest with the Speaker—with- out recourse to hearing at the Bar—to deal with disorder by strangers, an occasional outburst like this might meet with punishment that would surely end it. With greater care on the part of Members sucb troubles might be made very rare. That is the alternative. But the speaker is no doubt well advised in taking the step he has to give time for consideration of the 133 st way to meet the evil.
The air has been full of

THE MAYORALTY, rumours this week as to developments in the election of Mayor on Nov3mber 9th. As the whole town knows the caucus meeting of the Town Council selected Alderman Forshaw to succeed Alderman Smethurst, after a number of names had been considered. The choice, though not absolutely unanimous, was a good one, and especially so as the Alderman was the senior of those gentlemen who were willing to entertain the offer of the Mayoralty. It is worthy of note that such opposition as there was, did not come from Alderman Forshaw's political opponents, the Liberals, but from a malcontent section in his own party. Some of these gentlemen, with a want of both discretion and good taste, were anxious to " run " Councillor W. B. Roberts as a candidate for the Mayoral seat. Mr. Councillor Roberts may be a very excellent man personally, but he has yet to win his spurs in public life. Possibly he realises this quite fully, and it may be that his friends have gone further than he desired, but at any rate Councillor Roberts has publicly intimated that he will not allow his name to be put forward as a candidate for the Mayoralty. This is a very wise decision on his part, :for we do not see how he could hope to have commanded anything like solid support at this juncture. Alderman Forshaw will make a capable, courteous' and painstaking Mayorior we are mistaken in the man, and we hope he will be elected by the unanimous vote of the Council.

Few men have accupied the THE RETIRING Mayoral chair of a County Msyon. Borough like Warrington for a period of two years, and given such general satisfaction throughout that time as has Alderman Smethurst, our present retiring Mayor. Probably no one would contend that he has been one of the most distinguished holders of this honourable position, for Alderman Smethurst has his limitations, and is fully aware of the fact. But he has attended to his duties with a zeal and enthusiasm worthy of all praise. Neither he aor his good lady have spared themselves in the slightest in well-doing during the past two years, and the community is grateful to an extent which it is difficult to express here. Alderman Smethurst has, at least, made his mayoralty notable by his devotion to duty, his strict impartiality, and his exceeding generosity and kindliness. Even the children have learnt to know and love our genial Mayor, who has paid particular and unusual attention to the rising generation. Many things have been accomplished during Alderman S meth urst's mayoralty, but in one failure we deeply sympathise with him. He would have relinquished the robes of office with more satisfaction had he been able to urge the Warrington Bridge scheme to comple- tion. We had hopes that during his period of office as chief citizen of the Borough, Alderman Smethurst would have succeeded in gratifying his ' own very laudable ambition in this direction, but fate and a dead-weight of sullen opposition have proved too strong for him. We noted, with some surprise, that in his speech to the Council on Tuesday the Mayor regretfully abandoned the 'cantilever scheme for widening the Bridge and advised the Council to go in for a new structure. There has been so much delay already that this is perhaps the wisest course, though we are still convinced that the widening scheme which the Council actually passed so long ago would have answered the purpose for ten years at least.

Monday next is the polling THE ELECTIONS, day for the elections in Orford and St. John's Wards, and there is every prospect of a severe struggle taking place between the five candidates who are contesting the two vacant seats. In Orford there is a three-cornered battle between Liberal, Conservative and Socialist, but the vigaur of the combat between the two former seems to have dwarfed the candidature of the latter. Mr. Peacock has many claims for support, not the least of which is that he refrains from introduc- ing Imperial politics into an election which should concern itself solely with the welfare of the town and the representation on the Town Council of the ward inhabitants. The other side is still trying desperately hard to trade on such a catch-phrase as "religious liberty," though the record of the Tory party in the past in regard to liberty of any kind does not make pleasant reading. If the electors are really concerned about religious or any other kind of liberty they will take care to vote against the return of a Tory candidate, and particularly of one who is a servant of the trade which causes more people to lose not only liberty but life itself than any other factor in our social life. We would say to the electors of Orford Ward : Vote for Peacock aud real representation ! Ia St. John's Ward Mr. J. Ball is fighting an unequal battle, against the combined forces of Toryism and class privilege. His opponent does not seem to have much qualification for repre- senting so large a body of ratepayers, and even the laudable desire of Mr. W. P. Rylands to see St. John's "all Tory"should not weigh with ratepayers who have very material interests at stake. Mr. Ball has proved himself a very enlightened and progressive representative during his past three years in the Town Council. He has the advance- ment of the working classes at heart, and he has never lost an opportunity of furthering those schemes which are for the benefit of the com- munity. St. John's is a working-class Ward with many congested areas, and a record death-rate. Unless it is represented by men of Mr. Ball's stamp it will make very slow progress towards the era of better things. We hope the electors will consider these facts carefully and vote solidly for Mr. Ball on Monday.

Not at Warrington—at ANOTHER No-. Barnsley this time. The TRADING Yorkshire town is at present AGITATION, being stirred to its depths by just such another agita- tion as shook Warrington and put an end to a demoralising syEtem of trading between the Council and some of its members. A Mr. John Harvey is taking the lead in the Barnsley fight, and at the first big ratepayers' meeting last week this gentleman emunerated charges against the Town Council which have a very familiar appearance to Warrington eyes. There is another Waterworks scandal at Barnsley—an estimated expenditure of £170,000 actually totalling up to over £355,000. This beats the Lawson Contract apparently ! Then there are defalcations by the late Collector which have cost the town thousands of pounds, Council meetings "in committee," refusals to supply information and produce orders for payment &c. A public inqulry is demanded. Mr. Norbury Williams attended this first meeting of Barnsley Non-Traders, and judging from a speech occupying two columns and a half in a local paper he was in his element. He promised the Barnsley Council some lively times, and considering the material he has to go upon—it includes limited companies with trading Councillor-shareholders—he will fulfil his promise. Warrington was, of course, held up as a shining example of what had been done and what could be done. Mr. Williams said at the outset: Barnsley was not the only English borough which had gone to sleep and had to suffer for it. Looking round that great assembly he could not help thinking of another borough, 'Warrington in Lancashire, which was also in a state of dap sleep seven years ago. At Warrington in 1901, they started what was perhaps the finest series of muni- cipal meetings ever held in one borough in the country. They held 18 meetings in a hall which would hold 2,000 people, and every meeting was crowded. They began with an honest deter- mination to change the complexion of the Council and in three or four years they effected such a change in that Council that its best friends would not have known it."

The Warrington Women's WOMEN LIBERALS. Liberal Association has every reason to congratu- late itself on the valuable part it has taken in the propagation of progressive principles and ideals in the constituency, and judging from the success of the annual social gathering on Monday evening there is no likelihood of waning interest or enthusiasm. On the contrary, the members manifest a praiseworthy desire to keep themselves well informed on the political issues of the day, and lose no opportunity of advancing the interests of the party. Tae presence of Mr. A. H. Oros field, M.P., and Mrs. Crosfield lent special interest to Monday's meeting, and the enthu• gestic greeting which they received must have been highly pleasing to the Member and his wife. In a characteristically well- reasoned address Mr. Crosfield touched upon a variety of topics which are occupying the attention of the Government, and made special allusion to the problem of unemployment and to the Licens- ing Bill. The Government is making a brave attempt to grapple with the situation and, as Mr. Croslield wall pointed out, its work will not be confined to the palliatives which are necessary in view of the acute distress prevailing in many quarters, but determined steps will be taken to cut at the root of the evil. It is a task of great magnitude but we believe the confidence of the people in the Government's ability to tackle it in a drastic and permanent way will be fully justified by events. Meanwhile the Licensing Bill is a decided step in the right direction and the fact that it has such a powerful backing from the moral and progressive forces of the nation is a tribute to the wise statesmanship of Mr. Asquith. Mr. Crosfield touched upon several subjects of special concern to women and the sympathetic way in which he views their aspira- tions fully justifies the association in a continuance of its whole-hearted support of his efforts. Mrs. Osborne, the capable hon. secretary, presented a most interesting report on the Federation meet- ings in London from which it was evident that the Liberal women of England are fully alive to the importance of the issues forming the groundwork of present-day politics.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

We hear that the local organisers of the Women's Suffrage Society are going to make a strong effort to persuade Miss Christabel Pankhurst to come to Warrington and address a Parr Hall meeting, when she has completed her ten weeks imprisonment for inciting a crowd to" rush "the House of Commons. * * There was a unique incident at the Council meeting on Tuesday when the formal resolution of thanks to the retiring Mayor was passed. After eulogistic speeches from Alderman Tinnion, Alderman Bolton, Alderman Bennett and others, the resolution was put to the meeting. The Council not only carried it unanimously but with musical honours, the whole assembly rising and singing "For he's a jolly good fellow " with great heartiness. This is the first time there has been such an occurrence in the Warrington Council, where business rather than sentiment usually prevails, and it was an eloquent testimony to those qualities of heart that have distinguished Alderman Smethurst during his Mayoralty.

* *-* The London and North-Western Railway has been subject to many strange prohibitions and restrictions, particularly in its early years. `• It shall not be law- ful for the railway company to use any locomotive engine upon the railway within the town of Liverpool," enacts the Liverpool and Manchester Railway Act of 1826 ; but the why and wherefore of this drastic enactment does not appear, even in a preamble. An amusing enactment is contained in Clause 16 of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway Act of 1892,which provides that " no steam-engine shall be set up in the township of Burtonwood or Winwick, and no locomotive shall be allowed to pass along the line within those townships which shall be considered by Thomas Lord Lilford or by the rector of Winwick to be a nuisance or annoyance to them from the noise or smoke thereof."

* * * Seven candidates for municipal honours have been returned unopposed and with one exception they are all Councillors who have been re-elected. The only newcomer is Mr. T. Birtles, one of Warrington's oldest and most respected tradesmen, and a suitable representative for Town Hall Ward. There is just ' one feature of these returns which strikes us as being oddly amusing. Councillor Pemberton was adopted as the Conservative candidate by the very men who in times past, tried so hard to defeat him. Whether the Latchford Conservatives were influenced by real admiration, or by the cogent reasoning that if they could not defeat Mr. Pemberton they had better claim him as an ally, it is hard to say, but Councillor Pemberton is entitled to consider his unopposed return to-day as one of his greatest municipal triumphs. * Scene at the Dolgelley Urban Council last week. Mr. Lewis Richards is suspended for impolitely addressing another member. He still attempts to speak. The Chairman: You have been tried by a jury of your own countrymen and suspended from taking any further part. I ask you to withdraw. Mr. Richards: Who is going to compel me to withdraw? The Chairman: You are suspended, and cannot take any further part. Mr. Richards; But I The Chairman : I tell you, Mr. Richards, that you are a dead man here to-night. And mind you now, unless you keep quiet I shall send for the police. This was too much for the " dead man." He got up, called the Council a "chamber of horrors," and departed. * * * " F.E.G. " writes to the " Westminstor Gazette" as follows : "Sir,—The following extracts from Horace Walpole's letters suggest that this wonderful autumn has not been without precedent. On September 13th, 1759, he writes : "This noble summer is not yet over with us. I never write without talking of it, and should be glad to know in how many letters this summer has been mentioned.' On October 11th we are told, I don't know if it proceeds from the menaced invasion, or the last comet, but we are all dying of heat. Everybody has just put out their fires, and if it lasts I suppose will next week make summer clothes. The mornings are too hot for walking; last night I heard of strawberries.' Finally, on October 21st, he explains his continued absence from town : Can one easily leave the remains of such a year as this? It is still all gold. I have not dined or gone to bed by a fire till the day before yesterday." * * Two Scottish Lord Rectors were elected on Saturday, and in both cases there were three candidates and Cabinet Ministers were defeated. At Glasgow Lord Curzon just managed to beat Mr. Lloyd George by twelve votes, Mr. Keir Hardie (despite the fact that he is "ten times better known and a hundred times more respected" than either) having to be content with 122 votes, just an eighth of Lord Curzon's 947 or Mr. Lloyd George's 935. Mr. Lloyd George was only selected comparatively late in the day, for Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman was the original Liberal choice. At Edinburgh Mr. Wyndham defeated Mr. Churchill by ninety-nine votes. Here, again, the purely party pitch was queered by a third candidature, in this case a much more formidable one than at Glasgow. Dr. Osier, who stood as an Independent and received a great deal of support from the medical students, was bottom of the poll (the correct place, apparently, for third candidates), but he polled 614 votes against Mr. Wyndham's 826 and Mr. Churchill's 757. * * Manchester, which is doing its best to deal with the local unemployed, is this week making an interesting effort to assist women who have no work. Out of 7,000 cases of distress inquired into, 800 were those of women who are" either solely responsible for the upkeep of a home, or contributors to that upkeep i whose assistance cannot be done without." It s to assist these that the experiment is being made to pro- vide them with needlework. A work-room has been fitted up, and two batches of women will each be supplied with three days' work a week. The wages are to be 2s. a day and a midday meal. This should be a valuable help to many. Unfortunately, the crisis there is becoming daily more acute. The cotton stoppage is having a very serious effect upon numerous workers who depend indirectly for a living upon the staple industry. In the past the women at times like these have been too often o verlooked, and it is very gratifying to see a sensible effort being made to mitigate to some extent the distress that is now pre- va irmg among them.

The proceedings against the three Suffragette leaders could only end in one way, for despite Miss Pankhurst's cleverly irrelevant advocacy there was in reality no defence to the charge made against them. They did not dispute that they invited and incited the nten and women of London to "rush" the House of Commons--a deliberate incitement to use force,which in any case would have been indefensible. When the day came for the "rash," the Suffragists were joined by unemployed and nondescripts, with the result that a serious riot was almost certainly only averted by the most elaborate police precautions. We regret (says the " Westminster Gazette ") that these women should go to prison; but it is their own choice. The law provides the appropriate remedy in being bound over to keep the peace, and -P it is the women themselves who by refusing thus make prison inevitable. In their franker moods the 1 Suffragists admit that their action is in itself inde- fensible but say they are entitled to do it on the principle that all's fair in love or war. Our reply to that is that this incitement to " rush" the House of Commons was from every point of view a grave mistake. Even if it had succeeded, what would have been the legitimate moral to be extracted from it ? There is no sounder principle than that the Palace of Westminster must be;kept free of access to all its members, and free from physical pressure on them. For our part, we believe that, even judged by the test of expediency, the "rush " did not pay the Suffragists.

div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
[FRou OUR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.] WHAT THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD

HAS DONE. If it were possible to narrow down to a single point the disagreements between the President of the Local Government Board and his critics on the Labour benches, it would be found in this, that Mr. Burns disapproves of relief works, as such, and Labour members like Mr. Crooks and Mr. Keir Hardis believe in them. For the accusation that the Local Government Board .has _minimised the industrial
crisis, or been slack in endeavouring to meet it, amply disproved by the figures which Mr. Asquith quoted last week and Mr. Burns repeated on Monday. Mr._ Balfour wanted to know_ what the Government

had done for the unemployed this autumn that they did not do last autumn. Well, the answer is plain and forcible. From August to October, 1907, there were five loans to local authorities sanctioned for giving work to the unemployed in the locality, with a total value of £3,560. in the same months this year ninety loans have been sanctioned for the same purpose, with a total value of £719,000. In the first three weeks of October, loans to the amount of £547,000 have been sanctioned, or are awaiting sanction, and a further amount of £326,000 will be promptly dealt with. If all loans to local authorities for works of public utility are reckoned, and not only - those specially designed for the assistance of the unemployed, it will be found that between June and October, 1907, £3,589,000 were sanctioned ; between June and October, 1908, £4,388,000. , AN OLD SYSTEM BUT NEW VIGOUR. To argue, as Mr. Keir Hardie did, that, because the - proposal for local authorities to expedite their loans lis one which has been made on previous occasions it is useless to push it forward at a special crisis, iS , 1 to confuse words and things. Mr. Burns has used the machinery of the expedited loan on a scale entirely different from anything attempted before, and he has ' seized a peculiarly favourable opportunity for apply-- ing this machinery to the relief of unemployment, since the local authorities had been forced to hold back from many enterprises during a period- of dear money, which has only recently come to an end. , 1 Before an unfavourable verdict is passed upon the , system of expediting loans and organizing municipal 11 work so that the bulk of it falls in the months of slack employment, the system should be tried on its merits, that is, on the amount of its contribution to 1 the wages fund. But Mr. Keir Hardie appears - - satisfied to dismiss it contemptuously because it has been adopted before on a different scale and under idifferent conditions. MORE ELASTICITY. Not only has Mr. Burns pressed the local authdrities to take advantage of a period of cheap money to embark on new schemes of public work when the depression of private trade has thrown a large body of men out of employment. The Government, by giving greater elasticity to the conditions under which the Central Grant is distributed, by doubling the amount actually expended last year, so that £300,000 are at once available, and by relaxing the special regulations in regard to the work to be aided, so that persons who have received poor relief during the past twelve months and persons who have been assisted under the Unemployed Act during the last two years are no longer disqualified, have placed the Distress Com- mittees in a much better position for effectively assist- ing the unemployed. As the difference between the cost of contract and of unemployed labour will be made good to the local authorities by the Exchequer there is a considerable inducement for them to under- take constructive works now, when they can borrow cheaply, and so furnish employment to a large number of workers. They have nothing to lose, and much to gain, since the undertakings which they tv ill be putting in hand are of real utility, and would in any case be carried out at some later date, when money might be dearer ; and they might, too, be only diverting labour from private undertakings, in which it could be as beneficially employed. OTHER DEPARTMENTS HELPING. .

Though --tii-e-fir-st-h-r:irnio-iTfi'etine—m-piJy;e; crisis naturally falls upon the Local Government Board, other Government Departments are actively engaged in giving aid. The Office of Works will employ some 500 or 600 men in the loyal Parks, and by hurrying on the erection of the new offices for the Commission- ers of Woods and Forests, will provide work for 200 more. The Commissioners of Woods and Forests

have decided to spend some £lO,OOO on road-making. The Board of Agriculture has acquired 14,000 acres for small holdings and 13,000 for afforestation. The War Office is prepared to absorb, during the winter, in the Special Reserve 24,000 able- bodied men at a cost of about £200,000 while the permission granted to Reservists, up to the number of 10,000—a permission of which (1,300 have already availed themselves—to seek work in the Colonies, will give relief in another way. An expenditure of about £2,500,000 will be placed this year by the Admiralty' upwards of six weeks in advance of the time originally -proposed. The ante-dating of the programme should, lir. Asquith has calculated, give £200,000 more to be spent during the winter than would otherwise have been the case. And the Post Office will find emplor- ment at Christmas for 8,000 men at a wage increased, on the instance of the Po ter-General, from 20s. to 255. IS THE EXPENDITURE SUFFICIENT? Altogether,it is probably no exaggerated estimate to fix, as Mr. Burns does, the sum about to be devoted to new public works between now and March, at five millions. Except for the difference between the cost of contract and unemployed labour, the public will obtain full value for this money. It is by better organization of employment, not -by an artificial creation of work which involves the frittering away of public money on purposeless tasks, that the Govern- ment is proposing to remedy the acute distress of? period of economic disturbance. True, the expendr ture would be hopelessly insufficient if Mr. heir Hardie's computation of the number of unemployed came anywhere near to accuracy. But Mr. Burns had no difficulty in showing that the computation could not be accurate. The ratio of pauperism per thousand in London has arisen from 24-1 in 1907, to 247 this year. So slight a rise is altogether incompatible with the assumption that there are from two to three millions of men out of work, with from six to six and three-quarter million persons dependent on them 112 the country as a whole. That a situation of much gravity has arisen no one disputes. But there is.no advantage in looking at it through the distorting medium of panic.

THE PRACTICAL ASPECT. In a rambling and inconsequent debate, the practical aspect was almost lost sight of. Otherwise there would have been much more said about the sufficiency or insufficiency of the expenditure to the needs of the case, and about the wisdom or unwisdora of empowering local authorities to raise a penny rate for the direct employment of unemployed labour. Mr. Crooks declared it was not money, but an organized system that was wanted. Mr. Heir Hardie, While urged that power should have been given to the local authorities to spend a penny rate on wages, ignored the one consideration which alone could docile whether this power was desirable or not. Mr. Asquith 0 decision, as he had declared when he made his state-- ment of the Government's intentions, was based crl the fact that the districts in which unemployment prevails will get out of loans a great deal more they could out of a penny rate. It was a practical question which the Government had to settle-0 best to obtain the necessary money for an immediate object. But the Government's critics were not yr' pared to look at matters from a practical standpalt-

COMPENSATION FOR LICENCES. The discussion of tha question of compensation for licences suppressed on the ground of redundancy was carried over from Friday to Tuesday. As Mr. Asquith said, the object of the Government was, in the first place, to lay down a clear definition of value, and in the second place, to apply to all cases one uniform standard. At no stage during the progress of the measure of 1904 were the words dealing with the . method of assessing compensation ever discussed. It Iwas not surprising, then, that when their effect became ` the subject of litigation, an interpretation was put , tpon them which the firamers probably never intended. - Whether the late Government intended it or not, the compensation clauses in their measure have given to ~ the owners of tied houses more generous compensation , than is awarded in the case of free houses. The , principle which the present Bill follows is to adjust compensation on the lines of assessable value. If the , result is said to be unjust, the admission is necessarily , made that the licensed houses have not been taking their fair share in the burden of the rates. The Government are accused of being the publican's enemy; but they insist upon the licensee participating in compensation. The Conservative Government shut : their eyes to the rights of the publican.

The Rev. Herbeatt Dunnico, of Kensington Baptist Church, Liverpool, who recently received an invita- tion to become pastor of Ernmuel Church, Leicester, has, in response to the urgent appeals of his people, declined same. l'he rev, gentleman announced he decision on Sunday evening, to a congregation which filled the spacious building, and over-flowed into the aisles. The utmost enthusiasm prevailed, and hun- dreds took the opportunity at the close of expressing their appreciation. We understand that the living is of considerably more value than that now held by Mr. Dunnico, and his decision has given immease delight to his friends. Table, Floor, and Hanging LAMPS. FARM FED BACON from Arley district at ASHLEY'S. Advt. Penny Popular Concerts. These was again a crowded attendance at the penny popular concert at Bold street school on Satur- day evening and it is evident that the entertainments are highly appreciated by the public. The programme was well up to the usual high standard, and each item was well received. There were songs by the Misses Hewitt and Armstrong and Messrs. L. Aukland and I. Clayton. all of whom acquitted themselves admirably. Mr. W. Parkinson entertained the company with a series of animated pictures, including a very humorous set entitled " Tommy and the glue pat," which canted the schoolroom to resound with peals of laughter. " A trip round Killarney" was splendidly depicted,giving an extensive idea of the beautiful scenery to be seen in that well-known spot. The pictures included the sights to be seen while on the way to Bristol, leaving Fish-guard harbour, the voyage across to Ireland, scenes on the journey from the sea coast inland to the Lakes of Killarney, showing the wild and uncultivated land on either side of she line, and the extensive area of boggy land to be found on the " Emerald Isle." The concert on the whole was a complete success. BRASS AND COTEER HEARTH SITES, see window display for now and artistic patterns.—J. S. I GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge-street, Warriugton.—Advt. Drowned in Latchford Locks. An inquest was held at Grappenhall on Monday by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, touching the death of a ship's cook, named Michael Macnamara, aged 24, son of James Macnamara, Cross Molina, County Mayo. The evidence showed that on the 15th inst. Macnamara came up the Ship Canal on board the Lancashire, and tbe captain, Mr. Albert Spicer, gave him permission to go and see some friends in Warrington. He left the ship at 9.15 p.m., and was told to be back by one o'clock. Macnamara went to his old lodgings at 15, Pierpoint-street, and at ten minutes to eleven he left the house, saying he was going straight back to the locks. He was then cheerful and well. No one appears to have seen Macnamara alive again. When the Lancashire came down the Canal at about four , o'clock he was not to be found. The captain was ' obliged to go on, but at Eastham telephoned to the locks to ascertain whether Macnatnara had been seen. On Saturday last, one of the Ship Canal employes, John William Lee, 45, Thelwall-lane, noticed the body floating in the lock, and it was recovered. Constable Wood examined it, but found no marks of violence. In answer to the Coroner, Captain Spicer said Macnamara was a particularly steady and respectable man. The jury returned a verdict of .-!` Found drowned." , ASHLEY'S for PROVISIONS, 4,I3ITTTERM ARKET-ST.--AdVt. Security of Tenure for Secondary Teachers. At a meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Branch (East) of the Incorporated Association of Assistant Masters on Saturday in Manchester, he two following resolutions were passed: 1) That this branch thanks his Majesty's Government for the greater security of tenure pro- vided for Assistant Masters by the Endowed Schools (Masters) Act passed at the end of the last Session of Parliament; but notes with extreme regret the acceptance in the House of Commons of an amend- ment depriving masters summarily dismissed of the right to be immediately informed of the reasons for such dismissal. (2) That this Branch expresses its gratitude to the Incorporated Association of Head Masters for their most effective co-operation in endeavouring to obtain greater seem ity of tenure for assistant masters in Secondary schools. The above Act was the direct outcome of the two actions brought by the Asssistant Masters' Association in the High Court and the Court of Appeal in the notorious Richmond (Yorks) dismissal case, which showed that, by law, masters had less rights than domestic servants, or rather,no rights at all. The law expenses have cost the Association nearly seven hundred pounds. WIIITE TOASTING CHEESE Gd. per lb. at As IILE Y'S.--AdV t. School Children and the Infirmary. A meeting of head teachers of the elementary schools of the town was held at the Infirmary on Wednesday afternoon to consider the question of the endowment of a cot in the children's ward. There was a representative attendance. Mr. W. H. Stans- field (president of the Teachers' Association) was elected to the chair. Mr. J. H. Smethurst, represent- ing the Board of Management, explained the scheme. They had now a sum of about £3l or .C 35 towards the endowment fund, and he had called that meeting, to see if they might be willing to give their practical assistance. He suggested that one or two days each year should be set apart and called " Children's Cot Day," on which a collection should be made from the school children. If they got a penny per child throughout the Warrington schools it would realize £6O or £O5. ile thought they could stir up the interest of the children in this way. They were not going to ask the children to give semething for nothing, but they proposed to give a certain number of them facilities for visiting the Infirmary one Saturday afternoon per month to be shown throughout the institution and the various appliances such as the X-rays. (gear, hear.) —Mr. E. Wallington said the scheme had his heartiest approval. The suggestion of Mr. J. H. Smethurst to have one or two days set apart each year for collections was a good one. Another way was to give the children collecting books Ito tollect from their parents and relatives. The sug- gestion with regard to the children visiting the Infirmary was an admirable one. (Applause.) —After further discussion it was decided, on the proposition of Mr. Moore Murray, seconded by Mr. Wallington, that a committee be formed to go into the details, and if possible to arrange for the first collection hefore December. The( followinri committee was appointed : Miss Mary Taylor, Miss Finney, Miss Beardmore, and Messrs. Wallington, Stansfield, Parker (secretary), Robson, Moore Murray, and Kilburn; with Mr. J. H. Smethurst and Mr. J. H. Hampson (ex-officio) repre- senting the Infirmary.
The Examiner Saturday, October 31, 1908.

the trade" Mr. Rushworth would not have a free voice in the Council. In that ward there were some 400 Catholic voters, so it would be readily recognised that their vote was a power. He was told that at a Tory meeting a scurrilous attack was made on the Catholic Young Men's Society. He was there to defend the fair name- of that organization. The Catholic Young Men's Society, as a body which was representative of the Catholic opiaion of Warrington, sent questions to each candidate for municipal honours and they were answered to their perfect satisfaction by Mr. Peacock. (Applause.) He urged the Catholics of the ward to record a solid and unanimous vote for Mr. Peacock and show that they would not be gulled by the talk of the Tories. When Councillor Toole appeared on Mr. Rushworth's platform it was nothing more or less than an unfortunate incident,and it had been wiped out since by the support Councillor Toole had'given to Mr. Peacock. Had Councillor Toole known that Mr. Peacock was coming before the electors he would never have been on Mr. Rushworth's platform. (Applause). Mr. Joffe UPSON in seconding strongly denied the ' charge that the interests of Orford Ward kad suffered in the hands of its progressive representatives. They had the finest and the first Council school in that ward ; a recreation ground, and the only branch reading-room ; and something had been done in the direction of the removal of slum property. The association of the Conservative party with the cry of " religious liberty " was one of the most bare-faced , things he had ever met. (Applause). The Conserva- tives were the party who dented the franchise to the Jew; who withheld emancipation from the Roman Catholics until Ireland was on the point of revolution ; who kept the Nonconformists for hundreds of years from rank in the army and navy and the civil service, as well as from participation in municipal government and employ ; who closed the Universities to all but those of their own religiol.3 faith ; whe had for hundreds of years made social pariahs of those who were not of their faith and Church ; who to-day in 7,000 parishes in the land held the only school to which children of all denominations were cempelled by law to go and in many of which the children were taught doctrines in which their parents did not believe or were taught that their parents' doetrines were wrong. Lie had never heard Mr. Rushworth and his colleagues protest against that gross injustice to many tens of thousands of their fellow countrymen. The attempt that was being made to alienate a section of voters in the ward from the support of Mr. Peacock was disgraceful. The education question did not enter into that or any other municipal contest. In Warrington the Act had been administered without friction, because all parties had united in promoting the interests of education and had thought first of all of the interests of the child. Mr. Upson dealt at some length with the Government Education Bill, and said that to characterise it as the endowment of any form of religion was to state that which was absolutely false. Earnest men were now engaged in trying to find a solution,but the Tory party had ignored that fact in their effort to catch votes. His (Mr. Upson's) opposition was not so much to Alr.Rushworth as a man, but to the business in which he was engaged; and to the dangerous effects of that trade upon the social well-being of the people of this town. They were all convinced that it was a trade which was followed by social degradation, poverty and unemploy- ment, by broken health and misery, and the robbing of little children of the joys, comforts and blessings of life. An addition to the already large representation o,f the trade on the Conneil would render largely' impossible many of the schemes of social reform in which the people were so deeply interested. The trade must have its power broken and its might taken away. (Applause.) Mr. JOSEPH HOWES supported. He said Mr. Rush- worth in a speech at the Junior Conservative Club the other evening let the cat out of the bag. He said : They were always told that the success of municipal candidates was the first step towards success in Parlia- mentary elections. He hoped that the members of the club would do their utmost to secure victories in Orford and St. John's Wards and thus help to bring back Warrington to its old-time Conservatism." That was the game the Conservatives always played. They were neutral candidates during the fight and the day after the election it was a great Conservative victory and the people were fooled. If they were fighting the general election through these bye-elections, as he knew they were, it was necessary that progressives should know what they were doing. We were on the eve of great and important changes in this country. The Government had already done great things, but they had still greater things in hand which would affect the municipil life of all parts of our nation. What members of the Radical party had been struggling for for years, was at last to be realized to some extent. We were decentralising and localising. We were not going in for Government control of every- thing, but for local control. We were marching forward to the municipalization of a lot of things that affected our every-day existence, and the next few years would be a most trying time for the great municipalities. There was every reason to suppose that the Housing Bill which Mr. Burns had in hand would confer immense power on the municipalities for the better housing of the people. It was singular to him that a Tory dare show his face in a municipal fight. We would have had no municipal life if the Tories had had their way. The Tories would have held to the old rotten close Cor- porations where the local landowner used to appoint his nominees and get everything snugly tucked up under his own arrangement and controlled by his own power. The great party of reform broke through that and gave home rule to the towns. It was a degrading thing that the sacred matters of religion should be dragged into municipal contests. Wnatever their religion might be, they had a right to exercise their citizenship and to vote for the man who was most likely to ,do the best work for the people in the ward. (Applause.) Continuing Mr. Howes said it was of the greatest importance to send to the Council Liberals who had sympathy with the Old Age Pensions Act, in order to see that in January next we got as many people as possible on the list. (Applause.) Mr. Howes expressed the hope that the Government would soon find it possible to allow old people in receipt of parochial relief to be transferred to the pension list, for it would immensely liberate local taxes. The great schemes the Government was about to hand over to the municipalities must be man- aged by progressives, or they would fail miserably. The taxation of ground values, to which the Government was pledged, was the great secret of success for the municipal life of the country. (Applause.) In conclu- sion Mr. Howes said that at the last general election the town was emancipated from the brewers and they wanted to maintain that state of emancipation by returning to the Couucil men who had sympathy with the aspirations of the toilers and would see that the measures handed over to the Council for adminis- tration were not used to prop up a monopoly bet to extend the rights of the people. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGE WALKER in supporting said he objected to the influence the trade Was securing in the Council. He also emphasised the importance of taxing ground values and urged the electors to return to the Council a man who would endeavour to do his utmost for the general welfare of the town. (Applause.) The resolution was than put to the meeting and carried with great enthusiasm. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings. After the meeting the candidate received an ovation from is large crowd assembled outside his committee Vora.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
TWO CONTESTS ON MONDAY NEXT.

There will be two contests for municipal honours at Warrington on Monday next. In Orford Ward a three-cornered fight is being waged with great keen- ness, the candidates being : Mr. Peter Peacock_ (L.) __ . _

Mr. J. Hampson (S') Mr. J. A. Rushworth (C.) All the candidates have been hard at work holding meetings, and excitement runs high. Mr. Peter Peacock has a splendid backing, and his meeting on Thursday evening was one of the largest and most enthusiastic we have ever witnessed in a municipal contest. He places a capital progressive programme before the electors, and his commercial training eminently fits him for Council work. Oa the question of religious education, his opinion gives entire satis- faction to the Catholic Young Men's Society, and a representative of that organ:zation strongly supported Mr. Peacock's candidature at the meeting on Thursday. In St. John's Ward another stiff fight is in progress the candidates being : Mr. James Ball (S.) Mr. F. T. Lashford (C.) ' Councillor Ball has a record of good work on the Council and Education Committee and makes a capable and energetic representative of the working classes. His meetings have been most encouraging and if the enthusiasm is maintained he should be returned triumphant on Monday. Councillor Ball possesses the ability to place his views intelligently before the electors and on Wednesday evening he delivered an hour's address which was listened to with keen atteatioa and appreciation.

div.head: ORFORD WARD.
div.p: ORFORD WARD.
Mr. Peter Peacock's Candidature. ENTHUSIASTIC MEETING AT SILVER-STREET.
Roman Catholic Support.

Mr. Peter Peacock's campaign in Orford Ward is meeting with splendid support, and his many workers are leaving no stone unturned to ensure his triumphant return. On Thursday evening a public: meeting in support of Mr. Peacock's candidature was held In Silver-street schools and proved an unqualified success. The room was crowded to overflowing, and the greatest enthusiasm prevailed. All the speeches were received with hearty approval, and there was evidence of a determination on the part of this large gathering to do its utmost to place the Liberal candidate at the head of the poll. Cauncillor John Wilkinson presided and was supported on the platform by the candidate, Councillors Locker, Dickenson and Connington ; Messrs. J. Upson, A. M. Crowe, Joseph Owen, Frank Hughes, NV, Clegg, J. Elwell, G. Walker, J. Critclaley, Joseph Howes, and Joseph Howes, jun. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Peacock was a self-made man and had worked his way from a humble position to a most important appointment under one of the largest and oldest firms in the town. That was evidence that he had energy and ability as well as commercial train- ing. (Applause). While he was in the Council he proved himself to be a man of courage and independence ever ready to stand up for his own principles, without fear of party or association. (Applause. Warrington would in the near future be in need of such men because a tremendous amount of work confronted the Council which would be for the general improvement of the town and the betterment of the conditions of the working classes. They were all proud of Bridge-street now that the widening had at last been completed, but the Council intended to tackle the other three main streets and endeavour to complete them in a shorter time than it took to improve Bridge- street. Other schemes demanding attention were the enlargement of the baths and the provision of recreation grounds, and he was also hopeful that much good would result from the work of the newly-formed Towns Committee, whose object was to encourage manufacturers to start new industries at Warrington. He believed Warrington was second to no other town in England for railway and other means of transit and if the committee succeeded in its work it would be a grand step towards the solution of the unemployed problem. (Applause.) PEICOCK said he contested the ward not lbecause of any feeling against Mr. Rushworth person- ally, but because Mr. Rushworth was a publican and there were already six publicans and brewers in the Council. It was a scandalous shame for Warrington to allow a seventh to attempt to enter the Council. (Applause.) Mr. Peacock proceeded to criticise Mr.Rushworth's election address. Alluding to his advocacy of the Orford Ward recreation ground scheme, Mr. Peacock said he believed that scheme would have been completed if he had remained in the Council. It seemed somewhat strange for Mr. Rush- worth to advocate the provision of pnblic bowling greens when he had one attached to his own public house. The Tories endeavoured to gull the electorate into believing that they were the party to prevent unemployment and Mr. Rushworth practically said: " Sand me to the Council and I will cure every- thing that is wrong." What had the twenty-one Tory Alderman and Councillors been doing during the last three years? They had apparently been looking after themselves and leaving it to the Liberals and Labour men to help those who could not help themselves. (Applause.) If the Tory party were so anxious about the unemployed, how was it that the painting of the baths was not allowed to be proceeded with this winter ? He would like to know where the twenty-one Tories were when police were being imported from other towns—from everywhere but Warrington. (Applause). It appeared to him that the publicans thought it would not be safe to have Warrington men to do Warrington work. (Applause). Unemployment was the most important problem to be dealt with. He believed in spending Corporation money on Corporation improvements which would bear fruit not only in find- ing work for the unemployed but in benefiting the inhabitants in years to come. With regard to the " religious liberty cry" his statement on the education question was clear and distinct. He believed the 1902 Act was a good one and he was sure it had given every satisfaction in Warrington. The reason was that about the time it came into operation they had on the Council men like Councillors Wilkinson, Clegg, Upson and others and a proper understanding was arrived at with the result that everything had worked happily. It seemed most peculiar that a publican of all others should be fighting for the churches at election times. The Tories who were trying to bluff the Roman Catholics on this question did not tell them how they ousted the late Mr. Maginn from the Council. He hoped such hypocritical clap trap would have its deserts on Monday. (Applause.) If returned to the Council he would do his utmost to see that educational matters were fairly dealt with. It was a lie to say that because Councillor Toole spoke at one of the early meetings in support of his opponent, the Catholic instruction was to vote for Mr. Rushworth, because he was informed that had Councillor Toole known that he (Mr. Peacock) intended to come forward he would not have lent his support to Mr. Rushworth. Councillor Toole and the Catholic party knew that in him (Mr. Peacock) they had a friend who would always support what was right. (Applause.) Mr. Rushworth said he believed that friendly societies should be represented on the Old Age Pensions Committee. Where were the twenty-one Tory friends of the work ingclasses when it was decided to have no friendly society or trade union representatives ? Mr. Peacock dealt with many matters of interest to the ward. He had, he said, been described as "the rejected of Bewsey Ward ' but Mr. Rushworth was actually rejected by the Orford Ward electors live years ago, and he (Mr. Peacock) hoped they would reject him again. (Applause). With regard to the Socialist candidate, he (Mr. Peacock) believed he could serve the workingmen far better because he had been in the Council before. He had been in touch with the Trades and Labour Council on various questions and with Councillor Stott, and they recognized in him a friend of the working classes who could be trusted to look after their interests because he was not tied to any party. (Applause.) Mr. A. M. Caown moved a resolution of confidence in Mr. Peacock. He said he was there as a ratepayer, a Catholic and an Irishman. He did not come before them as a party politician but simply to support a good man against a rotten and insidious trade. (Applause.) Mr. Peacock's conduct while in the Council showed that they could not have a better representative of the working classes and especially of Orford Ward. He (Hr. Crowe) maintained that as a representative " of

div.head: ST. JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD.

div.head: Councillor Ball's Candidature.
div.p: Councillor Ball's Candidature.

On Wednesday evening a public meeting in support of the candidature of Councillor James Ball in St. John'a Ward was held in Hamilton-street schools. The approaches to the building were thronged with children who hooted the arrival and departure of those attending the meeting, and sang some doggerel about "voting for Mr Lashford." Many of them stood on the window sills and while the meeting was in progress endeavoured to make themselves as objectionable as possible. There was a crowded attendance at the meeting and great enthusiasm prevailed, not a single dissentient being recorded when the vote of confidence was put. Mr. E. BLIN'3TON, secretary of the Trades and Labour Council, presided and strongly urged the importance to the workers of direct labour representation. The asser- tion had been made—and it was one of the vilest that could be made at election time—that Councillor Ball was an atheist. The striking feature was that in that very ward a church existed where a Bible class was held and Councillor Ball had addressed it on Biblical subjects. He did not think the members of the Church of England would look to an atheist to teach them the Bible. Mr. Plinston referred to the valuable work which Councillor Ball had done on the Education Committee and to the help which he would be able to give in the administration of two measures which were of vital importance to workingmen—the Feeding of School Children Act and the Medical Inspection of Children Act. The cry of Mr. Lashford was " Religious Liberty." He (Mr. Plinston) believed in religious liberty. He believed that people had a perfect right to demand for their children the faith they believed in. C ouncillor Ball had answered the questions submitted to him satisfactorily and the candidates were therefore equal on that subject. Too much was, however, being made of the question. It was simply being used by the Constitutional party of law and order—though there was not much order shown by their representatives at a meeting last week—to divert the feeling of the electors from direct labour representation. (Applause.) Councillor BALL spoke for upwards of an hour and was listened to with keen interest. Alluding to his attitude on the question of exemptions from school attendance, he said that wherever it was possible he still believed that a child should go to school until it was fourteen years of age, but he found from later thought and experience of the wages paid in Warrington in the large majority of cases, that to press the point at the present time would be an exceedingly harsh pro- ceeding. The withdrawal of two or three shillings which a child of thirteen might earn would be a depriva- tion to the younger children of the family.On that point alone he had decided that he would not press for the raising of the school age until the workers of Warring- rington got a living wage. (Applause.) With regard

to the feeding of school children, he did not sugges that it should be a premium to the idler and the shirker, because he said as a Socialist and a supporter of family life, that the first duty of the breadwinner was to see that his children were properly fed, and so long as his income was sufficient he ought to do it himself. Where the parents could not afford it, the children ought to ba fed by the cornunity at large. Councillor Ball referred to his "advocacy of the abolition of school fees, particularly at the Beamont School. In Warrington, he continued, there was no religious difficulty. He had satisfied his Roman Catholic friends but he was not sure whether he had satisfied his Church friends, because he had not yet received a reply from them. If parents desired to send their children to schools where they would receive a certain class of religious education, they could do it in Warrington without fear or favour. Alluding to the insinuation of atheism, Cauacillor Ball said that if he was so irreligious as the Tories would like to make out, how was it that on three separate occasions he had been specially asked to go and address a men's Bible class on Sunday afternoon at St. Peter's Church ? Councillor Steel mast admit that that was absolutely true because he (Councillor Ball) had gone to the Church at Coun- cillor Steel's invitation to address men upon a religious subject. Speaking on municipal affairs, Councillor Ball said that if they had any complaint about the present condition of the town they could only blame the Tory party who for twenty years had had the voting power on the Council. The price of gas to day was threepence more than it ought to be owing to Tory iufluence in times gone by. When the Corporation in promoting a Bill sought power to purchase the annuities which were being paid in respect of the gas undertaking, the Tory influence was surficient to cause that clause to be cut out and for many years the ratepayers had been paying £3,000 per year out of the gas profits to those annuities. With regard to unemployment, it was promised by the Government that grants would be given for relief work and the money would have to be used and distributed by the Town Councils and local authorities. They would have to suggest what kind of work should be 'done for the money and to submit schemes. It was therefore necessary to have somebody in the Council who was not only able to take an interest in the workers but who could also express his views clearly. What he (Councillor Ball) suggested was that as much Corpora- tion work as possible should be carried forward to the winter months when trade was usually slack. The I Corporation ought also to let as mach land as they owned as was suitable for cultivation. The profits made from municipal undertakings should be used on some necessary work instead of borrowing money. We wanted a new Witrington Bridge which would cost £20,000, and also a bridge at Howley. He recommended that some of the insanitary property in that ward should be cleared away, thus finding work for the unemployed, and a recreation ground provided on the site. It might be asked how high would the rates become if the profits were diverted an this way? Until they taxed land values they would not get the necessary money to carry forward reforms for the town and country. Councillor Ball dealt exhaustively with the land question and said the result of Tory legislation and ownership of monopoly had been that the cost of town life had been increased. He declared himself strongly in favour of the taxation of land values. (Applause.) Mr. W. Pon: having addressed the meeting, questions were invited. _ .

Only one was submitted : Is the candidate in favour of a public slaughter house? Councillor BILL said he supposed he was asked that question because his opponent was a butcher (Laughter.) On general principles, and without think- ing of his opponent as a butcher, he was in favour of a public abattoir for Warrington. The reason was that in a public slaughter-house, the conditions under which the meat was killed and the restrictions under which it was examined almost ensured that the meat sold to the public was at least in a good, healthy and proper con- dition. (Applause). The Ca %ARMIN announced that the Citizens' Temper- ance. League at its Executive Committee meeting that evening had decided to support Councillor Ball's candidature. (Applause). On the motion of Mr. HUGHES, seconded by Mr. ELLISON, a vote of confidence in Councillor Ball was carried unanimously. Last evening anottie7 meeting in support of Councillor Ball's candidature was held in Brick-street school.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There is infinite variety provided by the programme at the Palace and Hippodrome this week. Effie White creates a great sensation as a kaleidoscopic and fire dancer, and anything more beautiful tha—n the effects produced with the aid of two lanterns could hardly be imagined. The dancer is one moment a butterfly of gorgeous hue, and next she is seen entwined by glittering snakes or bowered among roses and pansies. She has a fine " repertoire " of slides and produces a turn of remarkable charm and beauty, of which her graceful dancing is a notable feature. Nat Clifford, known as the " nimble one," justifies his cognomen with some clever dancing. As a humorist he excels, and the Warrington crowd has rarely laughed with greater heartiness than at Nat Clifford's jokes and songs. A unique item is provided by Dm lfferrett, the world's champion exhibition bass drummer. Merrett beats the drum to orchestral accompaniments. We were not struck with the drum as a musical instrument, but Dan Merrett's wielding of the drum-sticks was marvellous. Indian-club play I was not in it for rapidity and dexterity, and all the ' time he was beating the drum with the necessary precision. " The Meet " is the title of a hunting ab3urdity which provides Keith and Merson with opportunities for some rapid and side-splitting cross- talk. They are a funny pair, and their exhibition of eccentric dancing is uncommonly clever. Munroe's black and white comedy team specialise in mirth, melody, and music, and gain an appreciative round of applause. The Three Temples (including Madam Louie Gilbert) distinguish themselves as operatic vocalists. Their singing of "The Soldier's Chorus " from " Faust " evoked rounds of applause. A quaint comedian is Happy Attwood, who raises a smile immediately ho appears and keeps it fixed on the faces of the audience till he has finished. Mr. Wicltlop's orchestra has some choice instrumental work which 13 always well done. The cornet solo in the interval by Mr. W. Ryder was deservedly encored. Jessie Burnett, comedienne, and the biograph, com- plete a capital bill of fam

div.head: SACRED CONCERT.
div.p: SACRED CONCERT.

The first of a series of sacred concerts promoted by the Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Musicians' Union in aid of the benevolent fund of the Union and local charities was held at the Palace on Sunday evening. Unfortunately the venture did not receive that measure of public patronage which it deserved but those who did attend were delighted with the high class programme submitted. The orchestra, under Mr. E. A. Widdop's baton, gave some choice selections in a manner which *evidenced intelligent study, their most pleasing contributions being the selection from Gounod's "Faust" and " Spanish Dances" (Mosx- -Iwwel.) Other acceptable features were a saxophone solo "Romance " (Lc•-tr) by Mr.J. Payne, and a 'cello solo (a) " Berceuse ' (b) "Dance Rustique " (.S'quirc), by Mr. E. W. Malpass. The vocalist was Miss Annie Worsley, who sang " 0 Divine Redeemer (Conned) and 0 Rest in the Lord " (MendelsBohn) with deep feeling.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

A splendid programme is announced foe next week and should attract large audiences. The bill is headed by the Austral Trio who will present their refined versatile act entitled "A musical evening." Geoff reys and Benson will appear in one of their comedy sketches and the other artistes will be : —Albert Letine in his female impersonations; the Prinellas, in their farmyard scene ; the Jackley Trio in a refined and recherche drawing room entertainment,includtng the famous whistling comedian, George ; Flo Burnett vocalist extraordinary ; Irma Orbasany's cockatoos, introducing a complete vaudeville performnce and pantomime : Jack Rae, novelty gymnast.

div.head: Buckley-street S.S. Band of Hope.
div.p: Buckley-street S.S. Band of Hope.

A grand concert in connection with the above was held on Monday night. There was a long programme to be resorted to when the President (Mr. J. Knowles) took the chair at 7.30. Numerous solos and recitations were rendered by some of the juvenile members of the society and the audience was delighted by Mr. .1. Urmston's rhetorical powers. There was a pleasing dialogue entitled "Sign the Pledge" by 13 little girls. But the item of the evening was the humorous dialogue entitled "Miss Diddle's Lodgings" in which Miss Kindon took the part of Miss Diddle and earned rounds of applause. Mr. H. Keen caused much laughter as Sambo, and Mr. A. Hall as Mr. Lovewater, Ur. Longworth as Mr. Pressman, Mr. Taylor as policeman, and Miss Brittain as Cluppins. It seemed as though each acted his or her proper role. Buckley-street Dialogue party are not behind as regards dialogues and someane to act them. _
Take Woods' great Peppermint Cure, for Coughs and Colds ;it never fails. Is. lid., 2s. U.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
BOGUS COLLECTOR SENT TO GAOL.

Mary Sandford, a married woman, of 59, Chancery. lane, was charged at St. Helens on Wednesday with obtaining threepence by fraud from Mr. A. Dromgoole. —The evidence was that the previous day the woman went to Mr. Dromgoole's shop in Liverpool-road and produced a collecting book. She said she was collect- tog for the burial of a child which had been burnt to death, and was not insured. Her story was believed and she was given threepence. Later a policeman saw her going from shop to shop, and took her to the police station. She then said that her mother had sent her out, and then that her husband made her go out begging and give him the money.—She repeated this latter state- ment to the magistrates, but they sent her to gaol for twenty-eight days.

div.head: GALLANT RESCUE BY A BOY.
div.p: GALLANT RESCUE BY A BOY.

Thomas Ashton (12), of Halton-road, Runcorn, on Wednesday sight had a narrow escape from drowning in the old quay dock of the Ship Canal. Oa an impro- vised raft he was gathering wood for a gunpowder plot bonfire, when his frail craft upset him into the water. ' Another boy, Ernest Shaw, of Perry-street, jumped in ' and seized him, but his strength was not equal to his i courage. Ashton had sunk when John Harvey,apprentice fitter, son of Captain Harvey, appeared on the scene, and diving to N% here he saw bubbles, brought the drowning boy to the surface and safety. Ashton was unconscious, but revived under proper treatment.

div.head: WIDNES ELECTIONS.
div.p: WIDNES ELECTIONS.

November 2nd will see two interesting elections out of six lots of nominations in Widnes. In Victoria Ward, Covacinor T. J. Peters is to be opposed by Mr. Dan Garghan' the nominee of the Amalgamated Union of Labour. The latter has unsuccessfully fought on two occasions for a seat in the gilded chamber. In Farnworth Ward, Councillor Edwin Wood has as his opponent Mr. T. A. Bullough, who last year was defeated by Councillor George Davies in Simms Cross Ward. In the remaining four wards the following will be returned unopposed West Bank Ward.—Councillor D. Lewis. Waterloo Ward.—Councillor R. Hurst. Simms Cross Ward.—Councilor P. Caldwell. Halton Ward.—Councillor D. Welding. THE ST. BEDE'S-ROAD SCHEME AT WIDNES. Widnes Town Council on Tuesday discussed for hours whether a 50 feet wide thoroughfare, a mile long, bisect- ing the upper portion of the town, shall or shall nut be made forthwith. The question of making this road, to be called St. Bede's-road, has been discussed on countless occasions during the last year. Those who live in the neighbourhood strenuously object on the grounds that the road would divert the traffic° and reduce the import- ance of this district. The chief objection that of expense, has been met by the committee, who have ' obtained valuable concessions from the landowners, reducing the estimated cost by many thousands of pounds. After three hours' debate the Mayor called an adjournment, and tea was handed round. At a later hour the Council decided to adjourn the discussion fo la month. One hundred ratepayers were present, and largely-signed petition against the road was presented

div.head: WIDNES VIRAGO SENT TO GAOL.
div.p: WIDNES VIRAGO SENT TO GAOL.

Annie Jones, of no fixed abode, was charged on Monday at the Widnes Police Court with being drunk and disorderly, and further charged with breaking a plate-glass window at the Bath Spring Vaults.—Police- constable Scarborough said that at 11.45 on the 23rd inst. he saw the prisoner run towards the Bath Spring Vaults and deliberately break the window with her left shoe, and had he not arrested her farther damage would have been done.—Superintendent Strickland stated she had been forty-eight times before the court, and had also been sent to goal for a similar offence.—The Chairman addressing the accused, said it seemed to him that she spent most of her time in gaol. It was a very sad case. She had been given several chances to reform, but she never responded to them. Therefore she would have to go to goal for one month for drunk- enness and two months for breaking the window— three months in all. • Prisoner wept bitterly during the of the proceedings.

div.p: FRODSWAM MORTUARY.

At a meeting of the special committee appointed to deal with this question the architect submitted plans and estimate of £lBO. The Committee considered that amount excessive, and gave directions for modifications. The architect had now submitted an amended estimate of £l2O, and the committee recommended its adoption subject to the size of the building being reduced, and also that tenders be obtained. div.head: CONSTITUTION OF TIIE HOUSE CONIMITTEE.
div.p: THE CONSTITUTION OF TIIE HOUSE CONIMITTEE.

Admiral Jones-Parry, in accordance with notice he hsd given,moved that the House or Visiting Committee consist of eleven members. He said the only objection he had ever heard to his proposal was that every mem- ber of the Board wished to have a finger in the pie. That was all very well, and the members had that opportunity at the Board meeting when the minutes of the Committee were submitted. He was certain that a small committee would be listened to with much greater care and trust when they presented their report. Under the present conditions members could not give the necessary attention to inspecting the house. A small committee would feel a greater sense of responsibility. Mr. Linaker formally seconded in order that the matter might be discu.sed. Mr. Morris opposed the resolution. The House Com- mittee was one of the most important committees where most of the money was spent, and he would rather stay at home than be a member of the Board if he were debarred from attending the meetings of the committee. Mr. Spruce, as chairman of the House Committee, said he could not agree to the change. He failed to see wherein the committee had failed to discharge its duties and until the admiral could advance some good grounds for the proposal he believed the present arrangement was the best they could have. Mr. Stokes said the change would be a backward step. When they had a small committee some years ago it gave great dissatisfaction to those who were not members. It was at his instigation that the committe was made to include the whole of the members of the Board, so that all should have the opportunity of going through the house and taking a direct part in its managetiaent. Mr. Woodward said he was glad Admiral Parry had brought the question forward in order that it might receive its quietus. The vital reason why no change should be made was that if matters had to be fully discussed at the Board meetings they would have to arrange another day for the meeting of the Rural District Council.

Mr. Linaker said he thought that before introducing such a motion Admiral Parry should have been able to show that the present administration was failing in its purpose. He thought the visiting committee worked very well under the present conditions. The resolution was defeated,Admiral Parry not having a single supporter.
