div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
Sr. JOHN'S SOCIAL,

A social for the young pehle of St. John's parish was held in St. John's Parish Hall, Legh-street, on Saturday. Mr. Pilling's band was in attendance, and an enjoyable evening was spent. ACCIDENT AT E.ARLESTOWN STATION. I At eleven o'clock on Tuesday mornin; several carriages left the rails at the Earlestown Station cross- ing on the main line for Manchester and Liverpool. They were, luckily, empty carriages going to St. Helens. A gang of men were soon on the spot, and the traffic was resumed shortly afterwards. SETTING A WAGGON IN MOTION. At Newton Petty Sessions? on Thursday, eight boys were charged with setting in motion.a waggon, the property of Richard Evans and Co., Haydock. It appeared that the boys uncoupled the waggon frons others standing in a coal siding. The waggon was stopped when the boys found they were approaching the main line of the Great Central It dlway.—The Bench said that the lives of railway passengers had been endangered, and that this was a very serious case. —Prisoners were each fined 10s. KILLED BY A FLY WHEEL. SEQUEL TO A SURREPTITIOUS GAME OF CARDS.

Mr. S. [Brighouse, county coroner, conducted an inquiry at the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday, into the death of Thomas Chesters, sixteen, of Rathbone- street, Earlestown, an apprentice wheelwright, employed at the London and North-Western Rail- way Waggon Works, who was killed by a Ily-wheel in the works, on Saturday raorningy From the evidence it appeared that at 9.30 on Saturda. morning a surreptitious game of cards was in progress during working hours in a corner of one of the shops. The sudden appearanca of the chief foreman of the works caused a general stampede through the engine- house, and in an endeavour to find a hiding place Chesters opened the door of a cupboard, which guards a huge flywheel and stepped in. The amount of space in the cupboard was said to be only 81in., so that Chesters must have practically stepped on to the wheel and been killed instantly.—William Crosby, another apprentice wheelwright, said he saw Chesters enter the cupboard, but he did not report the matter until inquiries were ' made some two bouts later. The machinery was then stopped and the unfortunate boy's body was found at the bottom of the flywheel pit in a shockingly mutilated condition.—A verdict of "Death from misadventure " was returned. •

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
FOUR MOTORISTS FINED AT ST. HELENS.

At St. Helens County Magistrates' Court,on Tuesday, Captain R. S. Ramwell, L.A., of Bowdon, was charged with exceeding the motor-car speed limit. He was said to have covered a quarter mile in thirty-six secondq—a rate of twenty-five miles an hour—on Sunday, October 18.

Jack Last, chauffeur, of Birkdale, pleaded guilty to driving a car on Saturday, October 27, at the rate of thirty-one miles an hour. Robert W. Sutton, plumber, of St. Helens, did not appear. He was stated to have driven a car at over twenty-four miles an hour on October 10. Robert 11filsall, chauffeur, of Southport, denied that he drove at the rate of twenty-four miles, on October 10. Sergeant Fiddling and three officers described how the time was taken. Each of the defendants was fined £l, includingosts.

div.head: FATAL BURNS.
div.p: FATAL BURNS.

Mr. Brighouse bold an inquest at St. Helens on Tuesday on Elizabeth Worswick, aged thirteen, who died in the Providence Hospital on Saturday from burns. Mrs. Knowles, the grandmother, said that the girl had lived with her at College-street since she was eighteen months old. Her father was a collier living at Black Brook, Haydock. Last Saturday week the girl went to her aunt's house in William-street to look after the baby. In the afternoon when left alone in the hoase, she was cleaning the grate and her clothing took fire. She rushed into the street enveloped in flames, and she was afterwards taken to a doctor and then to the hospital where she died.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. ST. HELENS ELECTIONS.

The preparations for the seven contests in St. Helens on Monday next are being most vigorously pure -ed on both sides at St. Helens. The result of Saturday's contest in Hardshaw Ward was disappointing to the Labour party, who had hoped that the Conservatives would have been beaten. The whole of next week's elections are being contested between the Conserva- tives and Labour Party. The Labour party are in the position of having to defend four seats. In North Eccleston Mr. Hamblett is opposed by Mr. W. J. Ellison (C.) In Hardshaw Mr. Pugh is opposed by Mr. Brace Davidson (C.) In West Sutton Mr. R add is cdposed by Mr. J. H. Bottomlev, the well-known Con- .-ervative speaker; while Dr. Graham has taken up the task of defending the Labour seat in South Eccleston, in place of Mr. Forshaw,who has accepted an impertanz. position in connection with the Newton Parliamentary Division Labour party. In Parr Ward Mr. Woodward is opposed by Mr. R. Wareing, the Labour organiser. In south Windt° Mr. APLachlan,one of the old Liberal party, has retired, and the Conservatives have put for- ward Mr. Haslana Fox who is opposed by Mr. R. W. Thomson ; while in East Sutton Dr. Bates (C.) is opposed by Dr. O'Keeffe, who was formerly a member for the Parr Ward.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " Mrs. Ponderbury's Past.",
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " Mrs. Ponderbury's Past.",

The Warrington public have hardly supported the excellent company which is producing "Mrs. Ponderbury's Past" this week as well as it deserves. There have certainly been some good "houses," but the building ought really to have been crowded every night to witness Sir Francis Burnand's high-class comedy. Nothing funnier has been written and staged for a long time, and Mr. Percy Hutchison's company does full justice to the many farcical situa- tions which arise. Mr. George Mule undoubtedly carries off chief honours in the fine role of Ur. Ponderbuiy, who is not merely a hen-pecked husband but an abject slave to the imperious and virtuous Mrs. Ponderbury. The part has infinite possibilities, but we cannot recall to mind any actor who would have realised them more fully and adequately than Mr. Mudie. His interpretation of the part is a creation in itself, and he certainly makes poor Ponderbury a very real personality. The " story of the.knife " is one of the cleverest humorous conceptions in the whole comedy. and to hear Mr. Mudie relate the story of how the knife became a family fetish is killingly funny. Like most fetishes, its virtues are exploded in the end, and even Mrs. Ponderbury does not come through the ordeal with her "past " unsullied. This dictatorial lady is capitally represented by Miss Annie Stalman. Another lady who is responsible for much of the fun, and for all the scrapes poor Ponderbury gets into—and out of —is Madams Modjiski, formerly Stella of the " halls." Miss Florence Wiz makes her a dashing and delightful young person, without a suspicion of the prudery which so often dilates the nostrils of Mrs. Ponderbury-. The studio scene was full of riotous revelry between her and Ponderbury, and the audience rocked with laughter. Of the three scenes, however, we thought the first the best. It gives Mrs. Mudie's subtle) humour such scope! Peter, the ancient butler, plays a considerable part in the piece, and Mr. Alfred Ibberson's treatment of the role was masterly. Mr. Drew Mackintosh and Miss Florence Wellesley also played their companion parts very creditably, while Mr. Charles A. Staite skilfully pourtrayed the insipid Ur. Hyacinth Grayling. "Mrs. Ponderbury's Past"- was preceded by the one- act comedy by Mr. Muffle entitled "His Landlady." It was very well acted by Messrs. Ibberson and. Mackintosh, and the Misses Wellesley and Elswick, but the misunderstandings which made the mirtls. 1 eemed a little too obvious.

Hollingworth, T, Praise is due to Mr. A. Troughton (exhibition manager Miller, .7. B. Bugloss, Mr. W. Farness, Mr. J. A. Groom for the completeness of the arrangements, .. (founder and secretary of the homes), and Mr. A. ale Troughtcn (manager of the exhibition). The Rev, E. C. E. CARLETON haying offered prayer, Mr. GROOM delivered an explanatory address. He said the Watercress and Flower Girls' Christian Mission owed its existence to the efforts of that truly Christian nobleman, the seventh Earl of Shaftesbury. It was over forty-two years since he (Mr. Groom) had the honour of laying before Lord Shaftesbury, an account of the sad condition of that vast constituency of London's poorest of street poor—namely the children, girls and women who were seeking to earn their living by the sale of flowers, watercress and other articles in the London streets. Lord Shaftesbury thought it a pity that so much young life should be allowed to run to waste, which if rightly directed might be a benefit to the community as well as to those poor creatures. Hence the institution was inagnrated for the social, moral and spiritual uplifting of this vast clasa. It began as a small local market effort and it bad now, by the goodness of God, attained to national importance, ministering eve-y week to over 6,000 children,girls and women who came under its care.l hey had an orphanage which accommodated 250 fatherless and motherless little girls, received without any question of age, creed or physical infirmity. They were kept until they were fit to go into service, provided with an outfit and a general oversight kept of their future. The institution had also its own cottage hospital and convalescent home, and a seaside holiday home for blind andcrippled girls. There were also eight centres in London, and at the flower market an early breakfast and club room was Provided as a counter-attraction to the public-house. In over 3,000 oases they had been successful in dealing with the able-bodied, but it never seemed to him to be Christ-like to care for the able-bodied and leave the afflicted uncared for. Unless something was done for them the only outlook was that they would drift to the Workhouse or become a permanent drain on charity. He held that unless they raised the recipient above the need of charity, charity had failed in her real work. Mr. Groom showed how the artificial flower industry was started at the institution in order to pro- vide a means of livelihood for the blind and crippled girls. There were now 268 girls undergoing that train- ing, and they were all paid for the work they did. They handed to the institution ss. per week for board and lodgings and kept the remainder, and when he stated that they could earn from 10s. to 15s. per week he thought he could claim that they had in some measure solved the problem of how efficiently to train afflicted, blind and crippled girls. Over £2,000,000 worth of foreign made flowers were imported into this country every year. The Duke of Argyle told him (Mr. Groom) to try and bring back to England her long lost trade of artificial flower-making. That was what he was try- ing to do, and last year the crippled girls competed successfully with the foreigner to the extent of over £lO,OOO. (Applause). In giving up the office, which 1 may Connell and the committees. He had given every one say Ido with some regret, I would urge upon my suc- of them a'fair hearing, had been most impartial, and cessor the necessity of pushing on with one or the other had, in fact, been the essence of fair play. He had ,of the bridge schemes which have been before the upheld the best traditions of the chair—(bear, hear)— Council, and °f should like to assure him in that matter, and they felt very much indebted to him for the as in all matters which he will have to take in hand as gentlemanly and courteous way in which he had acted, Mayor, I shall only he too glad to render him every He had laboured long and strenuously, as Alder- possible assistance. (Hear, hear.) I beg to thank the man Pierpoint had stated in his letter. He had officials most .heartily- for their services—the Town thought no duty too greit or too small for him to Clerk, the Deputy Town Clerk and Mr. Spinks Mr. undertake. He had khowdif o party or creed, and had Spinks has rendered great assistance to the Mayoress in been everyone's Mayor. Therefore he bad been a connection with the children's parties and other fun- popular Mayor. He had 'discharged his duties willingly tions ; indeed hie services have been invaluable. Mr. and with grace, charm and sweetness. One thing that Longdin, Mr. Fairhurat and all under them have also stood out prominently was the fact that he had been been extremely kind and have rendered me every the children's Mayor. His (the speaker's) own children possible assistance. The townspeople have also been good and I have received kind letters from many of had said what a nice, kind gentleman Alderman Smethurst was. That was an appreciation anyone them as well as from several children expresing regret that I Ral about to give up the office of Mayor. There is might be proud of, becaase it was genuine. He felt that the same kind of thanks would be accorded to the Mayor by the men and women of the town of all sections and partici. Whatever he had done he had done with whole-heartedness and kindness. He was blessed with a large and tender heart, and had he been blessed with a large pocket he would have "made the ' wilderness blossom as the rose and the desert and the solitary place glad." (Applause.) The ' Mayoress, at all the fnnctions which she had graced by her pressence, had made everybody' happy and contented, and he felt sure Alderman Smethurst must be proud that he had such a wife and his family proud that they had such a mother to render such great and vslnable work as she had done as Mayoress. He (Alderman Tinnion) could only hope that the ilayor would long be spared to come amonmat them and assist in carrying out the good work they had in hand, and also to continue his deep interest in the social and other affairs'of the town. (Applause). The DEPUTY-MAYOR, as the oldest member of the Council, seconded with great pleasure. He said it was the prerogative of the f leader of the opposition "to move the vote of thanks, and he took it as a graceful act that the " opp mition" had expressed such apprecia- tion of alderman Smethurst's services. He (Alderman Bolton) did not think the Mayor could have possibly done better than he bad. The Mayor had done his best and they had very little cause to complain in any direction. He had attended all the functions he possibly could ' • BM kindly and genial face was always welcome ; and he had sheen that he had appreciated the position he had held. The Mayoress had certainly done her best. (Hear, hear.) She had been a worthy Marmess and had attended many functions at con- siderable inconvenience to herself. He did not think, that the Council would be doing its duty if it did no heartily and thoroughly thank the Mayor for his sel- vices during the two Tears he bad been the chief magis- trate of the town. He had been very attentive to his duties and had given every possible consideration to everybody. He hoped all the members of the Council would endorse the vote of thanks as heartily as they did the other day at the meeting of the General 'Pur- poses Committee. Alderman Beseerr, in supporting, said it was one of the proudest recollections of his life, that he proposed the election of Alderman Smethurst as Mayor of the Borough, and he had never bad occasion to regret having done so. On the other hand ha had had matiy reasons to be sincerely thankful he took the course he ' did. Alderman Smethurst's work had justified his ' appointment up t ) the hilt, and he felt sure that that was the unanimous feeling of the members of the Council. He had been endeavouring to find a suitable quotation to express the work of the Mayor. He had found an extremely hackneyed one; but, after all, nothing be had seen better summed up what he wished to say about the matter and it was this : Howe'er it be it seems to me, 'Tis only noble to be good. Kind hearts are more than coronets, And simple faith than Norman blood. (Applause.) As he had said it was a very hackneyed quotation, but it was quite true; in fact, he did not know any in the whole range of English literature that would better describe the Mayor. If he might dwell more upon the public side of the appointment he might say that the Alderman had equally justified their con- fidence; and they respected him uot only for his kind- heartedness but for the admirable manner in which he had discharged his duties; while with regard to the civic life of the town there were many things upon which he would be able to look back with pleasure, particularly upon the widening of Bridge-atreet. There was only one episode with which the,/ had occasion to feel disappointed and that was that his sincere wish that his term of office should be crowned by the completion of the bridge had not been realized. Alderman Smethurst, had however, done his utmost for that scheme, but had had to contend with greet difficulties. Many interesting events had occurred during his Mayoralty. He had taken part in the opening of the extended Infirmary, the New Post Office, and the Bolton Council School, while in the realm of pleasure he hadtaken some part by laying the foundation stone of the Palace and Hippodrome—hear, hear—and it was a happy idea that he should have visited once in every year the schools of the borough and have awarded medals to, the best boys and girls. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Mayor bad succeeded in raising large sums of money for the Nursing Institution and for Wigan relief fund, and he believed that in the long annals of the Mayors of Warrington there had not been one who had won more sincere and more extended respect and regard than Alderman Smethurst had done. The same remarks applied to his good wife who had been untiring in her work. (Applause). Councillor EVANS also supported, and said that in the work of the Mayor there was a great deal for which they bad every reason to he thankful, and they were especially indebted to the Mayoress who had supported her husband most loyally in his manifold duties, at genie self-sacrifice. The work of the Mayor and Mayoress had far exceeded the expectations of the people generally. Councillor PEMBERTON said that he, more than any other member of the Council, had bad a varied experi- ence since he became a member of the 'Corporation, but he could say that the Mayor had always acted fairly and impartially in conducting the meetings. The posi- tion of the Mayor at first was not an easy one, but easily difficulty bad been surmounted. Allusion was made to the Mayor's kindness to children, and Councillor Pemberton said that a bad man never got a child's appreciation. That was the real essence of true appre- ciatior, because it, was unbiased. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURTON said the Mayor and Mayoress richly deserved every word that had been said about them. Hu Worship's work in connection with the Infirmary end Nursing Association and other Institu- tions would stand out prominently for many years to come. (Applause). The resolution was then pnt to the meeting end carried with enthusiasm. Alderman Tinnion then led the Council in singing that familiar air " For he's a jolly good fellow." It is believed that this is the first time it has ever been sung in the Council Chamber at the conclusion of a Council meeting. Cheers were also given for the Mayoress and family. The MAYOR, who was received with cheers, said : Centlemen, I must in the first place thank the mover, the seconder, and the other members who have spoken on the resolution you have just passed, for the kind words they have used and the sympathy they have shown to me in the discharge of the difficult duties of the Mayor. I must also thank the whole of the Council for their unanimous vote which conveys to me such a hearty expression of their appreciation of my services. I must also thank the speakers for their kindly reference to my good wife, and I shall have much pleasure in telling her what you have said. My wife, often under great difficulties as you know, has done her utmost to assist me and to render to the town such services as were within her power. (Hear, hear.) May I say here that it is mainly due to the consideration I owe to my wife, and the arduous task which owing to the condition of her health she had often found difficult to perform, that I was compelled to decine the unanimous request of the Council to accept office for another year? And I say this in order that I may express my gratitude to you for the great honour you again offered me. In reviewing my year of office I should like to refer to the deaths of those who have served their town as members of the Council, Mr. James Fairclough, Mr. EL W. Fraecomb, Mr. W. D. Houghton, and Mr. John Magian have gone in one short year, but I feel sure that the work they did for the town will
A RUMOUR

... cone abroad to which I refer to for my own sake and for the sake of those who may follow me. It has been said that I receive 1 the support of Sir Gilbert Greenell and Mr. Parr with regard to my expenses. May T say that I have never received a penny in my life either from Sir Gilbert or Mr. Parr ? This was stated in a r way c itriage by a man who ought to have known better, but he made the charge with such emphasis—not ill-feeling—that I was bould to con- tradict it. This gentleman, who has bean seeking the position of a inemher of the Council, said other things. I shall tell him about it some day. I thought it was due to myself and to my family, and those who will come after me, to say, that snob a statement, so far as I am concerned, is utterly undue and unfounded. i thank you most heartily for the kind manner in which the resolution has been received. (Applause).

div.head: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.
(By PEDO).

The sport is booming. Glowing accounts of club doings are coming from many new districts. The old clubs ate Otai cling a rush of new blood. The enthrsiasna i 3 not confined to this country, as reports from the continent and colonies go to show that our neighbours and cousins mean to give the old country's represents- tives something to ch in future international competi-

lhe stream of old blood which hns during late years flowed from het'e into Ctnada and Australia, may be relied on to instil the right spirit into the rising genera- tion of crost-country runners there, and Canada particu- larly-shMO shine. • It.is wcirthy of.note that the United States are taking great interest in tong distance running. Alf Shrubb's ramblings have not been nithout a result, and it is reasonable to ASSZIM3 that with his coaching " Harvard University " will develop a cross•ootintry team capable of a warm rterformance.' Alf was extra at the game. Ile will have apt pupilo, and expenses will not to cousiderol.

11,e War °Tice officio, s invriabTy move on the slow but sure plan- They are understood to have under con-' sideration a scheme to adapt " eross-Conntry [tanning' as a portion of winter drill, insto id of some of the exercises at present in use. To the sceptical this should prove a shaker. It has long been recognised by the most 'competent judges of athletic =, what an important branch in the development of the athlete this sport providcl, and also the lasting good,derived ham participation in a sport whicli repre eats the pure-t form of amateurism and it is possible to. e working' lad, although in many instances clubs have pltfyci the exclusive game to their own detriment, as instanced by the figure they cut when opposed to a team of working lads who have bad proper schooling. • Alter the Bareness entailed by early efforts has worn off, beginners are surprised at the ease vcith which they can get over a rem of 7 or 8 miles, especially when they recollect how tired they previously felt after a walk over a similar distance—proper tuition and perseverance work wonders.
SATURDAY RUNS.

Sutton Harriers visited Thatto Heath where St. Austin's provided a five mile con: e for their St. Helens and District League fixture which provided another easy win for Sutton; resell—Sutton : Welding, 1; Straw,'2 ; Whittle, 3 ; Barrow, 4 ' • Morris. 5 • Devlin, 6 ; total 21; St. Anstins : Meredith, 7 ; Rigby, 9 ; Mercer, 12 ; Greeuall, 19 ; Lowry, 20 ; Wharton, 21; total 88 points. Sefton Harriers mustered well for a -run otalmost seven miles. J. T. Rimier acted as whip until the lot lined up for a break over the last mile, when he acted as pace and easily finished at the head of the field. It should be mentioned that the Northern Charnpion, W. T. Clark, was an absentee, but there was great jubilation in the Sefton camp when the nesi.a arrived that Tommy " hal Won the Scottish Marathon Race, with something like half-a-mile to spare. lie is credited with having covered a distance of 16 miles in 1 hour 23 minutes 51 seconds, which represents a good per- formance even if the distance was a half-mile short, which is afa ir,estimate. Tommy finished aL a very fast paco and was warmly applauded. Broughton Harriers ran over about seven miles of grand country in the neighbourhood of Denton. Three packs totalling 31 runners had a good .time and E. Walker was prominent in the fast nice. - Crewe Harriers had a strong pack out for a six mile run in the Sandbach district. Bowyer and Bennion did not get away much from H.Bradley. These three led the field and finished in the order given after fine set to. Bradley is a find. Warrington A.C. bad a run of about six miles over the usual quarter, the pack of 23 were set a merry pace by J. T. Mulhall and were whipped in by H. K. Jepson (captain). All thoroughly enjoyed the run, Siddall, Litherland, Hewitt, Millington and Whittaker being prominent. Despite the inclement weather 16 turned out for a ran on Tuesday evening. At a subsequentl Committee meeting it was decidc I to' hold two novice ' races, the first to take place on November 11th, and be confined to those who have previous to this season ton across country ; the second race,on December 19th, will be open to all who have not previously obtained an award for crosr-counta f running. Club medals will also be awarded to the brat novices home in two of the inter club fixtures. „

The Points competition will be decided on the results of the intm. club fixtures and will give added interest to the following : November 28th, Warrington United at Sankey. December 12th, Crewe [farriers at Crewe. January Oft, Warrington United from Bridge Inn. Jenvlry 23rd Crewe Hu.iers from Bridge Inn. - .
The annual four-catuered encounter c;ith Felton, Sutton and Broughton should this year be under the guidance of Safton Harriers who have not yet fixed the date 8:c.

In addition to these, further competitive races will be providt by the Club Championship, Annual Christmas Handicap, Northern, Livorr 30l and District, and National Championship ishresting times are in store for the more se?soned runners as well as the novices for whom handsome provision is evidently Laing made. Fast and slow racbs will be formed for to-day's run at 330 and for Tuesday's run at, 8.15 p.m. from the Bridge Inn. Members and intending members are requested to attend early end regularly so as to derive full benefit from the qualifying runs.

div.head: Warrington. Women's .Circle.
div.p: Warrington. Women's .Circle.

Mrs. Lloyd-Jones presided at the Circle on Sunday, assisted by Mrs. Clatworthy and Mrs. Davies. An old-fashioned address on the best lines was given by Mrs. Owen on" Home-making." God made woman to he the complement of man, not to usurp his place, and sent both into the world differently equipped mentally and physically for their own sphere of work. Women had rights, but their true and best rights were not what is often understood by "Women's Rights." Whetkier the birds love to return depends on whether we make of our homes nests or cages. It was evident that many agreed with Mrs. Owen's views. Miss Hayes was the soloist : " God that madest earth and heaven" and "He shall feed His flock" ; and the girls sang " Tell it over once again," Misses Bates and Tynan taking the duet.

div.head: FOR ELDERLY FOLK.
div.p: FOR ELDERLY FOLK.

Get from any good chemist, Tincture Gentian Com- pound, one ounce; Syrup Rhubarb, one ounce; Barkola Compound, one ounce; and Syrup of Ginger, five ounces; and mix by shaking well in a bottle. Take in teaspoonful doses, one afor each meal and one at bedtime.

This is the prescription and the directions as given by an eminent authority on kidney diseases, who makes the statement that this simple home-made mixture will relieve almost any kidney disorder, or backache, or bladder weakness. This should prove of untold value to all elderly folks, who always suffer, more or loss with their kidneys and bladder at this time of year.

div.head: BAPTIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD, Annual Sale of Work. '
div.p: BAPTIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD, Annual Sale of Work. '
MR. W. LONG AND THE LICENSING BILL.

The schoolroom attached to the Baptist Church. Latchford,. presented a bright and pleasing scene on Wednesday afternoon when the annual sale of work was opened by Mr. William Long. The stalls were attractively arranged and heavily laden with tempting wares. They were in charge of ladies-of the congrega- tion, who had worked untiringly for the success of the sale. There was an encouraging attendance at the open- ing ceremony, the pastor (Rev. J. Matthews) pre- siding. Amongst those present were the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Rev. J. S. Hughes, Rev. H and Mrs. Wall and Mrs. James Dodds. After the Rev. C. Harvey Cook had offered prayer, The Rev. J. F. MATTHEWS explained the necessity of the sale in order to maintain the funds of the Church in a satisfactory condition. He referred with gratitude to the help rendered by the band of workers and to the progress which the church wes making. He was also proud to say that the Sunday school had considerably I grown, and he had seen as many as one hundred children in that room. That was the tenth sale of work they had had since he (Mr. Matthews) commenced his ministry there. In conclusion Mr. Matthews announced that he had received donations to the amount of £lO 63. and expressed the obligation of the congregation to Mr. Long for his kindnes in coming to open the sale. Mr. LONG said that when be got a note from Mr. Matthews and the members of the committee asking him to open the sale he consented with pleasure,because he had a very warm feeling for Mr.Matthews' work and for all those who were trying to make a stand against the sin and misery in the world. The fight that was going on now in connection with the Licensing Bill ought not to be a party question. It was a fight against what he would call the trade. The success of "the trade" meant the ignominy and debasement of the people and if there was anything of which he could speak with approval it :ia4 the way in which John Burns stood up in the House of Commons the other nighkagainst what ha (Ur. Long) believed was only a temporary attack upan him, by stating the amount that was spent in drink in England by the working classes every year. The Government would want all the support they could have to carry the measure through and it was one of the things they should all work for. Mr. Long commended the good work which the churches were doing and urged the importance of working unitedly with a right motive. (Applause.) An innovation at this year's sale was the passing of a vote of thanks.

The Rev; J. S. HUGHES, in proposing that such a vote b.. 1 accorded to Mr. Long, said that their church was not a rich one, and even if they put their hands deep into their pockets they could not pull much out. (Laughter.) Therefore they had to hold sales of work to attract the h-lp of many of their outside friends, and to. maintain the good Work which the Church .was doing. Mr. CONWA.Y seconded.

The Rev. J. F. MATTHEWS, in supporting, cordially acknowledged the loyal support the members of the Church had given him during his eleven years' ministry there, and mentioned that they had on two occasions raked his salary. _

The vote was heartily passed and in responding, M. LoNG said Mr. Matthews was one of the best known ministers in the district, and had gained the esteem of all. He wished the sale eve 7 success. (Applause). . THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. -
The sale was opened on Thursday afternoon by the Rev. John Yonge._ _ _ _

The Elev. J. F. ikaTmews said that they at Latch- ford tried to face any ditlicultias squarely and honestly and to put their shoulders to the wheel,so that unitedly they showed year by year a fair amount of progress. He was very much struck that afternoon with the exquisite peacefulness and quietness of the scene around the church and it struck him that anyone standing by the railway bridge and looking at that building would think that nothing was ever done there and that it was such an out-of-the-way place that very little influence could radiate from it as a centre. Happily that dream was only a dream. They tried to do a little work there which -was generally appreciated in the neighbourhood and in the town in which they lived. Referring to Mr. Yonge's presence, Mr. Matthews said that those who were present at the birthday gathering at Wycliffe last week were not only struck but delighted with the keen appreciation in which Mr. Yoage's name and work were held in ou,r beloved town. The town had become a place which he (Mr. Matthews) loved very much indeed. One could not work amongst people for eleven years without in some sense getting to love those who were more or less deflaitely associated with the work of his own church and of other churches. They were delighted to see Mr. Yonge looking so hearty and well and they hoped he would be spared for rainy years not only to ctrae down to Latc'dord, which he did as fre- quently as opportunity would allow,hat to continue the good work which he had been doing at Wycliffe for thirty-two years. Might he continue to enjoy that delightful friendship they all felt towards him and that warm affeotion with which they regarded him. Nfr. Matthews announced that Wednesday's proceeds amounted to RP Mr. James Dodds had promised a donation of two guineas and he had also received cheques of 10s. each from Mr. James Gandy and Dr. Edward Gaudy. (Applause.) The Rev. J. YONGE said that although their church was outside the boundaries of the town it had for many years been the centre of great good, the place of many holy seasons and happy work for the Master, where many a soul had been fashioned after God's image and where the blessing of the Holy Spirit had attended the ministrations of succesAive ministers, and not least, the ministry of their pastor, Mr. Matthews. He (Mr, Yonge) was always interested in the fortunes of Wash Lane and looked back with pleasure to many happy times spent there. He always felt that the friends of that church had a warm coiner in their hearts for him and he heartily reciprocated the feeling. They had his heartiest good wishes for the success of the sale. (Applause.) _

IY.-CLOYD-Jons in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Yonge said that was an appropriate occasion on which to wish Mr. and Mrs. Yonge many happy returns of the day end a much longer life of usefulness. They were all glad to see Mr. Yonge looking sp well, despite the weight of years on his shoulders, and his fife was an inspiration to the younger men to follow in his footsteps. Mr. Yonge had always been a close and sympathetic friend of Latchford Baptist Church—in fact they almost looked upon him as their bishop. (Laughter).

Mr. S. ALIIINSoN seconded. He said Mr. Yonge thought well of Latchford and the Latchford friends thought well of Mr. Yonge. (Applause). The vote was heartily accorded, and Mr. YONGE briefly responded. The total proceeds of the sale amounted to £Bl Os. GI and included the following donations :—Mr. F. R. Roberts. £2 23. ; Mr. James DAcis, £2 2s. ; Mr. Edwin Marsden, £1 is. ; Mr. Fred Pendlebury, Z 1 is.; Mr. C. E. Parker, £l. is. ; Mr. Ziba Armitage, £1 ; The Pastor, £1 ss. • 111 r. Frank Fish,los. Gd. ; Mr.ltichard Boardman, 108. ; %fr. John Lunt, 10s. ; Mr. Joseph Bailey, 103. 6d.; A Friend, 10s. ; Mr. J. Gandy' 10s. ; Mr. E. Gandy, 1 os.; Mr. James Kenwortby, ss. ; Mr. William Hough, ss. ; Miss Blanche Lawton, 2s. 6d. ; Miss Rees, 2.5.

div.head: SKIN DISEASES
div.p: SKIN DISEASES
OVERCOME BY THE WONDERPUL BLOOD PURIFYING PROPERTIES OF DR. MORSE'S INDIAN ROOT PILLS.

A person suffering from eruptions of the skin has much to endure. It is not merely the dis- comfiture and irritation and painful sensation, but life is made misera- ble by depression of spirits. The liver is torpid and the kidneys are partially inoperative, and you feel languid and weak. The disease is in the blood and when the system is not cleansed through the usual channels Nature asserts herself and forces portions of the impurities through the skin in the form of Pimples, Boils, and Blotches. NO DROPPING OFF.

" James!" cried the merchant from his pri- vate office. "Yes, sir," answered his office boy. "I am tired, and lam going to have an hour's rest in my chair here." "Yes, sir," "If I should happen to drop off, call me at four o'clock." "Yes, sir." So the merchant lies 'back in his chair, folds his arms, closes his eyes, and is soon in the land of dreams. He is awakened by the clock striking five, and calls, indignantly, " James I" " Yes, sir I " "Why didn't you call me at four o'clock, as I told you to do?" "Well, sir, ye told me to call ye if ye had dropped off! I looked in on ye at four O'clock, and ye hadn't dropped off I Ye was sitting on the chair, sound asleep. 7.

This is the story:—One day, when it was very hot, an exPress train from Plymouth to London ,was flying along at the rate of sixty , miles an hour. When it stcpred at ,kwindon. for a few minutes, many pscpie, gpt out and many people got in. Presently the train moved on, and they just whizzed through the stations. On the way, in one of the carriages there were two people, one was a small youth, the other was an elderly lady, the, sort with a very straight face that never notice litfle boys and girls except to stop them when they 4. are having a little harmless fun, and with her hair brushed back very stlif and ye-4 s:raight. - She had a little black pug dog 'in her lap that she fed on plum cake and jujubes. Juot opposite her sat the young man, wlo had no pug dog, but he had a nice black -bliar pl-., in his pocket, and, after looking out of the window two or three times, and sadly wishing that he could have seen the label on the window with " Smoking" on it, and after looking' at the stern face in front of I.irn two or three times, and wondering to himself if he dared, he took it out cf his pocket. There was a look on hls face like a schoolboy who has been found out, all the time he was filling it. The lady frowned! He pulled a match out of his pocket, and commenced putting , away, when there were sparks, not frcm the pipe, but from the lady. Said she, very mud- den-like, as though she were in a great hurry, - "Do you know, I strongly object to smoking, especially when boys smoke. Pnt it out at once, or I will pull the communication cord and stop the train." And, suiting the action ; to the word, she sprang up, but, ins:cad f the "cord," she seized hold of the briar pipe, and flung it out of the window, saying, as she did so, "Nasty thing." Not to be outdone. the , youth amide a grab at the dog, and threw him out of the window. Neither of them ever ex- pected to see that pipe again, or poor doggie alive, but, judge of the surprise of them both, when the train steamed -into Paddington Sta- tion an hour afterwards, there was the little black pu jig on the platform, wagging his tail, with the pipe in his mouth. _ - WILLIE Covraow (age 3 years). For further particulars see "Post Office Guide," at any Post Office. POSTAGE STAMPS. Books containing 12 penny and 23 halfpenny stamps are now on sale at each post office. Price 2s.

INLAND CORRESPONDENCE. The term" Inland Correspondence" means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels

o) (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be traus- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter pot, the only limitation being that of size.

_ TATTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows.:— Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... id. A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth. POST-CARDS.

_ The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card h one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 53 inches in length by 33 inckes in width, or be less than 3+ inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and finch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter.

div.head: HALFPENNY PACKET POST.
div.p: HALFPENNY PACKET POST.

The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz in weight. Printed matter, ,&c., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is id. a Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter. PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: Fora parcel ... ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 ft exceeding 1 lb. • 2 lb. 0 4 PI ff 2 lb. 9 I 3 lb. 0 5 r, „ 3 lb. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. 6in. in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. Gin. round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker ' • thus, if it measure no more than 3ft. in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel" Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sander should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving.

PARCELS .(FORTHGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. • MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d. •, £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 6d. ; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of ad. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. _ _

These are obtainable at ;;;;;;Vney order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by fid., from 6d. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are up to 2s. 6d.; Id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,colleb:ing and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d., which covers 12 words, and an additional id. for each extra word. 'This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is Li is. TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are, accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.

These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is .£1 or over, a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. Any amount up to and including £1 may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account Was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can bee xpedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegram!. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINE CHAIIGE9.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
MOUNTAINS AS MAGNETS.

Magnetic observations of the extinct vol- cano called the Puy de Dome, in Central France, have brought out the curious fact i that the mountain s magnetised not merely at certain points, but as a whole, the top of the dome acting as a south magnetic pole. Singularly enough, similar observations on the Kaiserstuhl, a mountain in Germany, in- dicate that it possesses a north magnetic pole at its summit.

div.head: GREAT SALT LAKE DENSITY.
div.p: GREAT SALT LAKE DENSITY.

Everybody knows that the water of the Great Salt Lake in Utah is very dense as well as very salt, but many will be surprised to learn that its density varies to a remark- able degree from time to time. For instance, in 1885 the density was 1.1223, aud the per- centage by weight of solid constituents was 16.716; in 1903 the density had increased to 1.2206, the greatest ever recorded, and the percentage of solids to 27721; in 1907 the density, had diminished to 1-1810, and the per- centage of solids to 22920. Of the solids in 1907, 12.67 per cent. was chlorin, 7.58 per cent. sodium, 153 per cent, sulphate radical, 0.72 per cent. potassium, 0.45 per cent. mag- nesium, and 0.04 per cent. calcium.

div.head: MAJESTIC ICE-WALL.
div.p: A MAJESTIC ICE-WALL.

In a letter from Professor Edgeworth Davis, a member of the British Antarctic Expedition to the South Pole, addressed to Professor W. J. Sollas, in England, there was a vivid description of the Great Ant- arctic Ice Barrier. "It is a sight," says Pro- fessor Davis, "that beggars all description. Imagine a continuous ice-wall, 500 miles long and 100 ft. to 2001 t. high, the exquisite blue of the crevasses contrasting finely with the dazzling white of the weathered ice on either side of them." They followed • the barrier eighty miles without finding a place where they could establish a base. " Balloon Inlet," used as a base by the expedition of 1901, had completely disappeared. Finally they went to MacMurdo Sound, as the only base now available.

div.head: RUBY GLASS.
div.p: RUBY GLASS.

In his book on "The World of the Infi- nitely Small," Professor Gruner, of Berne, gives an interesting account of ruby glass. Genuine ruby glass is expensive, because it is prepared with gold. It owes its colour to the presence throughout its mass of particlee of gold too small to be seen with the micro- scope. Only the 'ultramicroscope, which ren- ders visible objects perceptible by means of their diffusion of light, is able to shew the existence of these minute particles. With the ordinary microscope the glass appears as a uniform transparent mass, but the ultra- microscope shews that it is filled with points of light resembling stars on a black back- ground. These points indicate the presence of the particles of gold to which the colour of the glass is due.

div.head: WANTED-A METAL.
div.p: WANTED-A METAL.

Professor Henry Louis, adaressing the In. of Civil Engineers in London re- cently, said that one of the greatest needs at the present moment, in the industry of min- ing, is a metal that shall be strong, tough, and very considerably harder than quartz. The production of such a material, he be- lieved, would conduce more to the technical advancement of several branches of mining than almost any other discovery that could named. The metal is needed as a substi- tute for diamonds in drills. The only kind of diamonds suitable for this purpose are dark, opaque stones, shewing no cleavage, and known in the trade as carbons." They are very scarce, and proportionately dear. The chilled iron shot used of late years will not answer for the harder rocks.

div.head: GROWTH WITHOUT LIFE.
div.p: GROWTH WITHOUT LIFE.

At the British Association meeting Dr. Dawson Turner discussed growth due to osmosis, or growtS without life. He exhibited a specimen and photographs of the curious growths which Professor Leduc had produced by the purely physical process of osmosis, and explained that an artificial seed of one part of sugar and of two parts of copper sul- phate was sown in a 6 olution of gelatine and potassium ferro-cyanide. This seed began to grow as though it were alive: it might attain a height of lft. to 2ft.; and it presented organs analogous to those of vegetables, such as roots, stems, leaves, and terminal organs. Functions which had hitherto been con- sidered as _ characteristic of life, such as nutrition by intussusception, organisati)n, growth in thickness and in length, were thus realised by purely physical forces; and physiologists were therefore led to conjec- ture whether those functions in living plants and animals might not be aue to the same cause.

div.head: "BALLOON SICKNESS."
div.p: "BALLOON SICKNESS."

At a meeting of the French Biological So- ciety, MM. Crouzon and SOubies gave an ac- count of some experiments on balloon-sick- ness which they had carried out. They made a balloon ascent with the• object of testing the relative value of inhalation of pure oxygen and Agazotti's mixture for aeronauts, which consists of 87 per cent. oxygen and 13 per cent, carbon dioxide. One observer ex- perienced symptoms of sickness at a height of 13,282 ft., indicated by a pain at ,the back of the head and 'in the nape of the neck, fol- lowed by venous congestion of the face, drowstness, and mist before the eves when looking earthwards, and *a heavy 'feeling in the eyelids. At 14,7641 t. the breathing be- came panting, and on attempting to sit down the observer fMI to the bottom of the car At a height of 15,7481 t. to 16,401 ft. the ob- server was overcome with drowsiness; and did not reply to questions, which symptoms were rapidly removed -by the inhalation of gas, but they returned after a short interval. The symptoms were/removed equally well by means of Agazotti'd mixture. At a height of 14,922 ft. the latter removed the respiratory distress in about ten seconds•, but at it height of 16,000 ft. it - was found that oxygen alone was of any use.

div.head: GAS BY THE POUND.
div.p: GAS BY THE POUND.

A development 'in Germany which "should offer great possibilities in this country, says Chambers's Journal, is the supply of gas in cylinders adapted for the lighting of coun- try houses and rural districts. The gaa has been invented by Hermann Blau, a chemist, and is distilled from oil and other materials. Manufacture is carried out upon new and novel lines. The oil is fed into the retort and distilled at a. lower temperature than that employed in coal-gas manufacture. The by-products are secured, and the gas cleaned and scrubbed in the usual manner. It is then compressed at great pressure in cylinders similar to those employed for the transporta- tion of oxygen, the effect of this pressure being a liquefaction of the gases. • The permanent gases which distillation has yielded, such as hydrogen, methane, and car- bon monoxide, the chief constituents of coal- gas, are then dissolved to the required ex tent in the liquid gases. When the pressure is relieved the liquid volatilises, carrying off certain proportion of the gases which were dissolved. The light obtained is of great brilliancy, while the gas is

PERFECTLY PURE AND HARMLESS. The cylinders are of varkng lengths and capacity, it being pcosible to acquire a small vessel holding 11b. of gas, suitable for tra- velling, boating, or camping-out expeditions, up to large reservoirs containing heavy sup- plies suitable for extensive country seats. The medium size, adap4d for use in small villas, will supply enough gas to meet re- quirements for some eight weeks. All that it is necessary to do is to install the charged cylinder in the receptacle supplied for the purpose outside the building, connect it up to a small tank in which the pressure is regu- lated, and then admit it to the ordinary pip- ing-system of the house.: When a cylind3r is empty it can be easily and quickly disconnected, and a full cylinder replaced, the empty one being returned to ill works for a fresh charge. There is no possibility of explcsion, and no technical knowledge is necessary for its manipulation. The, only attention required is the ehamainu of the cylinders as they become exhausted. The system is cheap, highly efficient, and free from danger, and even the smallest vil- lages can become possessed of a complete gas-distribution plant at a nominal outlay.

Warrington Still Losing.

Warrington took a re-oganised team to Broughton on Saturday, the whole of the threequarters being "A" team players. Dickenson and Taylor were absent through injury, and some of the other regular hands were suspended for inattention to training. The team made a very plucky fight but had to submit to rdefeat from a better side. Fine weather prevailed and 7,000 people watched a fine, open game. Teams : Broughton Rangers—Barlow, back; Hardyman, Harris, C. James, and Hogg, threequarter backs; Stirrup and Flynn, half backs ; Ruddick, Grainey, Beetbam, Mottram, J. L. Clampitt, and R. Clampitt, forwards.

Warrington—Tilley, back : Bradshaw, Daintith, Landor, and Cartwright, threequarter backs ; Lloyd and Jenkins, half backs ; Belton, Nield, Dowell, Naylor, Hewitt and Chester, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. C. Lumley, Leeds. The game opened extremely fast. One of the." Wire- pullers" getting offside, Harris tried a place kick at goal, but the shot failed. Smart work followed, and Mottram was foiled when he seemed sure to score, but h Warrington man was penalised for not playing the ball, and Barlow easily kicked a goal. The Rangers were working well together, and some splendid passing took place, Harris falling at goal. The Rangers being penalised for offside play and obstruction, Landor and Tilley bad kicks at goal, but both shots went wide. Hardyman, who had been neglected up to this point, received the ball and made a capita run and passed to Beetham, who was pushed into touch. The Rangers had by far the better of the game, and Barlow,receiving the ball about 30 yards from the posts, coolly dropped a beautiful goal. This was followed by Hogg scoring another try from a well-judged pass by Harris' but the latter again failed to place a goal. Just before half- time Warrington bad another shot at goal, but Landor again failed. Half-time :—Rangers 3 goals 2 tries (10 points) ; Warrington nil. After the interval Warrington rallied and passed smartly, and Daintith raced over with an excellent try, I but injured himself in doing so, delaying the game for a few minutes. The goalkick failed. Then followed a sensational tackle by Barlow, who rushed up and charged Landor when nearing the line and prevented the latter scoring. Luck was against Warrington for Bradshaw seemed a scorer when after punting over the line, he was beaten in the race by Claude James. After scrambling play, Hogg mulled the ball and let in Cartwright, who scored cleverly, Landor again failing with the kick.

The forwards were playing a great game, the War- rington men with the greater zest, but the Rangers had the measure of their opponents, and Mottram got an excellent try. Barlow placing a goal, while the score was quickly added to, by Claude James, who completed a fine try, after dodging several of the Warrington backs. Barlow kicked n goal. Final : Rangers, 4 goals, 4 tries 20 points; Warrington, 2 tries 10 points.

div.head: WIGAN v. RUNCORN.
div.p: WIGAN v. RUNCORN.

Upwards of 15,000 spectators were present at Central Park to witness this match. The opening half was of an, even description, and the solitary goal which accrued was credited to Runcorn. Padbury, some 20 minutes from the start, taking a penalty kick, which resulted in the leather striking one of the uprights, and then rebounding over the tar. Immediately after the resumption, Creevey scored a fine try, and the points were augmented by Leytham landing the goal. In the subsequent play the home representatives gained a complete mastery, Thomas registering a try Leneath the cross-bar, though Leytdhm failed to add the goal points, whilst Creevey again bent tbe opposition, for Thomas to further increase the lead. Result :—Wigan 2 goals 3 tries (13 points), Runcorn 1 goal (2 points).

SWINTON V. ST. HELENS. At Swinton' before 4,(100 spectators. A very poor game resulted, play during the major part of the pro- ceedings being of a very scrappy a haracter. In marked contrast to previous matches, Swinton combined poorly, and the services of Fairhurst at half backwere sadly missed. Trenwith played a good game at half back for the Saints. The only score of the game was a goal dropped for Swinton by Walbrook. Result :—Swinton, 1 goal (2 points) ; St. Helens, nil.

div.head: WIDNES v. BARRY.
div.p: WIDNES v. BARRY.

Played at Widnes before 2,000 spectators. Widnes at once attacked and 0, Aspey dribbled over the line and scored. Jones placed a goal. A brilliant round of passing by the home backs ended in Ince getting over at the corner, bat the place-kick failed. %Vick:es con- tinued to have the best of matters, and more tries were scored by G. Aspey, Taylor and Hicks, while Jones placed two goals. Canter scored an unimproved try for Barry, after a scramble on the line. Half-time score : Widnes 3 goals and 5 tries (21 points), Barry 1 try (3 points). The game was more even in the second half. McCarthy and Lloyd crossed the line for Widnes, and Jones placed two goals. For Barry, Cheeseman scored an unimproved try. Result :—Widnes 5 goals aud 7 tries (31 points), Barry 2 tries (6 points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.

WARRINGTON "A " v. BROUGHTON' RANGIERS "A." Wariington recorded another victory on Saturday when they met Broughton Rangers "A" at Wilderspool befare a large crowd of spectators. The home side iucladed S.Lees who has now recovered from his injury sustained last season, and Lambert, of( Salford St. Bartholomew's, who on several occasions has assisted the Warrington Combination team. The" Wirepullers" early on showed smart combination, and clever work by Oakes and Lees set up a permanent attack. The visit- ing custodian failed to repel a forward rush, and llarmer scored near the posts, but Fonter failed with the place kick. From a smart croEa kick by Oakes, Harries gained a try at the corner, and Mclntyre succeeded in con- verting from near half-way. Broughton Rangers made spasmodic bursts, but there was really no sting in the attack and another raid on the visitors' goal ended in Rangers getting penalised and Mclntyre placed a goal. The Rangers opened their seore in a similar fashion and near the interval Oakes put on the finishing touch to a good passing movement. At the interval Warrington led by two goals three tries (13 points) to Broughton Rangers, one goal (two points). Turning round War- rington had again the best of ittand Kay scored cleverly. Broughton rallied and line passing led up to a try, but from this point the leaders had matters as they pleased and won by $l. points against Broughton Rangers five points.

div.head: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS
div.p: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS
111.—If Imports of manufactures cause unemployment and poverty, why not keep them out altogether instead of merely taxing them 10 per cent.

Tariff Reformers constantly assert that it is our imports of manufactured goods which cause unemploy- ment and pauperism. Yet Mr. Chamberlain's programme only proposes to tax such imports 10 per cent. Now a 10 per cent. duty would only very slightly reduce our imports of manufactures. This is proved by the fact that the imports of manufactured goods into America, which has very high duties, are very great; indeed, greater than our own. If the Dingley high tariff, averaging 70 per cent, on manufactures, does not keep imports out of America, how could Mr. Chamberlain's milk-and-water 10 per cent. tariff keep imports out of Britain? If, therefore, it is true that imports are the cause of -unemployment and pauperism, why not prevent these evils altogether by the simple expedient of prohibit- ing imports?

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. Friendly Societies and the Pensions Committee.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. Friendly Societies and the Pensions Committee.

_ Sir,—At the quarterly meeting of the Warrington Consolidated District No. 4, of the 'lndependent Order of Rechabites (S.U.) held on Saturday, October 24th, 1108, in Friars Green Schoolroom, it was agreed that the following resolution be sent to the press : "That this District of Friendly Society workers regrets the action of the Warrington Town Council, in deciding not to appoint any persons outside the Council on the Local Pensions Committee and expresses disappointment in not electing representa- tives from Friendly Societies and other kindred organizations in Warrington, and thus iv:oring the pro- visions of the Act, and hopes that a meeting of representatives of Friendly Societies in the town will be called together at an early date for the purpose of considering and presenting their claims on this subject." W. WRIGHT (District Trustee), T. MASSEY (District Treasurer), 30, Marshhouse-lane, Warrington.

The Publican and Religious Liberty. Sir,—The trade seem now to have tacked on to their political creed another cry—the cry of "religious liberty "—vote for the publican and "religious liberty." You want a pretty long spoon to eat out of the same dish with his Satanic Majesty, but I am afraid a very long noon will be required if a party consisting of brewers and publicans and religious workers sit down and eat together. Politics like adversity makes strange bed-fellows and at present we have Satan posing as an Angel of Light. The Tory teetotaller and the Tory publican unite under the umbrella of " religious liberty" to try to get at least one more pablican i into the Town Council. Our memory s not so dull that we do not recollect who led in the van of religious liberty in the past. Certainly the brewer and the publican will never move on the car of religious liberty one foot in its onward march of progress. Though I am not a Socialist or a believer in Socialism lam thoroughly convinced that on the present occasion the interests of the working- class,will be best served by supporting the Socialist candidates—Messrs. Hampson and Ball—at this elec- tion. They will not be Sancho Panzas to any party, but will fight for working-class interests and the cause of justice, truth, and sobriety.-1 am., PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: Thomas Morris Charity.
div.p: The Thomas Morris Charity.

--- Sir,— Will you permit me through the columns of the " Examiner" to lay some facts concerning the position of this charity before the charitably-disposed inhabit- ants of this tcrwn and its surroundinr, neighbourhood? The sum of £l,OOO was left by the late Mr. Thomas Morris to be invested, and the proceeds to be distributed in the shape of blankets, flannel or other warm clothing to " all old women of the borough of Warrington, over GO years of age, not in receipt of parochial relief." The Inland Revenue Commissioners, out of their usual kindness of heart, made us pay a duty of £5O, so that there was only left £950, which was invested in the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and brings in a gross yearly income of about £27. The trustees are the Rev. Canon Willis, M.A., rector of Warrington; the Rev. John Yonge, of Wycliffe Church; the Rev. Father Neville Wilson, rector of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, and myself. For many years the number of applicants has far exceeded the outside number of blankets, &c., that could be given, and we have relunctantly had to disappoint the greater portion of most deserving widows. This year we have had 240 applications, all of which comply with therterms of the trust, and all are recommended most highly by the different clergy of all denominations, magistrates, and doctors and other leading townsmen, whose names subscribed to the applications are genuine guides to the trustees as showing the applicants to be most worthy of help from the charity. The trustees met on Monday last, and unfortunately could only elect 03 old women for blankets and 37 for red flannel petticoats, thereby cnly granting 100 applications out of the 210, most of whom are either absolutely dependent upon sons or married daughters for their maintenance and lodging, and the trustees concurred in my suggestion that I should lay these facts before your readers, and to ask if any of them will kindly send me a cheque towards gratifying the wishes of the 146 old ladies, who for the present are left out of the charity through no fault of their own. We reckon that if we received, say, about £25, we could satisfy such number with blankets or warm clothing. Any subscriptions, therefore, sent to me will be grate- fully acknowledged. I may add that we obtain the red flannel petticoats from Mrs. Joseph Harrison's Society, so that we there- by assist another most deserving charity, and the only cost of carrying through the work of the Thomas Morris Charity is for printing and postaa'es, as the routine work is gladly done by myself and staff voluntarily.— Yours, &c., ARTHUR BROWNE, Corresponding Trustee. 67, Sankey-street, Warrington. 29th October, 1903.

div.head: FALL FROM A TRAIN.
div.p: FALL FROM A TRAIN.
Passenger's Miraculous Escape at
Warrington.

An extraordinary accident occurred on the railway near Warrington on Thursday, resulting in serious injuries to Alexander Mortimer, a single man, 41 years of age, residing at 50, Dundas-street, Glasgow. It appears that he left London from Euston Station by the two o'clock express. The train passes through Warrington at 5.52 at the rate of CO miles an hour, the first stop being Preston. It is supposed that the man was leaning on the carriage door when it flew open, or that he mistook the door for that of the lavatory door, and fell out when the train was approaching Walton New Junction. He was dragged a distance of GO yards, and both heels of his boots were torn off. He lay on the line on the railway embankment in an unconscious condition for four hours, and subsequently crawled to the signal box at Walton. His face was covered with Mood, and he had sustained serious injuries all over the body and head. He was taken to the infirmary, where he was attended hy Dr. W. S. M'Cune. He is suffering from wounds and contusions all over the body, the most serious being on the head. "How he escaped being knocked to bits," said Dr. M'Cune, " I don't know." When it was discovered that the unfortunate man was

missing the communication cord was pulled, and the train drew up at Winwicir. The line was searched carefully up to Warrington, but before the party arrived at Walton the man had got to the signal box. He is said to be an ex-railway employ from India.

The Chamber of Commerce and Warrington Bridge. At a meeting of the Council of the Chamber of Commerce, held at Market Gate Chambers on Thurs- day last, the delay in widening Warrington Bridge was again discussed, and it was unanimously resolved '` That, in the opinion of this Council, the construc- tion of a new bridge across the Mersey, capable of adequately accommodating the increasing traffic on both road and river, has long been an urgent necessity and they again respectfully request the Corporation to take the earliest possible opportunity.of dealing with the matter in a bold and comprehensive spirit."
