div.head: WOMEN LIBERALS. 1 ANNUAL TEA AND CONCERT AT WARRINGTON. Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.
div.p: WOMEN LIBERALS. 1 ANNUAL TEA AND CONCERT AT WARRINGTON. Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P.

The Warrington Women's Liberal Association, which is one of the most active and useful of our local pro- gressive organizations, held its annual tea meeting and concert in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening, and the function proved a complete success. About 170 sat down to tea, the catering being in the hands of the Winmarleigh Cafe, Co. At the concert the members had the pleasure of a visit from Mr. A. H. Crosfleld, M.P. and Mrs. Crostield, and the member, although suffering from a severe cold, delivered lan interesting speech. Mr. C. E. Parker presided, and amongst others present were :—Mrs. Ziba Armitage (president of the Association), Mrs. Parker (vice- president), Mrs. Osborne (hon. secretary), Mrs. Walker (bon. treasurer), Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Councillor Locker, Mr. and Nlrs.a. Owen,Mr. W. Clegg, Mr. George Walker, Mr.E.England,Mr.and Mrs.J. Elwell, Mr. Joseph Howes, and Mr. Joseph Howes, jun.—A capital musical programme was submitted, including songs by Miss Cox, violin solo by Mrs. Haviour, pianoforte solos by Mrs. Crosfield and Mrs. Holmes, and a pianoforte duet by Hrs. Parker and Mrs. Holmes. MRS. OSBORNE'S REPORT.

During an interval Mrs. O,BORNE presented an inter- esting report on the annual meeting of the Council of the Women's Liberal Federation held in the -Memorial Hall, London, in May. It stated that since last year 32 associations had joined the Federation, making the total number of affiliated associations 635, with an approximate total membership of 01,62 L There had been upwards of 600 public meetings held by associa- tions, and never before had there been so much enthusiasm thrown into the work. That association was represented by Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Clegg, Miss Walker, and herself. The Memorial Hall was packed by delegates when the Countess of Carlisle took the chair. The declaratory resolution, which reads as follows :—" This Council declares its adhesion to those great principles which have been passed with practical unanimity for so many years by delegates assembled in Council, including Home Rule for Ireland, Welsh Dis- eqablishment, the Abolition of the Veto of the House of Lords and of the hereditary principle of that Chamber, the Settlement of International Disputes by Arbitration,hostility to every form of Official or State Regulation of Immorality, and the Amendment of the Divorce Act of 1857," was carried unanimously. The following resolution was passed This council affirms its adherence to the principles of

FREE TRADE, and urges upon all Women's Liberal Associations the necessity of holding meetings and doing educational work to combat the insidious proposals of the tariff reformers, and to show, by their action, that Liberal women are determined to resist them by every means in their power. It expresses its undiminished belief that any form of Protection or preferential tariffs would be disastrous to the well-being of the people, reduce the standard of living, and aggravate the evil of unemploy- ment; and further, would conduce to dissatisfaction among the Colonies, and be inimical to the interests of the Empire as a whole." Discussion was then con- centrated upon

_ THE LICENSING BILL. The following resolution was moved and seconded : "This Council heartily welcomes the Government's great and comprehensive measure of licensing reform, and assures his Majesty's ministers of the steadfast and enthusiastic support of Liberal women in their endeavour to carry it into law. At the same time, this Council expresses the hope that it may be found possible to strengthen the provisions of the Bill with regard to clubs, in the direction of national Sunday closing and the statutory exclusion of children from the bars of licensed premises." This, with the addition of the following amendments, was carried : "And deprecates any reduction of the time limit. After 'children ' insert' up to the age of 16.' Add at end 'and that associatiqns be urged to hold meetings in its support.' " On the question of Bird Protection, the meeting urged the necessity of legislation to prevent the wholesale destruction of bird life for the purpose of personal adornment. It was well known that women were the biggest sinners in that respect. (Laughter.) A resolution were passed in sup- port of the Government Education Bill, as fairly main- taining the principles of public control and no tests for teachers and providing a fair,kolution of the religious difficulty. The
OLD AGE PENSIONS Bill was cordially welcomed as the first step towards meeting the circumstances of the aged toilers. Dealing with the question of

THE UNEMPLOYED, the report said : Considerable discussion took place over the next resolution dealing with unemployment ; "That this meeting of the Women's Liberal Federation, while expressing satisfaction at the progress being made towards helping the unemployed, nevertheless urges the Government so to legislate as to make it possible for all those willing to work to secure employ- ment and under fair conditions." One lady caused the assembly to laugh derisively by stating that the Government ought to build more battleships. It was explained, however, by Lady Carlisle that the delegate came from Chatham, and then there was more laughter. The delegate who proposed an amendment welcoming Mr. Asquith's announcement that when the Poor Law Com- mission has issued its report the Government hopes to bring before Parliament some practical method of dealing with the chronic and most pressing problem of unemployment, declared emphatically that labour must earn its wage. We must make it able to earn its wage, we must not put it in competition with labour that does not earn its wage. If you do that you penalize the consumer. The amendment was carried. A resolution urging the Government to further legisla- tion and regretting the general statement of the President of the Local Government Board that the work of married women must be seriously curtailed, and expressing the opinion that each Parliamentary Bill which regulates the labour of women should be judged on its merits was carried, and concluded the business of the second day. On Thursday morning Lady Carlisle spoke on the Prime Minister's reply to the deputation of the Liberal M.P's. on the WOMEN SUFFRAGE QUESTION. The deputation consisted of about GO M.P.'s and was introduced by Mr. Stanger who asked for facilities for the further stages of his Women's Suffrage Bill during the session or for some promise that before the close of the present Parliament the Government would either deal with the question themselves, or allow the House to do so. After quoting Mr. Asquith's reply the report proceeds : The resolution which was to have been moved from the chain behalf of the Executive Com- mittee was withdrawn under the circumstances, by leave of the Council. Instead, the following resolution was moved from the chair and carried non con. :—" This Council rejoices that an Electoral Reform Bill is to be introduced by the Government before this Parliament is dissolved, and thanks the Prime Minister for his pledge that when an amendment to that Bill in favour of the enfranchisement of women is brought forward in the House of Commons, the Government could not, and certainly would not oppose such a proposal, provided that the change was upon democratic lines." The following resolution : "This Council, having regard to the urgent need of every Liberal Member of Parlia- ment being a firm supporter of the principle of the enfranchisement of women, urges affiliated assoclations, before they work at elections, to secure that the Liberal candidate shall make a declaration in favour of women's suffrage in his address, or that he shall give a definite pledge in his election speeches to support this measure of justice to women" together with the following riders : " And this Council further trusts that the associations will spare no effort to secure the return of those Liberal Members of Parliament who have in the past given earnest support to women's enfranchisement; "That this Council urges each affiliated association to approach the Central Liberal Executive in its constituency, with the object of securing the co-operation of such Central Executive bodies in making this pledge a sine qua non of the adoption by them of their respective candidates," was carried by a large majority. She had emphasized the question of women's suffrage, because it naturally appealed to them most. They had no desire to be out- rageous in their demands or inconsiderate in their actions seeing that the Prime Minister had pledged himself to include women suffrage on democratic lines in the next scheme of reform of the present electoral system. They held him by his promise knowing that he was an honourable man and would not fail them. The delegates had the pleasure of being invited to the House of Commons by Mr. Crosfield, and of taking tea with one of their newly-elected vice-presidents, whom they were all delighted to have with them that night, viz., Mrs. Arthur Crosfield. (Applause.)

div.head: PRAISE FOR THE ASSOCIATION.
div.p: PRAISE FOR THE ASSOCIATION.

The CHAIRMAN congratulated Airs. Osborne on her excellent report. The Women's Liberal Association, under the able leadership of Mrs. Armitage and others, did a grand work at the last election. (Hear, hear). It might be that the enthusiasm naturally went down somewhat between the elections, but it was for the members to show that they thoroughly believed in the principles which they then espoused. Let there be On the part of the Women's Liberal Association no dropping of the Liberal flag, but rather let them keep it aloft. They enthusiastically supported Mr. Crosfleld and put him in Parliament. They very enthusiastically, supported him when he took another very important step and got married. (Laughter and applause). He (Mr. Parker) 'remembered at one of their meetings, repudiating any responsibility in regard to that union but Mrs. Crostleld had so won them all over—and in fact bad so won the whole town over—that he thought everybody in Warrington would be prepared to make themselves responsible for the wisdom of Mr. Crosfleld's choice and the happiness of the union. (Applause.) It was a great pleasure to them to have Mr. and Mrs. Crosfleld with them that night. (Applause.) The member unfortunately, was suffering from a sore throat, and he had asked him (Mr. Parker) to preside in his stead. They hoped, however, that his throat trouble
would not prevent him saying a few words and they would all be glad to listen to anything he might have to say. (Applause.)
MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., who had a very hearty reception, said he felt it a privilege and a great pleasure to be allowed to say a few words to that admirable gathering of Warrington Liberal women. Mrs. Osborne in the excellent report which they had , , all listened to with great interest had covered a great deal of ground. There was a very significant allusion to the question of the unemployed and he imagined that not any of the other important questions that they had on their minds and which were before them for administration and for legislative work in the future, could compete with unemployment in regard to the seriousness and far-reaching importance of that grave problem. Speaking the other day at the Liberal Club he said that

_ UNEMPLOYMENT would be, with the licensing question, in the minds of of everybody at Westminster and he could assure them that all that one heard in the House and in the lobby amply confirmed that. They were dealing this year with palliatives. He hoped there might not be urgent need, but if we were in for hard times it was possible that those palliatives might have to be extended during the coming winter—extended somewhat beyond the splendid and important statement made by the Prime Minister the other day. He was sure everyone in Warrington had noticed the significant conclusion of that statement; how the Prime Minister said that while at present they were dealing, as they were bound to deal, with palliatives, faced with the urgency of this question, this Parliament was not going to be content with that and before it brought its work to a conclusion, efforts would have been made to cut at the roots of the whole problem of unemploy- ment. (Applause.) He said "roots "advisedly because they were all well aware that there was no single panacea or remedy for this great evil. Personally he called it nothing better than humbug to pretend that there was any single remedy —(hear, hear)—and he was bound to say he was glad that both Mr. Balfour and Mr. Long had made some pretty significant remarks in that connection which perhaps it would be well for local politicians to bear in mind. (Hear, hear.) He believed that meeting, as much as any assembly in Warrington would agree with him that one of the greatest efforts they could make to cut at the root of unemployment was to be found in the great and brave attempt the Prime Minister had made to deal with the question of licensing reform. (Applause.) In the report Mrs. Osborne presented she evidently amused most of those present by a slight reference to ladies' dress. "I don't mind confessing," said Mr. Crostield, " that I have realized the extent of masculine ignorance on the subject of ladies' dress much more fully in the last few months than I ever did before. (Laughter.) I dare say it is rather rash, therefore, to attempt any metaphor founded upon ladies' dress, but I am going to do it. (Laughter.) With regard to THE LICENSING BILL one hears amongst people of many different shades of opinion,—moderate temperance reformers and very advanced temperance reliormers—the view expressed that while this Bill is a splendid measure and one that will carry the country—(applause)—it would have been just as well not to tack on one or two ques- tions that are included in it. I can assure you Ido not think you have the least reason to disturb yourselves or to be uneasy on that account, for this reason : I have noticed that if a lady gets a very nice dress, sometimes little additions are made—a frill goes on here and there— (laughter)—and no doubt they are very nice and becom- ing. (Laughter.) But still, if a frill disappears and little changes are made, the dress remains and is still a good one. (Laughter). So with this licensing measure, it is possible that one or two frills dealing with questions that may be settled by Parliament twenty-one years hence, may be removed by the House of Lords. I am not saying this by way of criticising the Bill at all, but where people are dis- satisfied on that account I would ask them just to con- sider that there are a few questions—very important, it is true, but not quite essential to the main principle of that great Bill—which may possibly be amended in another place, but if those frills disappear the dress will still remain and the Bill will be a splendid one." (Applause.) Continuing, Mr. Crosfleld said he did not think they should attach too much importance to all the noise they heard in demonstrations against the Bill. He fancied there were a good many people connected with the liquor trade, and many people not a hundred miles from Warrington, who thought there was a good deal in the measure which should commend itseW to all fair-minded English men and women. (Applause.) They did not always say so, but public utteaance and private cogitation were sometimes not the same thing, (Laughter.) Allusion had been made in the report to what was really a very signal achievement by Mr. Herbert Samuel—the great Children's Bill, which one might very fairly call "THE CHILDREN'S CIIIRTE " —(applause)—for it covered so much ground and included so many admirable and excellent clauses. It would be out of place for him to attempt to enumerate all that the Bill did, for he was sure most of those present were more capable of appreciating the advantages of its various provisions than he was. At the same time he would instance one or two of the proposals embodied in the Bill. A certain amount of fun had been made—he had heard Mr. Balfour make fun of it and other people in the country had done the same thing—of the limitation of smoking, the object of which was to prevent boys under sixteen indulging in the pernicious habit of cheap cigarettes. Such smoking had done a lot of mischief and he was sure that if that provision was a humble illustration of the work of the Government it was nevertheless an example of a kind of work that would have the support of the members of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association.(Applause.) Another reform which was still more important was that it would now be impossible for any boy of fourteen and practically impossible for a boy of sixteen to be taken either to the Police Court or to prison. Lads who were convicted of petty offences were dealt with in another way and therefore spared coming into contact with penal contamination. If one con- sidered how long it was since America and some of our Colonies dealt with juvenile offenders in that way so as not to demoralize them, the only wonder was that we 1 in England had not done it long ago. (Hear, hear). We were doing practical things of that kind now that we had a practical Govetnment in power—a Government that laid itself out for real genuine, practical social reform. (Applause). Passing from children to the older offenders, there was another reform that Mr. Herbert Gladstone had in hand at the present time. Where a criminal of over sixteen was I convicted, instead of being kept in prison he might be treated under the Borstal system which gave him a ! chance of leading a better life if he so desired,and if he : did his duty and pulled himself together he might cease ' to be detained, be taken in hand by friends and saved from drifting into A life of permanent iniquity. (Hear , hear.) Of course, if a man would not take advantage I of the opportunities given to him' he was liable to • be sent back to prison and suffer the consequences. Therefore they saw that every inducement both cif hope , and of fear was given to men who came within the arra : of the law, to reform and lead a better life. He hoped they would think that, coupled with the legislation on behalf of children which covered all the questions of 3 infant life, over-laying, risk of burning and all ill- treatment of that kind which had been carried to terrible lengths in some parts of the country, the reforms I he had indicated were linked together, a step in the right direction. (Applause.) For many years past, continued Mr. Crosfleld, one had watched the develop- ! ment of opportunities for women in so many different spheres of life. In business, in the professions, in all : that was embraced in the world of art, and in many other spheres of activity a silent though none the less t certain

EMANCIPATION OF WOMAN had been going on which to his mind was an illustra- tion, if he might borrow for a moment the language of Matthew Arnold, of "that stream of tendency that makes for justice." No man who was not utterly selfish could fail to look upon that great development as perhaps the most important onward step in the march of civilization. He had heard, of course, in the House of Commons the further question of female suffrage discussed from many points of view. While I not wishing to say anything dogmatic that night, there ' were a few points he would like to place before them for consideration. He had alluded to the opportunities , that women now possessed even in the world of busi- ness. If under the heading of business was included manual work, one felt certain that as time went on there would be not only a division of labour which they were bound to have in business between men and women but also a revision of labour. Mr.Slaackleton made some ' very striking remarks on that point towards the end of 1 last week, and he (Mr. Crosfield) was sure they must all I hope that as man got more control over machinery, as the instruments of production gradually reduced the cost of manufacture, there would be less need, in the rougher kinds of work, at any rate, to call upon married women to take part, and that it would also be possible gradually to eliminate a great deal of the child labour 1 that we had in our midst—(hear, hear)—so as to give better opportunities for education in early life, and in a measure to withdraw a certain amount of undesirable competition from the labour market. On the other hand, there were many kinds of physical work now being done by women which they would probably con- tinue to do and which might even be extended with very great advantage, so that while there would no doubt be considerable revision of the present division of labour, both in physical and mental work, he felt convinced that the division of labour would remain. They knew that in the future women would play a greater part not only in the realms of business and art but in the sphere of politics than they were playing to-day. He did not under-estimate the influence and importance of the work done by women in politics now, for it was a great force and a great power in the country,but he for one earnestly hoped that that power and influence might be greatly increased. The point be would, however, like them to consider was a difficult one, the extent to which that increa,se was to be carried. The
The Examiner, Saturday, October 31, 1908.

div.head: EMMANUEL CHURCH.
div.p: EMMANUEL CHURCH.
Annual Sale of Work.
THE CHURCH AND SOCIAL ENJOYMENTS.

Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church is fortunate in possessing an active band of workers who every year throw themselves whole-heartedly into the labours involved in the preparation for the sale of work which is one of the principal means of raising funds to support the various church activities. When this year's sale opened in the Church Institute, Knutsford- road, on ~(ednesnay afternoon, it was evident that every effort had been put forth to ensure its success, for the stalls were laden with a tempting array of use- ful and fancy wares and the appearance of the room was most inviting. The stallholders were :—No. 1 stall, Mrs. Vaughan and friends ; No. 2, Mrs. A. Gandy and friends ; No. 3, Mrs. A. Booth and friends; No. 4 (refreshments), Mr. T. Allen and friends ; No. 5 (flowers and fruit), Miss Ada Bibby and friends ; No. G, Miss N. Gandy and friends; tea room, Mrs. E. Allen and friends ; Bah pond, &c., Miss 51. Booth and friends. The incumbent (Rev. F. Vaughan) opened the sale on I Wednesday afternoon, Mr. J. Bibby presidiog. I The CHAIRMAN said it took about £450 a year to I keep up the work of the Church and its various organiza- tions. Most of their organizations were self-supporting and paid their way, but the Church was entirely dependent on the voluntary offerings of the congrega- tion and the proceeds of the sale of work—in fact the sale was the backbone of the Church as far as raising the finances was concerned. Last year it realized 1120 after paying expenses, and this year they hoped to obtain £l5O, so that after allowing for Church expenses, they might be able to devote something to the reduction of I the debt on the Institute. (Applause). The Rev. F. VAUGHAN said their first duty must be the raising of their Ebenezer, because hitherto the Lord had helped them. For twenty-seven years that Church had carried on its work in Warrington, and many of those present had witnessed the growth of its work and enterprise, and the extension of its influence in the town. There was a tendency in these days, and there had been for some years, to raise money for spiritual work in ways which did not commend themselves to careful students of the word of God. They believed that throughout the history of that church every penny had been raised in such a way that they were not ri..hamPol to associate it with the most sacred phases of their church's enterprise. They had no endowment fund and not one single penny had been drawn from any society or any other source, except the voluntary offerings of the people. They had not even the time honoured pew rents. To say that they had been able to succeed and progress in the way they had done was a cause of very great thanksgiving. They claimed that their church was assisting to purify,to cleanse and to keep clean the moral atmosphere of the town. They were united with all their Christian brethren in deepening religious susceptibilities and stirring in the minds of young men and others a realization of the lofty purposes for which they had been sent into the world. They were witnessing against any unholy alliance between God-dishonouring and sinful practices and any public profession of the religion of the New Testament. Was there any need for Emmanuel Church to-day? He met Churchpeople in the town occasionally—very occasionally because as a rule they passed by on the other side—and found there was a notion in their minds that there was no need for Emmanuel Church from the point of view of Churchmanship. He wanted to say most definitely that the Reformed Episcopal Church was not a new sect. They claimed to be in fashion and in spirit a continuation of the most glorious days of the Established Church. They claimed to be a continua- tion of Protestant Evangelical Churchmanship and they stood in this town as a protest against priesteraft in every form and under whatever name it might present itself. They objected strongly to any compromise with Romanism as an "jam." They had nothing whatever to do as a Church with political party or anything of that kind. They stood pledged to the Word of God and anything they did they claimed they could justify by the spirit of that Word and by the best portions of the history of the nation. Mr. Vaughan referred to the large numbers of Churchpeople who were out of reach of the Church of England and never went near the churches,and said that if Emmanuel Church did nothing but appeal to them, there was still some work for it to do. Those people desired and appreci- ated the doctrines and the form of worship to which the Reformed Church were pledged. Without thinking one unkind thought or saying one unkind word about those who thought in other grooves, they claimed from

div.head: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE DEMONSTRATION IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE DEMONSTRA- TION IN MANCHESTER.

On Friday, October 23rd, a large meeting was held in Manchester to uphold the cause of Women's Suffrage. The Free Trade Hall in which it was held, is at all times a bailding of unusual beauty, bet on the night of the demonstration it looked more beautiful than ever with its artistic Suffrage banners and floral decorations.

At 7.30 Miss Ashton took the chair, and with her on the platform • there were, besides the speakers, such interesting personages as Mrs. Elmy, a beautiful old lady with sweet blue eyes aud white curls ; Mr. C. P. Scott, editor of the " Manchester Guardian," whose wife was one of the Girton pioneers ; and Mrs. Swanwick, who is the honorary secretary of the North of England Suffrage Society. Proceedings began with a son°. : " Of whole heart cometh hope," to the tune of "'For ever with the Lord," to the organ accompaniment of Miss Margaret Furness. Miss Ashton then made her opening speech and told how numbers of Members of Parliament had been invited to sit on the platform that night, and all save one, had refused. She said they would not have dare to absent themselves if they had been invited to a meeting by electors. Lord Courtney of Penwrith,was then introduced,and moved a reaolution in favtur of Wornen's Suffrage. His speech was largely retrospective and he recalled the fact that when John Stuart Mill had introduced a Bill into the House of Commons in favour of the Suffrage about half a century ago, he Lad been greeted with smiles of derision. Mrs. Despard s:conded the motion in a stirring, earnest speech, and told how she had refused to pay her taxes because taxation without representation was tyranny. Mr. Stanger, M.P., supported the resolution in a speech of dry humour. He hit hard at men who got women to work for them in politics and then said they were incapable of voting. He dealt with the inconsistencies of the Anti-Suffrago Manifesto, and gave it as his opinion that Mr. Asquith's promise about the suffrage was satisfactory. Speeches were then delivered by Mrs. Bury and Miss Abadam. Miss Abadam brought out an import- ant point. It had been proposed by a responsible 1 person that work should be taken from IN omen to give Ito unemployed men. In accents of fiery indignation she pointed out that the right to work was the right to be honest.

On Saturday, October 24th, Manchester had a Women's Suffrage procession. About 4,000 men and women walked in it, and the streets were thronged with sympathetic crowds. In Alexandra Park numbers of platforms sere erected. Here the Suffragists aildressed the crowds, each platform dealing with a different subject. Mrs. Despard spoke on "Social Ethics," Mrs. Billington Greig on "Prison Reform," Canon Hicks on "Temperance," and so on. The whole demonstration ought to do the cause a great amount of good. People are at least learning to know what Suffragists are aiming at, and when once they understand that, the cause is practically won.
.L.F.W.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
WILLIAM F. GRANT.
Who plays Jack Meredith in " With Edged Tools."
"NEXT WEEK'S PROGRA.MAk.

-.- Next week Messrs. 11. Armitage and Arthur Leigh's company will present the late Henry Seton Merriman's " With Edged Tools " a tale of love and adventure. Messrs. Armitage and Leigh found out what the public wanted when they toured Wilson Barrett's " Lucky Durham "and Charles Frohrnan's greatest success " Leah Kleschna " and in " With Edged Tools " they have again hit the nail on the head. It is adapted from one of the gems of English literature, in a word from Henry Seton Merriman's masterpiece, a novel which has been read by over 2,000,000 people. No novel can attain such popularity unless there be that in it, which appeals to all classes. It is a combination of good writing, tense situations, and sound common sense, and it makes a good fascinating play of love and adventure. Miss Phillis Relph plays Jocelyn Gordon, and Mr. William F. Grant who will be remembered here for his performances in Lucky Durham_and Leah Kleschna plays "Jack Meredith
_ a part which gives great scope for his well-known abilities. Others in the caste are : Mr. Campbell Goldsmid, Mr. Rosier, Mr. Hartopp, Miss Isabel Grey and Miss Marie Leonhard.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
" By Ova Mt."

Warrington's defeat at Broughton by 20 points to 6 seems to have given many people the idea that the team was outclassed. As a m'itter of fact the score does not in the least represent the game. The Warrington men were all triers and gave the Rangers a very lively time. In fact, ten minutes after the interval they looked like turning the tables completely on the home club, for they scored two tries in quick succession and both Bradshaw and Lander had hard luck in not crossing the line also. The Rangers got the next five points through a mistake by the referee, for the- scorer was certainly a lot off side. The final try by Claude James was a good one, but not much could be said for the rest of the Rangers' exploits.

Some of the young " A " Learners on the Warrington side played surprisingly well and were by no means out of their class. Bradshaw did brilliant work at times, and gave promise of making a fine wing. Daintith played a better game at centre than ever he did at half, while Landor was also a success. The weak man of the line was Cartwright, who seems to have lost all his early form. If Brooks had been able to go in Cart- wright's place the result might have been different for Hogg twice got past Cartwright when he. might have been pushed into touch. Jenkins was a long way the best half, and the forwards played a rare game, especially in the second half. O'Neill, Dowell, Chesters and Hewitt were the pick, the ex-Cardiff player making more than one opening for the backs. The worst feature of the team was the want of a goal- kicker, though Tilley and Lindor both made good attempts.

It should not be long before Warrington have a capable side, and begin to win matches. Some of the juniors are showing rare promise, and if another class back can be secured there should not be much evidence of weakness in any department. The return of S. Lees and Lambert should make a considerable difference to the playing strength of the club. Both of them played a brilliant game against the Rangers " A " on Saturday, and a thrashing by 31 points to ,5 was rather a surprise to the Manchester men. Lees showed all his old cleverness with the ball, and he will be welcomed back to the senior team. Neither Brooks nor Jenkins can work the " scrum " satis- factorily.

I should think Warrington have just about touched bottom now. With only two wins and a draw out of nine engagement; their percentage could not he very much worse. At present they are in the excel- lent company of Barry and Mid-Rhondda !
The League table, including Saturday's results, is as fellows : For Per _

To-day's match ought to provide an easy and certain two points. Merthyr were easily beaten by Warrington during the Welsh tour and should, there- fore, have little chance of success at Wilderspool. The home team still presents rather a peculiar appearance with such names as Fish, Dickenson, Taylor, and the two Boardmans all missing. Some of the old hands will hays to do hard training before they are selected. The Committee are determined to deal firmly with all shirkers in future, and those men who won't keep themselves fit, won't play!

George Thomas has returned to the fold this week, looking much thinner but hard as nails. He has been chosen to play to-day and has only to reproduce his old form to become a farrourite once more with the Wilderspool crowd.

The team was chosen on Tuesday night, as follows : Tilley, full back ; Bradshaw, Landor, Daintith, and A. N. Other, threequarters ; Lees and Jenkins, half backs ; Dowell, Thomas, Cheaters, Harmer and Naylor, forwards.

The " A.N. Other" turns out o ha Lewis Treharne the Wigan three-quarter, who was signed on by the Warrington Committee on Thursday evening, and will play against Merthyr to-day. Treharne is a speedy wing and a good footballer, but like Creevy, Gunn and David he was unable to get a secure place on the Wigan first team. He is 51t 81in. tall, and 11 stones 21b. in weight, and hopes to do Warrington good service. By the way, though Treharne went from Wales to Wigan he comes of Cornish stock as his name suggests.

div.head: KANGAIZOOS' FIRST DEFEAT.
div.p: THE KANGAIZOOS' FIRST DEFEAT.

The Kangaroos met with defeat at Leigh on Wednesday in the eighth match of their tour. The All Blacks reached their tenth match before they found a team which could beat them at Wigan. Leigh are entitled to credit for having inflicted the first defeat on the Australians, but they were by no means the best team. Truth to tell, the tourists were unfor- tunate. They played a capital game, they outclassed Leigh in speed and combination, and yet they lost. Moreover, at half-time they were leading by 11 points to six. Leigh got one try out of four as the result of combination. The other three were, more or less, gifts, and in the opinion of most people not partisans, the one which decided the Match was yards off-side. Mr. McCutcheon refereed excellently, but I think he was caught napping in this instance.

ft was a fine game to watch—brimful of incident, and carried on at a tremendous speed. The Kangaroos showed better form in combination than on any previous occasion, and are plainly settling down into a very powerful side. Messenger was everywhere, as usual,and some fine football was shown by Devereux, Frawley, and Bolewski, the full back doing some wonderful attacking work in the last quarter when the side was " all out " to win. Clarkson, Bennett and Johnson were the best of the Leigh backs, while O'Neill stood out conspicuously among the forwards. Bate was slow.

There was a huge crowd for a Leigh match, especi- ally in mid-week,and if there were plenty of unemployed with time on their hands they must have had shillings too. The whole town seemed to be on holiday for the occasion.

If a cold needs subjugation, Pray beware procrastination, Or you'll merit objurgation, For t'will lead to something worse ! If Woods' Peppermint Cure's not sent for, Curing colds is what it's meant for, Then your life's not worth a cent, for You will shortly need a hearse.—Advt.

div.head: MR. BLECKLY AND TARIFF REFORM. CRITICISMS BY MR JAMES COX.
div.p: MR. BLECKLY AND TARIFF REFORM. CRITICISMS BY MR JAMES COX.

In the November number of "The Ironworkers' Journal," Ur. James Cox, the secretary for the Iron and Steel Workers' Association, writes as follows : From three separate and independent sources have had a report of the annual meeting of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles forwarded to me with the remarks of Mr. W. H. Bleckly on" Fiscal Reform" specially marked. As a rule I take little or no notice of all the fantastic fairy tales put forward by directors at these annual gatherings of shareholders, though I must confess they make very entertaining reading. In the first place I want to congratulate the chairman —Mr. J. S. Harmood Banner —upon the matter and manner of his speech. It rather reads almost like a half apology for a 15 per cent dividend and certainly a good reserve fund ; but to wind up with a state- ment that " They would be quite content with lower dividends " deserves the Victoria Cross straight away. Mr. W. H. Bleckly begins his speech by reminding his audience that it is not the first time he has called their attention to this Fiscal question. That is quite correct; in fact the annual meeting of this firm would be quite lost without this hardy annual of Fiscal Reform being accorded a very prominent place. Some of us would rub our eyes and wonder whether the end had come if our old friend Fiscalities was left out in the cold. There is a delightful tit .bit to begin with, which must have made the shareholders smile both sides of their face. I quote from " The Examiner" : "He (Mr. Bleckly) had repeatedly called their attention to the great misfortune it had been to the trade of this country that the subject of Fiscal Reform was made a party question—as it was a trade affair pure and simple. Quite so! I have been saying that for years. I insisted upon that over and over again when I dealt with this subject in nearly every iron making district throughout the country. I said to workmen everywhere (including those of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles) "hang politics if you like, but here is a question affecting our labour, our wages—and the purchasing- power of our wages ; this to us is a question of work and living—it's our bread and cheese, and as such we must get to the bottom of it and see all that it means to us as workmen. Not only must we examine the effect of this upon us in the works but out of them as well. A man's life consists of something else besides Labour —at any rate some of us are men enough to think so—therefore we will examine this question not only from the standpoint of work but living as well." What I want to ask Mr. Bleckly is :—Who made this a party question? Who drove out of their midst those stalwarts of Free Trade whose judgment, whose ability, whose patriotism could not be questioned, and sacrificed them to a party caucus ? Does he think our memories are so bad as to have forgotten the party intrigues of three or four years ago which would not tolerate Protectionist heresies being examined and questioned by the broadest minds and best balanced brains of the party he belongs to ? So much for the sugar-coating of this Protectionist pill he wants us, as workmen, to swallow. "All their directors," he proceeds, " were fiscal reformers, not as politicians but as men of busi- ness, and their convictions were due to their daily experience of the iniquitous unfairness of the present system of foreign competition." All right ! Let us take this statement as being literally correct. But might I suggest to Mr. Bleckly that we, as workmen, are Free Traders and Free Fooders not as politicians but as working men. Is to be insinuated that we, as workmen, have no brains or ability to measure up the advantages of Protection in so far as they bear upon our own lives and interests ? Is the employer, the man of business, the only absolute safe guide in this matter of our work, wages, and living. Even in the matter of this so-called foreign competition,is it supposed we are not able to balance up fairly well its extent compared with our own British competition over the whole face of the earth?

"The country had now before it a condition of things such as employers of labour had been steadily approaching for some time and that was the scarcity and often the entire absence of employment of large sections of our working population."

Perfectly true! But will Mr. Bleckly dare affirm that Protection will prevent these recurring cycles of depression, or, can he point to any Protectionist country where these cycles of depression are not even worse and of longer duration than here ? What I protest against is this continued insinuation (he dare ' not make the assertion) that fluctuating employment I and fluctuating trade would cease by taxing it. Why don't these Protectionist advocates come out into the open and prove—either from the history of the past or from the present position of other highly protected countries—that once we adopted the same policy all our troubles of unemployment and fluctuating trade would cease to exist.

"They heard of iron and steel works being closed or working short time all over the country mainly because British iron and steel was being driven out of our old and best markets while the Government stood by and declined to do a hand's.turn to assist . . . .

employers to obtain work for their workpeople." As a bit of specious rhetroic with the sting in the tail this may be hard to beat, but again we ask for evidence and fact. Here once more is the insinua-

tion that no works would be closed or even working short time under a Protectionist policy. Where are these works closed? Surely they could be mentioned so that the facts might be properly tested, and we might then have an opportunity of finding out why they were scrap-heaped. Again I ask are the works in Protectionist countries—even America or Germany —working full time or even half time, and, if not, where is the point of the stutement, except to mislead? I would probably shock Mr. Bleckly if I were to say that I would hail with delight the closing of a few works I could mention as one of the best things that could happen to the trade—though I trust this remark will not be taken personally. "India was being wrenched from us by the sur- plus productions of Tariff countries being sold at less than cost price. Let this country take a leaf out of the foreigners' book and foster our trade with India and the Colonies, and the present appalling dilemma of unemployment would fade away, and leave behind it a contented and prosper- ous population." Probably Mr. Bleckly has forgotten that Mr. Chamberlain left India entirely out of his preferential scheme, and this is worth remembering. But at last the cat has jumped. Now, no trade can exist for any length of time by selling below cost price,though there is such a thing as cheap bankrupt stock. We hear all manner of statements about this surplus stock busi- ness, but no attempt to produce evidence. Let us, however, take it as it stands, and what does it amount to ? That Protection by granting a monopoly to the employer protected enables him to charge such a high price to the home consumer as would protect him from loss by selling his surplus stock abroad even below cost price. Protect the manufacturer by penalising, the consumer is the pill we are requested to swallow - It speaks volumes for the insight of the average work- man that he sees the barbed hook in spite of all the baiting by Protectionist employers. I want to put a, , few straight questions on this purely trade matter, which may further help us in judging the best course for us, as workmen, to pursue. Ist.—What articles of manufacture should be taxed? 2nd.—Would you tax raw material and food. Explain and specify the term "raw material ? 3rd.—What amount of tax would keep out imports? 4th.--If surplus products are sold to the foreigner cheap will not our home consumer have to pay a sufficiently high price to cover the gift of these cheap products to the foreigner. sth.—Will protection cheapen or increase the cost of production in this country, and how? 6th.— Will it cheapen or increase the cost of living? If either Mr. Bleckly or any other Protectionist manu- facturer will give us some plain unequivocal answers to these six questions, instead of all their airy plat' tudes without the shadow of an argumentative fart, we shall make some progress in testing the value 01 the statements made and the policy advocated. Y DEMI CHILDREN,— aciar U story ' .1 After reading the "Kindness to Animals" Essays through and through, I really felt that I was unable to decide the winner of the prize. I therefore called a lady, friend to my aid. She very kindly consented to judge the Essays, and I have pleasure in announcing the winners. The first prize of a nice little silver watch has been awarded -to Violet Sandy for a very good contribution. As I mentioned last week, I decided to award consolation prizes; therefore, I shall be pleased to send boxes of Fry's Chocolate to the following :—Beatrice Arnold,'H. H. Hayes, C. A. Blissitt, Hilda Mary Haigh, Clara Day, F. E. Dark, Dorothy Buck- ingham, M. E. Parker, R. Osborne, G. Kendall, and W. R. Farrar. . Will all prize-winners kindly send me their full addresses, when I will imrriediately for- ward the awards? I hope my little friends will be satisfied with this announcement. I must thank very heartily all the Competitors who contributed, and must say that the Com- petition has been most successful. Now I will speak of the Christmas plans. You will remember that we had a grand dis- tribution of Clothing last year. I think the senders of the articles can hardly realise the kindness they were doing when they sent the warm clothing for poor children, who were only half clothed. You know tile cold weather will soon be here, and I Want you to help some poor little children. Therefore, I propose to give to the sender of the best garment or garments P.O. for 55., and half a dozen other prizes to competitors. This competition is only open to girls. I think the subject of sport is dear to the hearts of all boys. I therefore propose to them that they should write a short Essay on "Which I pre- fer—Cricket or Football—and why." This should be a very easy competition. Then, for boys and girls, I offer prizes for the best short story or anecdote connected with Christrints. Contributions can be sent at once. If sent early, I shall publish' the best three or four each week,as received. Any questions I shall be pleased to answer through these columns. With Ipvit,

—ncle Ned,—Your story in the paper about the little dog that was drowned in the Irish Sea and came to life again is very nice. My diddy says, "It is very wonderful, if it is quite true," and he told me another "true" story this morning about another little doggy, or, perhaps, it might be the same one that had such a hairbreadth escape from a watery grave.

GREAT SANKEY AFFAIRS. A meeting of the Great Sanl.ey Parish Council was held in the Council Schools, Sankey, on Monday even- ing. It was presided over by Mr. %Vlthem Taylor, and there were also present :—Messrs. W. Furntss, J. W. Walters, H. Fairclough, W. H. Ireland and J. Smith (clerk).—The Clerk informed the members that he had written tc Mr. Joseph Massey with regard to his applica- tion for an allotment, and he informed him that he requited two acres in the township of Great Sankey. It was his intention to cultivate the land himself. He was a labourer, and he intended to work on the land in his spare time.—Mr- Furness proposed that the Clerk should write to the applicant asking him when he wanted the land, and that the owner be approached to see whether he would let it.—Mr. Fairclough seconded this, and the motion was carried.—The Clerk reported that he had written to the Warrington Corporation Gas Committee asking that now the price of gas was reduced in Warrington it should he reduced in their parish. He had received an answer stating that the request could not be entertained.—After much discussion, it was decided to put the matter on the agenda for the next meeting, with a view to ceiling a conference of the various Parish Councils to meet the Warrington Cor- poration. A parish meeting was afterwards held when Mr. Taylor presided over a fair attendance. The subject under discussion was the proposal to levy a special sanitary rate to meet the expenses of night-soil collec- tion. Mr. Furness explained that the Parish Council had done all that they were able to avoid a special sanitary expenses rate being levied upon the district. Every inducement had been brought to bear upon the man who had collected the night-soil and to induce him to continue his work on the same terms. He had been interviewed by the Clerk, but he replied that he was not getting paid by all the people for whom he worked and further that he did not feel justified in going on with the work under the present circumstances. He also said that if the District Council did not take all the responsibility upon themselves and pay him a lump sum he would not have anything further to do with the matter They paid 13s. 4d. at the present time as a gas rate and if they wanted to raise the money necessary to pay for the gas and the sanitary work it would mean paying a rate of 41d. on to the present lid. That would make a sixpenny rate which would realize £lBO. They paid £55 at present for gas rate and that would leave them £125. Mr. Whitfield's tender for collecting ' the night-soil was £lOO. The farmers were the people who would be effected mostly, but he thought the house- holders would be a little better off. If ever a tax was put on it very seldom came off and they now appealed to the parish to see if some means could be devised to obviate the necessity of putting a rate on. Mr. Pownall said he thought the time was not yet ripe for throwing a cleansing rite titym the parish if they could possibly be avoided. Mr. Snoddy said that he thought the time had arrived when a rate should be levied and ho made a proposition to that effect. This proposition was seconded by Mr. Millington. Mr. Pownall then movel an amendment that that the mattes be left in the hands of the District Council. This was seconded by Mr. Unsworth. Fifteen were in favour of the rule being levied, but the amendment was carried amid applause and it was decided to ask the District Council to keep the sanitary collection off the rates if possible. Votes of thanks were afterwards accorded to the Chairman (Mr. Taylor), on the proposition of Mr• Furness and seconded by Mr.Higgs.
